story.title: Theo and the Space Race Server
story.subtitle: One glowing block, one very late bedtime, and a race across the stars.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep in Orbit (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake, which was exactly the plan.

His tablet threw blue light across the ceiling. In Roblox Studio, he was building a rocket for his new game, and the launch effect was all wrong — flat, no shake, no WHOOOOSH. He tapped the fire button for the ninth time. Nothing.

Then the screen flickered black and green, like an old computer waking up from a long nap. A block appeared on his baseplate that he hadn't placed — a glowing green cube, humming faintly, stamped with one word: LAUNCH.

"That's not mine," Theo said.

He clicked it anyway.

The hum turned into a WHOOOOSH, and his bedroom dropped away. He landed somewhere that felt like outside, except there was no sound at all — just stars, a glowing dial, and a voice.

"New player detected," the voice said, sounding exactly like a loading screen. "Welcome to the Space Race server. I'm Nova. I run this place."

Nova turned out to be a blocky figure in a dented silver suit, hovering on a jetpack that didn't seem to be doing much work at all. "You're a little early for the Moon," Nova said. "We've got years of history to get through first. Buckle in."

Below them, something spun slowly in the dark — a silver ball with four thin legs, like a spider that had given up on two of them.

"What is that?"

"The first thing humans ever put into orbit," Nova said. "Orbit just means it travels around something, instead of falling back down. This one travels around Earth."

"It's kind of small," Theo said.

"About 58 centimeters wide. Roughly beach-ball sized — maybe two soccer balls stacked on top of each other. It launched **October 4, 1957**, from the Soviet Union. They called it **Sputnik 1**."

Static crackled from a speaker Theo hadn't noticed. Beep. Beep. Beep.

"That's it talking," Nova said. "A simple radio beep. People everywhere could pick it up on ordinary radios — no fancy equipment, just a dial and some patience."

Three channels glowed faintly in front of Theo. "Can I find it?" he asked.

"Try."

He turned the first dial — static. The second — silence. On the third, the beep locked in clean and steady.

"There it is," Nova said, and the silver ball flashed bright, like it knew it had been heard. "Nice tuning."

"It's basically a tiny radio ball in space," Theo said.

"Basically," Nova agreed. "But in 1957, nobody had ever heard anything like it. People everywhere stopped what they were doing just to listen to a sound falling out of the sky. Sputnik started the whole race. Once it was up there, everybody wanted to go further."

A little score counter ticked upward somewhere in the dark.

chapters.heading: Level 2: A Passenger for Sputnik (1957)
chapters.text:
Nova led Theo toward a second capsule, smaller, with a round window and a hatch that hadn't sealed yet.

"One month after Sputnik 1," Nova said, "the Soviets launched again. This one wasn't empty."

Theo pressed close to the window. A shape curled in the corner, dark eyes blinking back at him.

"Is that a dog?"

"Her name was Laika," Nova said. "**November 3, 1957**. She became the first living creature to ever orbit Earth."

Theo flattened his hand against the glass. "She looks pretty calm about it."

"She was a good traveler," Nova said. "Before her, nobody knew for sure if a living creature could survive a launch, or floating weightless, or any of it. Laika was how they found out it could be done."

A panel on the hatch blinked red, waiting for a code — three slots, each needing an icon. A tray beside Theo held a paw print, a rocket, and a star.

"I guess I seal her in properly," Theo said, sliding the paw print into the first slot.

CLICK. The hatch glowed green. The rocket and star slid into place after it on their own, and a small animation played — the capsule lifting off, trailing orange light.

"Good call," Nova said. "You just sealed the hatch for one of the most famous dogs in history."

"People made a dog famous for going to space?"

"There's a statue of her in Moscow," Nova said. "People still send her letters, if you can believe it."

"People send letters," Theo repeated slowly, "to a dog. From decades ago."

"People are like that about Laika," Nova said, managing a shrug despite being made entirely of blocks.

Theo watched the little capsule shrink into a dot of light, joining Sputnik 1's faint beeping somewhere out past the dark. It felt, for a second, like two tiny players finally on the same server.

"Next stop," Nova said, "is where the United States finally gets off the bench."

Theo laughed. "Took them a whole year?"

"A very busy year," Nova said, and the stars around them began to blur sideways, like a loading bar sweeping across the sky.

chapters.heading: Level 3: Mission Control Comes Online (1958)
chapters.text:
The stars snapped back into focus around a room full of blinking control panels and men in short-sleeved shirts, all of them staring at a single screen.

"Sputnik scared the United States badly," Nova said. "So badly that they built a brand-new space agency almost overnight. NASA started running on **October 1, 1958**."

"Just like that?" Theo asked.

"Just like that. And three months before NASA even opened its doors, the US had already launched its first satellite — **Explorer 1**, on **January 31, 1958**."

A glowing globe floated in front of Theo, wrapped in a faint ring of colored light he hadn't noticed at first. It pulsed, almost like a loading icon that wouldn't finish.

"What's that ring doing there?" Theo asked.

"That's what Explorer 1 found," Nova said. "Count the bands. Tell me what you see."

Theo leaned close, squinting. "One... two. Two rings, both kind of glowing."

"Correct," Nova said. "Two bands of invisible energy wrapped around the Earth, like belts nobody could see until Explorer 1 flew straight through one. Scientists named them the **Van Allen radiation belt** — belt, like you'd wear, except made of energy instead of leather."

"So the satellite found something nobody even knew was there?"

"Exactly. A tiny satellite, barely bigger than your arm, discovered something wrapped around the whole planet."

A tall man in the corner of the control room leaned over a drafting table covered in rocket sketches. "That's Wernher von Braun," Nova said. "He led the team that would eventually build the rocket big enough to reach the Moon. Keep that name in your head — you'll want it later."

Theo tapped the glowing globe, and the two rings locked into place with a soft chime, like a level clearing.

"Ring count: confirmed," Nova said, in the voice of someone reading an achievement banner. "You just discovered something the whole world didn't know was circling it."

"Not bad for a Tuesday," Theo said, though he had no idea if it was actually a Tuesday, in 1958 or anywhere else.

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The control room melted away into a launchpad, steam hissing off a rocket taller than any building Theo had ever stood next to.

"This is it," Nova said. "**April 12, 1961**. A pilot named Yuri Gagarin is about to become the first human being ever to leave the ground and not come back down."

A capsule sat at the rocket's tip, round as a ball, with one small window. Inside, a man in a white suit gave a thumbs up through the glass, grinning like he was about to win something.

"How long is he up there?" Theo asked.

"About 108 minutes," Nova said. "Long enough to circle the entire planet once."

A panel beside Theo lit up with a jumble of switches, clearly out of order. "Launch sequence needs sorting," Nova said. "Fuel, ignition, release. Get it wrong and we just waste a lot of very expensive steam."

Theo studied the switches like he was reading a script in Roblox Studio — find the order, test it, see what breaks. Fuel first. Then ignition. Then release.

He flipped them in that order. The rocket shuddered, then roared upward in a column of fire and smoke.

"We have liftoff," Nova said.

As the rocket shrank into the sky, Theo noticed something odd — a blank spot on a wall of photographs nearby, where a name plate should have been.

"Who's missing?" he asked.

Nova's voice dropped, almost conspiratorial. "The chief designer behind this whole program. A man named Sergei Korolev. He planned nearly everything the Soviets achieved in space — but his name was kept completely secret. Most people didn't even know he existed until he died in **1966**."

"They hid the guy who built it?"

"For years," Nova said. "Imagine making the biggest thing in the world and nobody's allowed to know it was you."

Theo looked at the blank name plate for a long moment. "That's wild," he said finally. "He's basically the best player on the server and nobody knew his username."

Nova actually laughed at that one — a small, surprised, static-crackled laugh. "Best way I've ever heard it put."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Ten-Year Dare (1961)
chapters.text:
Two capsules floated side by side, one small and round, one slightly different in shape. A single glowing arrow pointed at each.

"Less than a month later," Nova said, "the United States sent its own pilot up. Alan Shepard, **May 5, 1961**, aboard a capsule called Freedom 7."

"Did he go all the way around, like Gagarin?" Theo asked.

"No," Nova said. "His flight was suborbital — meaning it went up and came back down without circling the Earth. Shorter trip. Still the first American ever in space."

"So which one is his?" Theo looked between the two capsules.

"You tell me. One flew in a straight line up and down. One flew all the way around the planet."

Theo pointed to the smaller, boxier capsule. "That one. Looks built for a quick trip, not a lap."

"Correct," Nova said, and the capsule glowed in confirmation.

The scene shifted again — a podium now, a man speaking to a crowd Theo couldn't quite see the edges of. A single sentence floated in glowing letters above his head.

"President Kennedy," Nova said. "**May 25, 1961**. Just twenty days after Shepard's flight, he stood up and dared the entire country to land a person on the Moon — and bring them home safely — before the decade was over."

"Before 1970," Theo said, doing the math fast. "That's not very long."

"Nine years, give or take," Nova said. "A countdown clock for an entire country."

A big red button sat under Theo's hand, labeled simply: ACCEPT.

"Is this actually my call?" he asked.

"Someone's got to push it," Nova said. "Might as well be you."

Theo pressed it. A countdown clock blinked to life above them, ticking down toward the end of the decade, numbers scrolling fast like something out of his own game's loading screen.

"Nine years to build a rocket that can reach the Moon," Theo said. "That's a bigger project than anything I've ever built in Studio."

"Funny you should say that," Nova said. "Wait until you see the size of the thing."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Two Firsts, One Hatch (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
Two glowing doors appeared side by side, each with a blank card hovering in front of it, waiting for a name.

"Two more firsts before we get anywhere near the Moon," Nova said. "Your job: match the traveler to the record."

On a tray floated two photographs — a woman with a steady, confident smile, and a man in a bulky suit, tethered by a long cord that trailed off into darkness.

"Door one," Nova said, "**June 16, 1963**. First woman ever in space, orbiting Earth aboard a capsule called Vostok 6."

Theo slid the woman's photo into the first door. It locked with a soft chime. "Valentina Tereshkova," the panel read, glowing gold.

"She used to work in a factory," Nova added. "Then she went and orbited the entire planet."

"From factory floor to space," Theo said. "That's a pretty big level up."

"Door two," Nova said, nodding toward the man in the bulky suit. "**March 18, 1965**. First human to leave his spacecraft completely and float outside it in open space — a spacewalk, they called it. About ten minutes, tethered the whole time so he couldn't drift off."

Theo slid the second photo into place. CLICK. "Alexei Leonov," the panel confirmed.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound long," Theo said.

"Try floating outside a spacecraft for ten seconds," Nova said, "let alone ten minutes. Nobody had ever done it. He had no idea if his suit would even hold."

Theo studied the photo — the tether, the dark behind him, nothing but a thin line connecting him to anything solid. "That's either the bravest thing I've ever heard," Theo said, "or the scariest video game level of all time."

"Both," Nova said. "He got back inside fine, by the way. Suit held. Hatch worked. Totally fine landing after."

Both doors swung open at once, revealing nothing but more stars beyond them — which, Theo was starting to realize, was basically how every level on this server ended.

"First woman, first spacewalk," Theo said. "Both firsts, both huge. Why doesn't anybody talk about these as much as the Moon stuff?"

"They will tonight," Nova said. "Keep going. The Moon's close now."

chapters.heading: Level 7: Earthrise and the Giant Leap (1968–1969)
chapters.text:
The server shifted, and suddenly Theo was floating beside a small capsule window, Earth hanging below like a blue marble half in shadow.

"**December 1968**," Nova said. "Apollo 8. First humans ever to fly around the Moon. One of the astronauts, William Anders, looked up from his checklist and saw this."

A photo framed itself in front of Theo — Earth rising over a gray, cratered horizon, small and blue and completely alone in the black.

"He wasn't even supposed to take it," Nova said. "Not on the schedule. He just grabbed the camera."

"Can I line it up the same way?" Theo asked, already adjusting an invisible camera angle like he was setting up a cutscene in Studio.

"Try."

He nudged the frame until Earth sat exactly on the edge of the gray horizon, small and bright against all that dark. The shutter clicked on its own, and the photo locked into place, glowing faintly.

"Earthrise," Nova said. "Same shot. Nicely done."

The scene shifted again, faster this time — a rocket taller than anything Theo had seen yet, standing on a distant pad.

"Saturn V," Nova said. "**363 feet tall.** Taller than the Statue of Liberty. This is what finally got us there."

"**July 20, 1969**," Nova continued, as a ladder extended down from a spindly-legged lander toward gray dust. "Neil Armstrong is about to become the first person to ever stand on the Moon."

A single rung glowed at the bottom of the ladder, waiting.

"Last step's yours to confirm," Nova said. "Line him up."

Theo nudged the boot forward, millimeter by millimeter, until it touched the glowing rung exactly. Dust puffed outward in total silence.

"The Eagle has landed," crackled a voice from somewhere far above them — and then, a moment later: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

"Buzz Aldrin climbed down after him," Nova said, "while a third astronaut, Michael Collins, orbited alone above in the command module — the part of the ship that stayed circling the Moon the whole time, waiting to bring them home."

"So one guy just... waited up there? By himself? The whole time?"

"Somebody's got to fly the getaway ship," Nova said. "Not everyone gets to be the one on the dust."

Theo looked at the footprint glowing in the gray ground and grinned. "The Eagle has landed," he said quietly, mostly to himself.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
A warning light blinked red, and an alarm chirped somewhere close, sharp and insistent.

"**1970**," Nova said, voice suddenly brisk. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon. Crew's fine. Ship's in trouble."

Theo's stomach dropped for exactly one second. "Are they okay?"

"They're okay," Nova said immediately. "Scared, cramped, cold — but okay. And they stayed okay, because engineers back on Earth spent days building a fix out of whatever the astronauts already had on board."

A tangle of wires and a cardboard-looking panel floated in front of Theo, three connectors dangling loose. "Help me finish it," Nova said. "Match the shapes. Round to round, square to square."

Theo worked through it the way he'd debug a broken script — slowly, checking each piece before locking it in. Round connector, round socket. Square to square. The last wire clicked home, and the panel hummed to life, a small green light blinking steady.

"Fix confirmed," Nova said. "That's basically what really happened — not you personally, obviously, but engineers on the ground, puzzling out a fix with cardboard, tape, and the manual. The crew made it home safe."

"They got better," Theo said, mostly to reassure himself. "Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon total, right? Across six missions?"

"Between 1969 and 1972," Nova confirmed. "All of them made it home."

The stars shifted one last time, and two spacecraft drifted toward each other in the dark, slow and careful, like two kids approaching a handshake they'd been practicing all week.

"**July 17, 1975**," Nova said. "American and Soviet spacecraft, docking together in orbit — meaning their hatches connected and locked, so the crews could float between them."

A hatch creaked open between the two ships. Two gloved hands reached through, found each other, and shook.

"That's the end of the whole race," Nova said softly. "Not a winner. A handshake."

Theo watched the two ships hang there, joined together, lit gold by a sun with no up or down. "That's a pretty good ending screen," he said.

"Best kind there is," Nova said. "Speaking of — your server's calling you back."

The stars folded inward, and Theo's bedroom rushed up to meet him. His tablet sat exactly where he'd left it, screen glowing ordinary blue again. The green LAUNCH block was gone — except for one small gold badge now sitting in the corner of his rocket build, shaped like two tiny hands shaking.

His launch effect, when he tested it, finally worked. WHOOOOSH, with a shake and everything.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was soccer practice — but first, he had a server update to finish.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** launched on **October 4, 1957**, the first thing people ever sent to circle Earth.
It was about **58 centimeters wide** — roughly beach-ball sized — and sent out a simple beep anyone could hear on an ordinary radio.
On **November 3, 1957**, a dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States started a new space agency, **NASA**, on **October 1, 1958**.
The first American satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and found a hidden ring of invisible energy wrapped around Earth.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President Kennedy dared the country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his spacecraft, for about ten minutes.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts flew around the Moon, and one of them snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled **Apollo 13**, but engineers on the ground helped the crew fix it and get home safely.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit, and the crews shook hands, ending the Space Race.

story.title: Maya and the Biggest Ship in the World
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the real story of the Titanic

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Porthole Lights Up
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor with a flashlight under her chin, drawing a little sailboat on her pad.

Her night light was a small brass porthole, round like a ship's window, a gift from Grandpa. Tonight the glass fogged up green, and tiny ripples moved across it like real water.

"Permission to come aboard?" said a cheerful voice from inside the glass.

A round, friendly face blinked at her. "I'm Pip," it said. "I show people ships. Want to see the biggest one ever built?"

Maya grinned and reached out. **WHOOOOSH!** The porthole swallowed her flashlight beam, her crayons, and her, and the bedroom melted into salty sea air.

She landed on wooden scaffolding, towering over a half-built ship. Hammers banged. Sparks flew.

"Where are we?" Maya asked, hugging her drawing pad.

"**Belfast, Ireland**," said Pip. "The year is **1909**. Workers just laid the **keel** — that's the long backbone at the very bottom of a ship."

Maya counted windows along the hull. "It's HUGE."

"You bet," said Pip. "When she's finished, she'll be about **882 feet long** — nearly three soccer fields end to end."

Two years later, crowds cheered as the ship slid into the water for the first time, built by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard.

"They call her **Titanic**," said Pip.

Maya drew the huge hull sliding down the ramp, bubbles everywhere. "I want to see the rest!"

"Climb aboard, artist," said Pip. "There's plenty more ship to draw."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Funnels, Three Smokers
chapters.text:
Maya stood on the deck, neck craning up at four giant smokestacks painted bright orange and black.

"Why does that back one look different?" she asked, squinting.

"Good eye," said Pip. "Titanic had **four funnels**, but only **three of them carried real smoke** from the engines below."

"So the fourth is just... pretend?" Maya giggled.

"Pretty much," said Pip. "It made her look even more powerful. Big and bold, like a drawing with extra sparkle."

Maya flipped to a blank page and drew all four funnels, marking a tiny star on the fake one.

"That's my secret code," she said. "Star means fibber funnel."

Pip laughed so hard the porthole glass fogged right up. "I'm stealing that joke, Maya."

A sailor walked by, counting funnels on his fingers, and Maya waved her drawing at him. He tipped his cap and laughed too, pointing right at her starred funnel as if she'd caught him out.

"Four funnels, three smokers, one big fibber," Maya sang under her breath, skipping along the deck to see what else she could find to draw before the ship set sail.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Floaty Boxes
chapters.text:
Down a steep staircase, Maya found herself inside the ship's belly, surrounded by tall metal walls and heavy doors.

"Why are there so many doors down here?" she asked, running her hand along cold steel.

"These separate the hull into **sixteen watertight compartments**," said Pip. "Like sealed boxes inside the ship."

"Watertight... water can't get in?" Maya asked.

"Exactly," said Pip. "If one box got a leak, the others would stay dry, and the ship would still float."

Maya thought about her bath toys, the ones with air trapped inside that always bobbed back up no matter how she pushed them under.

"So people thought she couldn't sink," Maya said slowly.

"That's right," said Pip. "Everybody called her 'nearly unsinkable.' Remember that word, Maya. It matters later."

Maya drew sixteen little boxes in a neat row, labeling each one with a tiny wave. Underneath she wrote, in careful crayon letters, "Floaty boxes."

She tapped the metal wall gently, listening to it ring like a bell.

"Let's go meet her sisters," said Pip, tugging her sleeve toward the stairs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Three Sisters Set Sail
chapters.text:
Back on deck, two other enormous ships steamed past in the busy harbor, their horns blasting.

"Those look just like Titanic!" Maya said, pointing.

"They're her **sisters**," said Pip. "**Olympic** and **Britannic**. Same shipyard, same family, three ships total."

A deep horn sounded right beneath their feet. Sailors scurried along the ropes, shouting cheerful orders.

"It's **April 10, 1912**," said Pip. "Titanic is leaving **Southampton, England**, on her very first trip, heading for **New York City**."

Maya leaned over the rail and waved at the crowds on the dock, waving back with handkerchiefs and hats.

"Can I draw the flags before we go too fast?" she asked, crayon already moving.

"Draw quick," said Pip, grinning. "She's picking up speed."

The horn blew once more, deep and proud. **WHOOOOSH**, the water churned white and foamy behind them as Titanic slid out past the harbor wall into the open sea, gulls wheeling overhead like excited exclamation marks.

Maya tucked her finished drawing safely under her arm and watched the land shrink away behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Ice Came
chapters.text:
Four nights later, the sea turned glassy and still. The air smelled like frost.

Maya shivered on deck, pulling her sleeve down over her cold hand.

"It's **April 14, 1912**," said Pip quietly. "Around **11:40 at night**, lookouts spotted something ahead."

A huge pale shape loomed out of the dark, taller than a house. The ship turned hard, but its side brushed the ice, and a long scrape shuddered through the deck.

Maya grabbed the railing. "Are we okay?"

"The crew acted fast," said Pip gently. "**Captain Edward Smith** gave calm orders. He stayed at his post the whole night, helping everyone he could."

Lifeboats swung down into the dark water, one by one, lanterns glowing on their sides.

"There weren't quite enough boats for everyone," said Pip. "Only about **1,178 seats**. That's a lesson we'll come back to."

A passenger named **Molly Brown** rowed hard in one boat, keeping everyone around her calm and warm.

Maya watched the little lifeboats drift safely away from the ship, bobbing like candles on black water.

"They're going to be okay," Pip said softly. "Help is already coming."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Dots, Dashes, and Carpathia
chapters.text:
In a tiny radio room, two men worked fast by lantern light, a little machine clicking under their fingers.

"What's that noise?" Maya asked.

"That's **Morse code**," said Pip. "**Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, the wireless operators, are calling for help."

"CQD! CQD!" Maya tried tapping the pattern on the table herself. "What does that mean?"

"The old signal for 'come quickly, danger,'" said Pip. "They tried the newer one too."

"SOS! SOS!" Maya shouted, grinning, dot dot dot, dash dash dash, dot dot dot.

Far across the dark water, a ship called **Carpathia** turned hard and raced through the night, engines roaring, to answer the call.

By morning, Carpathia reached the lifeboats and pulled everyone aboard, wrapping them in warm blankets and hot tea.

"Not everyone could be saved that night," Pip said gently, "and it's still remembered as a sad night at sea. But so many people made it home safely, because of boats like this one, and brave people who didn't give up."

Maya nodded quietly, then drew Carpathia steaming through the gold morning light, wrapped in a little blanket of her own crayon strokes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lifeboats for Everyone
chapters.text:
Back on calm water, Maya noticed something odd: the ships nearby now carried extra lifeboats, stacked high along their decks.

"Why so many now?" she asked, counting them on her fingers.

"After that night," said Pip, "people made new rules. Every ship must now carry **enough lifeboats for every single passenger and crew member** aboard."

"That seems obvious," Maya said, wrinkling her nose.

"It wasn't, before," said Pip. "They also started the **International Ice Patrol**, ships and planes that watch for icebergs and warn everyone nearby."

Maya drew a little patrol boat with a flag that read "ICE AHEAD!" in big crooked letters.

"So next time, ships get warned early?" she asked, holding up her drawing proudly.

"Exactly," said Pip. "That's how we learn, Maya. Something hard happens, and smart people fix it, so it's safer for everyone who sails after."

Maya tucked the drawing into her pad. "I like fixing things."

"Me too," said Pip, the porthole glass glowing warm and gold, like a little sun was tucked inside it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Twelve Thousand Feet Down
chapters.text:
The scene shifted, and Maya floated in inky blue water, lit only by a small round light.

"Where's the ship now?" she asked, voice echoing softly.

"Resting on the seafloor," said Pip, "about **12,500 feet** down. That's deeper than ten tall buildings stacked on top of each other."

A shape loomed out of the dark, Titanic's broken bow, quiet and rusted, draped in soft ribbons of sea growth.

"In **1985**, an explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her," said Pip. "She rests in two big pieces, far out in the ocean."

Maya pressed her palm flat against the glass. "She looks sleepy."

"She's been resting a long time," said Pip. "People have brought up plates, shoes, all sorts of things, kept safe in museums now, so nobody forgets."

Maya sketched the broken ship gently, adding soft curls of seaweed drifting all around it like a blanket.

"Goodnight, big ship," she whispered, tapping the glass once, softly, like a knock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
Light swirled, and suddenly Maya stood before a huge silver building shaped like a ship's pointed front.

"This is **Titanic Belfast**," said Pip. "A museum that opened in **2012**, right where she was built, a hundred years later."

Inside, children pressed their noses to glass cases full of drawings, tools, and tiny lifeboat models.

Maya pinned her own drawings up beside them, the funnels, the floaty boxes, the glowing lifeboats, the ice patrol flag.

"I helped tell her story," Maya said proudly, smoothing the edges flat.

"You sure did," said Pip, glass glowing soft and warm. "Now, time for bed, artist."

**WHOOOOSH** — the museum melted away, and Maya blinked, back on her bedroom floor, flashlight dim, crayons scattered everywhere.

On her pad lay a fresh drawing she didn't remember finishing: a brass porthole, glowing soft green, with tiny letters underneath that read, "Smooth sailing."

The porthole night light on her shelf gave one last friendly wink, then settled into its ordinary quiet gold glow, waiting for the next adventure.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Smooth sailing until tomorrow.

true_facts.text: Titanic was built in **Belfast, Ireland**, by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard.
Titanic was about **882 feet long**, the biggest ship in the world at the time.
She had **four funnels**, but only **three** of them actually let out real smoke.
Inside, her hull was divided into **sixteen watertight compartments**, so people called her 'nearly unsinkable.'
She left **Southampton, England**, on **April 10, 1912**, heading for **New York City**.
Around **11:40 at night** on **April 14, 1912**, she hit an iceberg.
There were only enough lifeboats for about **1,178 people**.
**Captain Edward Smith** stayed aboard, helping everyone he could.
Passenger **Molly Brown** helped row her lifeboat and kept everyone calm.
Wireless operators **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** sent the signals **CQD** and **SOS** for help.
The ship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued the survivors from their lifeboats.
Afterward, new rules meant every ship must carry **enough lifeboats for everyone aboard**, and the **International Ice Patrol** began watching for icebergs.
In **1985**, explorer **Robert Ballard** finally found the wreck resting about **12,500 feet** deep on the seafloor.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow in the Puddle
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Puddle Paint
chapters.text:
Rain tap-tapped on Ivy's window. Tap, tap, tap!

Ivy painted big puddle shapes on her paper. Purple puddles, orange puddles, even a polka-dot one.

Then the real puddle on her windowsill started to glow. It glowed pink, then blue, then gold.

Ivy leaned close. "Ooooh," she said.

A tiny drop of water popped up and winked. "Hello, Ivy! I'm Splash," it said. "Want to see how rainbows are made?"

Ivy grabbed her paintbrush like a magic wand. "Yes, yes, YES!" she said.

Splash giggled. "Hop in, then. SPLOOSH!" And the puddle pulled her right in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Everything went quiet and round. Ivy and Splash were inside a raindrop!

Sunshine beamed through the clear, wobbly wall.

"Watch what happens," Splash said. The sunshine bent, just like a straw looks bendy in a glass of water.

Ivy gasped. "It's bending!"

"That's right," said Splash. "Light bends when it goes inside a raindrop."

Ivy touched the light with her paintbrush. It left a tiny rainbow smear in the air.

"I made rainbow paint!" Ivy cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bouncy Light
chapters.text:
Inside the drop, the light didn't stop. It bounced off the back wall. BOING!

Ivy giggled. "Like a ball!"

"Just like a ball," said Splash. "Then it bends again on its way back out."

Out came colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

Ivy counted them on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

She pointed her paintbrush at each color, one by one.

"I want to paint every single one," she said.

Splash laughed so hard he nearly splashed right out of the raindrop. "Then let's go find more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Turn Around
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, the sky was bright. But Ivy saw no rainbow yet.

"Where did the colors go?" she asked.

Splash floated beside her. "Turn around, Ivy."

Ivy turned her back to the sun. Now the rain was right in front of her, like a sparkly curtain.

WHOOSH — a rainbow arched across the sky!

"You have to have the sun behind you," said Splash. "And rain out in front."

Ivy clapped her paint-covered hands, leaving little rainbow handprints in the air.

"I found it! I found the rainbow!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sun and Rain Together
chapters.text:
A little cloud drifted close and sprinkled rain. At the same time, the sun peeked out.

"Both at once?" Ivy asked.

"Yes!" said Splash. "Rainbows need sun AND rain together, in the very same moment."

"That's why they pop up after a rain shower," Splash said, "when the sun comes out to say hello."

Ivy held up her brush like a little sun. She waved it over an imaginary puddle.

"Hello, sun! Hello, rain!" she sang.

The rainbow glowed brighter, like it was smiling right back at her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Color Mixer
chapters.text:
A sparkly triangle of glass floated by, catching the light.

"That belonged to a clever thinker named Isaac Newton," said Splash. "He shined sunlight through glass like this."

"Out came all the colors, hiding inside plain white light!"

Ivy mixed her paints on her palette. Red and yellow became orange. Blue and yellow became green.

"I'm a color mixer too!" she said.

Splash clapped his watery hands. "Just like sunlight, hiding colors until they come out to play."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Puddle Detectives
chapters.text:
Two more friends waved from a tiny, drifting cloud.

"I'm Ibn al-Haytham," said one. "I studied how light moves, a long, long time ago."

"I'm Kamal al-Din," said the other. "I used round glass balls to copy raindrops."

Ivy's eyes went wide. "Like pretend raindrops?"

"Exactly," said Kamal al-Din. "That's how I found the rainbow's secret."

Ivy pulled a round bead from her pocket. She held it up to the light, just like he did.

A little rainbow shimmer danced on her hand.

"I'm a puddle detective too!" she cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
Splash took Ivy's hand. "Time to go home."

SPLOOSH! They popped back into her bedroom puddle.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The whole yard looked washed and shiny.

Ivy looked out her window. A real rainbow stretched over the grass.

She had the sun behind her, just like Splash showed her.

Ivy grabbed her paintbrush and painted the whole arch. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple — every color in its place.

She set her painting on the windowsill, right next to the puddle.

Splash winked from the water. "Goodnight, Ivy. Paint bright dreams."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Sleep tight, and paint bright dreams.

true_facts.text: Sunshine goes into a little raindrop and it **bends**.
Inside the drop, the light **bounces**, just like a bouncy ball.
Then the light **bends again** and comes out as colors.
To see a rainbow, the **sun has to be behind you**.
The **rain has to be out in front of you**, like a curtain.
Rainbows need the **sun and the rain at the same time**.
That's why rainbows often show up **right after a rain shower**.
A rainbow appears when the **sun peeks out from behind the clouds**.

new_recurring.name: Splash
new_recurring.rule: A tiny, cheerful raindrop who appears in puddles, rain, or spray to guide Ivy on gentle science adventures. Speaks in short, happy sentences, always says 'SPLOOSH!' when traveling between worlds, and signs off with 'Paint bright dreams.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ivy returns to her bedroom puddle, paints the rainbow she saw over her yard, and sets the painting beside the puddle as the real rain stops outside.

story.title: Leo and the Night Express
story.subtitle: A sleepy train ride with Hoot the Owl

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: All Aboard
chapters.text:
Leo lined up his train cars on the rug. Red car. Blue car. Yellow car.

Outside, the sky had gone dark. Leo did not love the dark.

He flicked on his little owl lamp. Two round eyes glowed on the shelf.

"Hoot!" said the owl lamp. Leo jumped. Then he laughed.

The owl's eyes were not just lamp eyes. They blinked.

"Ready to see why people sleep?" asked the owl.

Leo looked at his train track. It glowed gold, like rails made of stars.

He tapped the track three times, the way he always tapped real train rails. CLICK. The little engine chuffed.

"ALL ABOARD!" shouted the owl.

Leo hopped on, feeling brave instead of scared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boy Who Twitched
chapters.text:
The train huffed to a stop in a quiet room. It was the year **1953**, in a city called **Chicago**.

A boy slept on a cot. Two grown-ups watched him close.

"That is **Nathaniel** and **Eugene**," said Hoot. "They are watching his eyes."

Leo looked. Under the boy's closed eyelids, his eyes were zipping side to side!

"His eyes are doing laps!" Leo said.

"Good eyes, Leo," said Hoot. "That fast-eye kind of sleep got a name: **REM**, which just means dream sleep. You found it, same as they did."

Nathaniel loved sleep so much, people later called him the sleep expert.

Leo puffed up proud, like a real conductor.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Loop the Loop
chapters.text:
The train rolled onto a big looping track. Round and round it went.

"Sleep loops too," said Hoot. "Every loop takes about **ninety minutes** — that's an hour and a half, like one long cartoon plus a snack."

"Then what happens?" asked Leo.

"Quiet sleep, then dream sleep, then quiet again," said Hoot. "Over and over, all night long."

Leo counted the loops out loud. One, two, three.

The train looped right along with him.

"I'm a sleep loop counter!" Leo cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Floppy as a Noodle
chapters.text:
Inside the next train car, Leo saw a sleeping puppy twitching its paws.

"That's dream sleep," said Hoot. "The brain is busy, almost like it's awake. But the body goes floppy, like a wet noodle, so the puppy can't act out its dream."

Leo tried to wiggle his own arm. It flopped, heavy and silly. He giggled.

"And during the quietest, deepest sleep," Hoot added, "bodies do their best growing. That's part of why kids like you need lots of sleep."

Leo stood up extra straight, as if he could feel himself growing right then.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Clock With No Numbers
chapters.text:
The train chugged past a giant clock with no numbers.

"That's a body clock," said Hoot. "It sits in your brain, just above where your eye wires cross. It tells you when it's day and when it's night."

"Like a station clock!" said Leo.

"Exactly," said Hoot. "Scientists have a fancy word for a clock that runs about one day long: **circadian**. It just means 'about a day.'"

Leo tried the word three times until it stopped feeling silly in his mouth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Friendly Dark
chapters.text:
Outside the window, the sky turned inky black. Leo's tummy did a small worried flip.

"The dark isn't spooky," said Hoot gently. "The dark is a helper. When it gets dark, your body makes a sleepy juice called **melatonin**. Scientists first found it in **1958**."

"It's like a cozy blanket, telling your body, time to rest."

Leo watched the dark sky again. This time it looked soft, not scary.

"The dark is just tucking everyone in," Leo whispered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleepy Zoo
chapters.text:
The train zoomed past a whole zoo of sleepers.

A dolphin swam by with one eye open. "Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time," said Hoot, "so one eye can watch for danger."

Next, a giraffe dozed standing up, barely two hours a day.

Then tiny bats hung upside down, sleeping almost all day long, **twenty hours** of napping.

"Bats win the sleepy contest!" Leo laughed.

"Owls like you stay awake at night, though, right, Hoot?"

Hoot winked one glowing eye and didn't quite answer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Rug
chapters.text:
The train looped back, gold tracks glowing bright. It rolled right into Leo's bedroom, quiet as a whisper.

Hoot's eyes dimmed to a soft nightlight glow.

"Every trip finally comes home," said Hoot, "the same way every sleep loop finally reaches morning."

Leo climbed into bed, pulling his blanket up like his very own sleepy blanket.

His toy train sat parked on the rug, lights low.

The dark outside felt like a friend now, not a stranger.

Leo closed his eyes, ready for his very own loops of quiet sleep and dream sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. All aboard for dreamland.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, two scientists watched a sleeping boy's eyes zip back and forth under his eyelids and discovered **REM**, or dream sleep.
One of those scientists, Nathaniel, loved sleep so much that people later called him the sleep expert.
A night of sleep loops around every **ninety minutes**, moving between quiet sleep and dream sleep.
During dream sleep the brain is busy like it's awake, but the body goes floppy so it can't act out dreams.
The deepest, quietest sleep is when bodies do their best growing.
A tiny body clock sits in the brain, just above where the eye wires cross, telling you day from night.
Scientists call that about-a-day clock **circadian**, a word that just means 'about a day.'
In **1958**, scientists found a sleepy juice called **melatonin** that the body makes when it gets dark.
Dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.
Giraffes barely sleep two hours a day, napping standing up.
Some tiny bats sleep about **twenty hours** a day, making them super sleepy.

new_recurring.name: Hoot the Owl Conductor
new_recurring.rule: A glowing toy owl who wakes when Leo is sleepy and guides him on a gentle night-train journey through a science topic, always starting with 'All aboard!' and ending each trip back in his own bedroom.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Leo's toy train carried him home from the Night Express, no longer scared of the dark, and he fell asleep with Hoot's eyes glowing softly as a nightlight.

story.title: Rosa, Isla, and the Sticky-Toed Gecko
story.subtitle: A climbing adventure with ladybirds, spiders, and one very sticky lizard

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Ladybird
chapters.text:
Rosa lay on her tummy. She watched her ladybird nightlight. It glowed a soft green.

Isla sat on the top bunk. She drew a climbing wall on paper. She drew little hand holds.

Then the nightlight blinked twice. CLICK. CLICK.

It did not do that before.

Rosa poked it with one finger. "Hello, ladybird," she said.

POP! The light popped open. Out crawled a tiny lizard with big round eyes.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Gordy the Gecko. I climb walls for fun."

Isla jumped off her bed. "Walls? Like rock climbing?"

"Just like that," said Gordy. "Want to see how animals climb? Even upside down?"

Rosa clapped her hands. "Ladybirds too?"

"Ladybirds too," said Gordy, winking. "Hold onto my tail. Here we go."

WHOOSH! The bedroom wall turned soft and green, like a jungle. Rosa and Isla tumbled through.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Gordy's Sticky Toes
chapters.text:
They landed by a big glass wall. It went straight up, up, up.

Gordy skittered right up it. He did not fall. Not even a little.

"How do you do that?" asked Isla. "Glass is so slippery!"

Gordy held up one tiny foot. "Look close," he said.

Isla looked close. She gasped. "Your toes have lines! Like tiny hairs!"

"**Millions of tiny hairs**," said Gordy proudly. "Each one grabs onto bumps so small you cannot see them."

Rosa reached out and touched the glass. "I don't feel bumps," she said.

"That's because they're tinier than a speck of dust," said Gordy.

Isla grinned. "So that's how geckos run up walls. And across ceilings?"

"Yep," said Gordy. "Upside down too!" He scurried across the ceiling to prove it.

Rosa laughed so hard she almost fell off her leaf. "Do it again!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
Gordy stuck to the glass wall. Then he peeled one toe up at a time.

"Wait," said Isla. "Is that glue?"

"Nope," said Gordy. "**No glue at all**. My feet never get sticky and messy."

Rosa touched his foot. It felt clean and dry. "Not sticky!" she said, surprised.

"I can let go fast too," said Gordy. "Just like peeling off a sticker. Toe by toe."

He peeled his feet off the glass. Peel, peel, peel, peel!

"That's so cool," said Isla. "No glue, but it still grips?"

"Tiny hairs don't need glue," said Gordy. "They just grab on, then let go."

Rosa tried peeling her own fingers off the glass. "Peel, peel!" she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Ladybird's Secret
chapters.text:
A little ladybird landed on the glass, right next to Rosa.

Rosa squealed. "A ladybird! My favorite!"

"Watch her feet," said Gordy. "She's a climber too."

The ladybird walked straight up the wall. She did not slip at all.

"Ladybirds are beetles," said Gordy. "Beetles and flies have **tiny sticky pads** on their feet."

"Sticky like glue?" asked Isla.

"A little bit like glue," said Gordy. "Tiny sticky drops help them hold on."

Rosa watched the ladybird climb higher and higher. "Go, ladybird, go!" she cheered.

The ladybird reached the top and flew away. Rosa waved. "Bye bye, climbing bug!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Eight Legs, Lots of Hairs
chapters.text:
Something dropped down on a thread. Rosa jumped. "What's that?!"

"Just a spider," said Gordy gently. "She's friendly. Watch her climb."

The spider climbed up the glass with all eight legs.

"She has hairs too," said Gordy. "**Thousands of tiny hairs** on her feet."

Isla leaned in close. "Like your hairs, Gordy?"

"Just like mine," said Gordy. "That's why spiders can climb glass too."

Rosa took a deep breath. "She's not scary. She's just climbing."

"That's right," said Gordy. "She's just going home to her web."

The spider disappeared over the top of the wall. Rosa waved goodbye too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Claws or Glue?
chapters.text:
Next, Gordy led them to a bumpy rock wall. Ants marched straight up it.

"Look at their tiny claws," said Gordy. "Perfect for rough, bumpy walls."

Then the ants reached smooth glass. They didn't stop at all.

"How?" asked Isla. "Their claws won't work on smooth glass!"

"They **switch tools**," said Gordy. "Sticky feet for smooth walls, claws for bumpy ones."

Rosa pointed. "Like changing shoes!"

"Exactly like changing shoes," laughed Gordy. "Smart little ants."

Isla nodded. "Cockroaches do that too, right?"

"You got it," said Gordy. "Claws and sticky pads, whichever works best."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Goats on a Cliff
chapters.text:
Suddenly the wall became a huge rocky cliff. Goats leaped from rock to rock.

"Whoa!" said Isla. "That cliff is almost straight up and down!"

"Mountain goats don't mind," said Gordy. "Look at their feet."

Rosa looked close. "Their feet are hard on the outside!"

"Right," said Gordy. "**Hard edges grip the rock**. But inside is soft and squishy."

"Squishy like a sponge?" asked Rosa.

"A bit like that," said Gordy. "The soft part molds around the bumpy rock."

Isla grinned. "Hard outside, soft inside. Perfect for climbing cliffs."

A goat leaped right past them and landed with a soft THUD. Rosa clapped.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Squirrel Speed
chapters.text:
A squirrel zoomed past them up a tall tree. Scritch scritch scritch!

"Whoa, he's fast!" said Rosa.

"Squirrels have **sharp, curvy claws**," said Gordy. "They dig into tiny cracks in the bark."

Isla touched the tree trunk. "I don't see any cracks."

"They're tiny," said Gordy. "Too small for us to see. But just right for claws."

The squirrel reached the top and sat down, nibbling a nut.

Isla laughed. "He made it look so easy."

"Climbing is easy," said Gordy, "when you have the right feet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Froggy High Five
chapters.text:
Rain started to fall. A tiny tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf.

"Won't he slip?" asked Rosa. "The leaf is all wet!"

"Watch his toes," said Gordy. "They're flat and a little bit slimy."

Isla peered closer. "They look like tiny stamps!"

"Good eye," said Gordy. "Those **flat, slimy toes** stick to wet leaves and glass."

The frog hopped higher, never slipping once. Ribbit!

Rosa held up her hand. "High five, froggy!"

The frog lifted one sticky toe, as if waving back. Rosa giggled with delight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more thing," said Gordy. "People wanted sticky feet too."

Isla's eyes lit up. "Like rock climbers?"

"Just like that," said Gordy. "Scientists are people who study how things work. They studied gecko feet. Then they made **sticky climbing gloves** for people."

Isla looked at her paper drawing of a climbing wall. "I want gloves like that!"

"Maybe someday," said Gordy, smiling.

WHOOSH! The green jungle faded. The bedroom wall came back.

Rosa was back on her tummy. Isla was back on her bunk.

The ladybird nightlight glowed softly green, just like before.

But on the carpet sat one tiny gecko-shaped sticker, shining faintly.

Rosa picked it up and stuck it on her hand. "Sticky toes," she whispered, yawning.

Isla smiled and tucked her climbing drawing under her pillow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Stick with it!

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across the ceiling. Their toes have **millions of tiny hairs** that grab tiny bumps.
A gecko's sticky grip isn't glue. He can **peel his toes off fast**, just like pulling up a sticker.
Ladybirds and flies have **tiny sticky pads** on their feet, with a little sticky liquid to help them climb.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, just like geckos, so they can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches **switch tools**: sharp claws for bumpy walls, sticky feet for smooth ones.
Mountain goats have hooves with **hard edges and soft, squishy insides**, perfect for steep rocky cliffs.
Squirrels have **sharp, curvy claws** that dig into tiny cracks in tree bark too small to see.
Tree frogs have **flat, slightly slimy toes** that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Scientists studied gecko feet and then made **sticky climbing gloves** for people.

new_recurring.rule: A cheerful, sticky-toed gecko who pops out of a glowing object in the children's room and guides them through nature's climbing tricks. Ends adventures with the phrase 'Stick with it!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Rosa and Isla return to their bedroom to find a tiny glowing gecko sticker left on the carpet, and Isla tucks her climbing-wall drawing under her pillow before sleep.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Dinosaur Brick
story.subtitle: A WHOOOOSH back to the time of giant teeth and tiny raptors

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the rug. Their giant brick tower stood tall. It had held all week, ever since that last big CLICK.

Suddenly the top brick glowed red. Light spilled across the carpet.

"It's doing it again!" said Milo.

Juno grabbed his arm. "Is it dinosaurs this time?"

The brick wiggled. Little studs popped out. Pieces snapped together, fast as blinking. CLICK, CLICK, CLICK!

A tiny LEGO creature stood on the rug. It had a long neck and small spikes down its back.

"Hello!" it said. "I'm Bricky. Tonight I built myself into a dinosaur, just for you."

Juno clapped both hands. "A dino-Bricky!"

"Ready for a trip?" Bricky asked, and spun around once.

Milo grinned his biggest grin. "Ready!"

WHOOOOSH!

Red light swallowed the whole bedroom. The rug disappeared. Soft ferns and warm mud appeared instead. Somewhere far off, something small went rustling through the leaves.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Very First Dinosaur
chapters.text:
Milo landed on soft dirt. Juno landed right beside him, giggling.

"Where are we?" Juno asked.

"Very, very long ago," said Bricky. "Before mommies and daddies. Before even grandmas and grandpas. **230 million years ago** — that's so long ago it would take forever to count that high."

A small creature scurried past their feet. It was about the size of a dog, quick and bony.

"That," said Bricky, "is one of the very first dinosaurs ever."

Milo crouched down to look closer. "It's tiny! I thought all dinosaurs were huge."

"Not this one," said Bricky. "Dinosaurs started small. Some stayed small. Some grew into giants later on."

Juno tried to copy the creature's scurry-walk across the mud. "Like this?"

"Just like that," said Bricky, laughing.

Milo noticed tiny footprints left behind in the soft ground. "Look! It's leaving tracks!"

"Good eyes," said Bricky. "Remember those tracks. We'll see more like them later."

Juno stomped her own foot next to one, leaving a matching print. "Now it's MY track too!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Terrible Lizard Name
chapters.text:
Bricky led them to a quiet cave wall covered in old drawings.

"Here's a riddle," said Bricky. "A long time ago, a scientist named **Richard Owen** gave this whole group of animals one big name. Can you guess what it means?"

Milo thought hard. "Something scary? Like... terrible?"

"Close!" said Bricky. "In **1842**, he called them 'dinosaur.' That word means **terrible lizard**."

Juno gasped. "Terrible lizard! That's the best name ever!"

"It is a pretty good one," Bricky agreed. "Even though not every dinosaur was a lizard, and not every one was terrible."

Milo smiled. "Some were probably nice."

"Exactly," said Bricky. "But the name stuck. People still use it today."

Juno marched around in a circle, chanting. "Terrible lizard! Terrible lizard!"

Milo joined in, stomping his feet to match her words.

Bricky watched them and clicked happily, his little LEGO spikes rattling. "Now you both sound properly terrible," he said. "Well done."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant and the Tiny Turkey
chapters.text:
The ground began to rumble. THUMP. THUMP. THUMP.

Juno froze. "Is that scary?"

"Not even a little," said Bricky. "Just a big friend walking by."

A dinosaur with a neck like a crane rose above the trees. It kept going, and going, and going.

"That's **Argentinosaurus**," said Bricky. "Maybe the biggest dinosaur ever. Over **100 feet long** — longer than your whole street."

Milo's mouth dropped open. "That's bigger than our LEGO tower times a hundred!"

Then something small darted between their legs, fast and feathery.

"Was that a dinosaur too?" asked Juno.

"Yes," said Bricky. "That's a **Velociraptor**. In movies they look huge and scary. But really, they were only about the size of a turkey."

Juno laughed. "A turkey with feathers?"

"Many dinosaurs had feathers," said Bricky. "Just like birds do today."

Milo watched the tiny raptor hop away. "So the biggest dinosaur and the littlest one were both right here?"

"Same world," said Bricky. "Dinosaurs came in every size."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Horns, Plates, and a Spiky Tail
chapters.text:
They climbed a little hill. Below, two huge dinosaurs stood munching leaves.

One had bony plates standing up along its back, and spikes near the end of its tail.

"That's **Stegosaurus**," said Bricky. "Those back spikes could swing like a club to keep it safe."

The other dinosaur had three horns on its face and a wide bony shield around its neck.

"And that," said Bricky, "is **Triceratops**. Three horns, and a big bony **frill** — like a shield — to guard its neck."

Milo, who always loved sharks and their teeth, grinned. "Sharks have teeth to stay safe. These dinosaurs have horns and spikes!"

"Everybody needs a way to stay safe," said Bricky.

Juno pointed at the Triceratops. "I want a frill for MY neck!"

"You'll have to settle for a blanket," said Bricky, and Juno giggled so hard she nearly toppled over.

The two giant plant-eaters kept munching, calm as could be, not bothered one bit by their visitors.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Dinosaur Nest
chapters.text:
Bricky led them down to a sandy, sunny spot. Round shapes dotted the ground in neat little rows.

"Eggs!" whispered Juno.

"A nest," said Bricky. "This kind of dinosaur was called **Maiasaura**. Her name even means 'good mother lizard.'"

A big, gentle dinosaur stood close by, watching over the nest.

"People found nests just like this one in a place called **Montana**," said Bricky. "That's how we learned dinosaur moms took care of their babies, just like your family takes care of you."

Juno leaned close, careful not to touch. "Hi, baby eggs," she whispered.

Milo noticed one egg had a tiny crack. "Is it hatching?"

"Not tonight," said Bricky gently. "But soon."

Juno looked up at the mother dinosaur. "She's a really good mom."

"The best," agreed Bricky.

They tiptoed away quietly, so they wouldn't bother the nest, Juno waving goodbye to the eggs the whole way.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Footprints in the Mud
chapters.text:
The ground turned hard and crusty, covered in strange shapes.

Milo crouched down. "These look like giant footprints!"

"Good eyes again," said Bricky. "Footprints like these have been found far away, in places called **Texas** and **China**. The mud dried hard as rock, so the shapes stayed forever."

Juno put her tiny foot inside one giant print. It swallowed her whole shoe.

"There's a desert called the **Gobi Desert**," added Bricky, "where people have found more dinosaur bones than almost anywhere else on Earth."

"Who finds them?" asked Milo.

"**Paleontologists**," said Bricky. "Scientists who dig up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived."

Milo stood up tall. "I want to be one of those."

"You basically are one right now," said Bricky, and Milo beamed.

Juno hopped from footprint to footprint, counting each one out loud. "One, two, three, four!"

"Keep counting," said Bricky. "There are dinosaur tracks like these all over the world."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sue the Giant and a Silly Old Story
chapters.text:
A roar rumbled across the field. Juno grabbed Milo's hand.

"It's okay," said Bricky quickly. "This one's friendly to visitors passing through."

A huge dinosaur with giant jaws stepped out of the trees.

"**Tyrannosaurus rex**," said Bricky. "Its teeth could grow up to **twelve inches long** — almost as long as your arm, Milo."

Milo stared at the teeth. "That's bigger than a shark tooth!"

"Way bigger," said Bricky. "One of the biggest T. rex skeletons ever found got a nickname: **Sue**. People found her bones in **South Dakota**, in **1990**."

"There's even a silly old story," Bricky added, "about a farmer's dog digging up part of a famous dinosaur. It's a fun tale, but probably not quite true. Still fun to tell, though."

Juno giggled. "A dinosaur-digging dog!"

The huge dinosaur turned and ambled off into the ferns, not interested in them at all.

"See?" said Bricky. "Nothing to worry about."

Juno let out a breath and grinned.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Where Did They Go?
chapters.text:
The sky began to change colors, soft and strange.

"A long, long time after all this," said Bricky gently, "something big happened, and most dinosaurs disappeared."

Juno's face fell. "All of them? Forever?"

"Not quite all," said Bricky, smiling. "One group of dinosaurs never really left."

A bird fluttered down and landed on Milo's shoulder, chirping.

Milo blinked. "Wait. Is THIS a dinosaur?"

"In a way, yes," said Bricky. "Birds today came from a dinosaur family. So dinosaurs never fully went away. They just grew feathers and learned to fly."

Juno reached out one careful finger and let the bird hop near her hand, without touching it.

"So every bird outside my window..." Milo said slowly.

"...is a little bit dinosaur," finished Bricky.

Juno gasped with delight. "I have dinosaurs in my backyard!"

The bird chirped once more, then flew off into the glowing sky, and Bricky began to glow red too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH!

The ferns spun away. The mud turned back into carpet.

Milo and Juno landed with a soft bump, right back on their bedroom rug.

Their giant tower still stood tall beside them, exactly where they'd left it.

Bricky's little dinosaur shape began to wobble.

"Time for me to go back to being plain old bricks," he said.

Juno hugged the air where he'd been. "Bye, dino-Bricky!"

CLICK, CLICK, CLICK. Bricky folded himself apart, piece by piece, until he was just a small red brick again, glowing softly on the carpet.

Milo picked it up and set it gently on top of their tower. It clicked into place.

"Terrible lizard," Juno whispered sleepily, snuggling into her blanket.

Milo grinned and pulled his own blanket up. "Night, Juno. Thanks for counting all those footprints."

Outside their window, a bird chirped once in the dark, then went quiet.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: The very first dinosaurs lived about **230 million years ago** — so long ago it's almost impossible to count that high.
A scientist named **Richard Owen** gave dinosaurs their name in **1842** — it means **terrible lizard**.
**Argentinosaurus** may have been the biggest dinosaur ever, over **100 feet long**.
**Velociraptor** was really only about the size of a **turkey**, much smaller than in movies.
Lots of dinosaurs had **feathers**, just like birds do today.
**Stegosaurus** had bony plates on its back and spikes on its tail to stay safe.
**Triceratops** had three horns and a big bony **frill**, like a shield, around its neck.
A gentle dinosaur called **Maiasaura** took care of her babies in a nest, found in **Montana**.
Dinosaur footprints have been found turned to hard rock in places like **Texas** and **China**.
The **Gobi Desert** is one of the best places in the world to find dinosaur bones.
**Paleontologists** are scientists who dig up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived.
A famous **T. rex** skeleton nicknamed **Sue** was found in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
T. rex teeth could grow up to **twelve inches long**.
Birds alive today came from dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never really went away.

new_recurring.rule: The magic red brick can build itself into a small LEGO creature shaped like the night's topic (a dinosaur, a shark, a rocket) to guide Milo and Juno; it unbuilds itself back into a plain brick when they return home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno land back on their bedroom rug, and the glowing brick unbuilds itself from its dinosaur shape before Milo clicks it onto the top of their tower.

story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Climbed Everything
story.subtitle: A sticky, stuck-together bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko Light Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor. Past bedtime. Way past.

He lined up his toy spiders in a row. Eight legs each. He counted them every single night.

On the wall above his bed glowed a little green gecko sticker. It was his night-light. It always just glowed, quiet and still.

Tonight it blinked.

Sam sat up. "Did you just wink at me?"

The gecko sticker peeled off the wall. SPLORP! It landed on the carpet and grew legs that waved.

"Hiya," said the gecko. "I'm Tiko. Tokay gecko. Best climber you will ever meet."

Sam grinned so big his face hurt. "Climbers are my favorite thing. After spiders. And bugs. And also geckos."

"Good," said Tiko, "because tonight, you ARE a gecko."

WHOOOSH! The room spun. Sam shrank down, down, down, until the carpet looked like a giant green ocean.

He looked at his hands. Little sticky toes, just like Tiko's.

"Why are my toes sticky?" Sam asked.

"Toes have millions of teeny tiny hairs," said Tiko. "So many, you cannot even see one. They let us stick to glass. Even upside down!"

Sam looked up at his bedroom window. Smooth. Shiny. Straight up and down.

"Can I climb that?" Sam asked.

"Only one way to find out," said Tiko.

Sam pressed one sticky toe onto the glass. It held.

"It's holding!" Sam yelled. "IT'S HOLDING!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Up the Window Glass
chapters.text:
Sam climbed higher. Toe. Toe. Toe. Each one stuck like it meant it.

"This is the best thing I have ever done," Sam said. "Besides catching the roly-poly behind the shed."

Tiko laughed, a little clicking sound. "Wait till you want to come back DOWN."

Sam stopped. "Uh oh. Am I stuck?"

"Nope," said Tiko. "Watch me."

Tiko peeled one toe off the glass. Then another. Then another. Just like pulling up a piece of tape.

"It's not even glue," said Tiko. "No mess. Nothing sticky left behind. Just peel, peel, peel."

Sam tried it. He peeled his front toe. CLICK. Then the next one. CLICK. Then the next.

"IT PEELS LIKE TAPE!" Sam shouted.

"Grown-ups study stuff like this for their whole job," said Tiko. "They're called scientists. They liked our sticky toes so much, they copied them. In 2014, they made sticky pads for human hands. A real person climbed a real glass wall. A whole human, climbing just like us!"

Sam pictured his dad climbing up the living room window wearing sticky gloves. He laughed so hard he nearly peeled off all ten toes at once.

"Let's keep climbing," Sam said. "I want to meet more climbers."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider in the Corner
chapters.text:
Up near the ceiling, something moved. Eight legs. Fast.

Sam's eyes went wide. "A SPIDER!"

"Don't worry," said Tiko. "Just say hi."

Sam waved. "Hi! I pick up spiders in my yard all the time!"

The spider waved one leg back. "Nice to meet a fan," it said, in a tiny, scratchy voice.

"How do you climb glass?" Sam asked. "You don't even look sticky."

"Same trick as Tiko," said the spider. "Tiny hairs on my feet too. Thousands of them. That's how I walk straight up your window, and you can't."

Sam looked at his own gecko toes, then at the spider's feet. "We match!"

"Kind of," said Tiko. "Spiders got their own version, all by themselves."

The spider scuttled sideways along the glass, quick as a blink.

"Race you to the top!" Sam said.

He pushed off with his sticky toes. Toe, toe, toe, faster now.

The spider reached the top first. "Too slow, gecko boy!"

Sam laughed so hard he nearly slid back down. "SPIDERS STICK TOO! Rematch tomorrow!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Sticky, Drippy Fly
chapters.text:
Something landed on the glass next to Sam. BZZZZT.

A fly. Rubbing its front legs together.

"Watch this," said the fly. It took one more step and left a tiny wet footprint. SQUELCH.

"Ew," said Sam, delighted. "What IS that?"

"My feet drip a little goo," the fly said proudly. "Like tiny drops of glue. That's how I stick."

Sam leaned in close. "Can I touch it?"

"Sure," said the fly.

Sam poked the wet spot. His toe stuck fast. SPLAT.

"I'm STUCK!" Sam yelled, giggling the whole time.

"Peel it, like Tiko showed you," said the fly.

Sam peeled his toe off, slow and careful. It made a tiny squelchy sound coming free.

"Beetles do the same gooey trick," said Tiko. "Different bug. Same idea. A little drippy glue on the feet."

"Bugs are SO good at this," Sam said. "No wonder I like them so much."

He poked the wet spot one more time, just for fun. SPLAT. SQUELCH. Giggle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Ants on the Brick Wall
chapters.text:
Tiko led Sam down to the garden, out past the window frame, onto a bumpy brick wall.

A line of ants marched straight up it, quick and tidy.

"How do THEY do it?" Sam asked. "This wall isn't even smooth."

"Ants carry two tools," said an ant marching past. "Sharp little claws for bumpy walls, like this brick. Sticky pads for smooth walls, like your window."

"You just pick whichever one you need?" Sam asked.

"Every single time," said the ant.

Sam looked closer at the bricks. Tiny holes. Tiny bumps. Too small to see before, but not too small now that he was ant-sized.

"The claws grab the little bumpy bits!" Sam said, pointing at one. "I found it!"

"You sure did," said Tiko. "Cockroaches do the very same two-tool trick too."

Sam dug his own toe into a bumpy brick. It held. Different from the sticky glass way. But it held.

"Two tricks are better than one," Sam decided, climbing on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Goat on the Rocky Cliff
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH. Tiko hopped them onto Sam's old fish tank rock, now looming like a whole rocky mountain.

A fuzzy mountain goat stood on a steep rock, calm as anything.

"Aren't you scared?" Sam called up. "That's so steep!"

"Nope," said the goat. "My hooves do the work." It lifted one foot. "Hard edges around the outside. Soft, squishy middle. The soft part squishes flat onto the rock and grips."

Sam squinted. "Like a shoe that changes shape?"

"Exactly like that," said the goat.

The goat hopped from rock to rock, never slipping once. Not even a wobble.

"I want hooves," Sam said.

"You've got sticky toes instead," said Tiko. "Way better for glass."

"Fine," Sam said. "I'll trade you for a window, not a cliff."

The goat laughed, a funny little bleat, and bounced away up the rocks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Squirrel in the Backyard Tree
chapters.text:
Back near Sam's own yard, a squirrel zipped straight up the big oak tree.

"Whoa, how is he not falling?" Sam asked.

"Claws," said Tiko. "Curved ones. They dig into teeny cracks in the bark. Cracks too small for you to even see."

The squirrel paused halfway up. "Little bumps, little dips. My claws grab every single one!"

Sam ran his tiny gecko fingers over the bark. Up close, it was not smooth at all. Bumpy. Crumbly. Full of tiny places to hold.

"It's like the ants," Sam said. "Everybody's got their own trick for their own wall!"

"Now you're getting it," said Tiko.

The squirrel flicked its tail and shot the rest of the way up. "Nuts don't collect themselves!"

Sam laughed so hard he nearly let go of the tree bark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Frog on the Wet Leaf
chapters.text:
A raindrop plinked onto a leaf below them. Sitting right in the middle: a small green tree frog.

"How are you not sliding right off?" Sam asked. "That leaf is soaking wet!"

The frog lifted one foot. Its toe had a flat little pad on the end.

It was covered in slippery wet stuff called mucus. That's just slimy goo, kind of like frog snot.

"Gross," said Sam, grinning. "I love it."

"My pads have tiny little honeycomb shapes on them," the frog said. "They grip the wet leaf, even slippery as it is."

Sam looked closer. Tiny six-sided shapes, like a soccer ball, covered the frog's toes.

"You're sticky even when it's wet," Sam said. "Tiko can't even do that!"

"Different trick for a different job," Tiko agreed. "Wet leaves need a wet-sticking expert."

The frog gave a little bow, and hopped off into the dark garden.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Snail and the Walk Back Home
chapters.text:
Near the garden path, something very slow caught Sam's eye. A snail, gliding straight up the garden wall.

"No claws. No hairs. No goo," Sam said. "How?"

"Slime," said the snail, not speeding up one single bit. "I lay down a trail of slime. Then I ripple my foot along it, nice and slow."

Sam watched the snail's whole underside ripple like a tiny wave. "That is so cool AND so slow."

"Slow and sure beats fast and fallen," said the snail.

Tiko chuckled. "Every climber we met tonight had their own trick. Sticky hairs. Goo drops. Claws. Hooves. Slime. All different. All brilliant."

"I want to try every single one again tomorrow," Sam said.

WHOOOSH. The garden spun. The brick wall shrank. The oak tree shrank. Sam grew and grew, until he was lying on his own bedroom carpet again, toy spiders lined up right where he left them.

The green gecko sticker was back on the wall above his bed, glowing soft and quiet.

"Climb well, Sam," Tiko whispered, and the glow faded down to sleep.

Sam pulled his blanket up, smiling at the ceiling, already picking which bug to find tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well.

true_facts.text: Geckos like Tiko can climb glass and walk upside down because their toes have millions of tiny hairs.
A gecko's sticky feet are not glue at all. There is no mess, and the gecko peels each toe off, one at a time, just like pulling up tape.
Spiders have thousands of their own tiny hairs on their feet, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny drops of goo that ooze from their feet like little bits of glue.
Ants and cockroaches use sharp claws on bumpy walls and sticky pads on smooth walls, switching between the two.
Mountain goats climb steep, rocky cliffs using hooves that have hard edges on the outside and a soft, squishy middle.
Squirrels climb trees using curved claws that dig into tiny bumps and cracks in the bark, too small to see.
Tree frogs have flat toe pads with tiny honeycomb shapes that grip wet, slippery leaves.
Snails climb walls by laying down a trail of slime and rippling their foot along it, slow and steady.
In 2014, scientists built sticky, gecko-style pads that let a real person climb a glass wall.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam grew back to normal size on his own bedroom carpet, right next to his lined-up toy spiders, while the green gecko night-light glowed softly above his bed and Tiko whispered 'Climb well, Sam' before fading to sleep.
