story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Golden Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A buzzy bedtime trip to see how honey is made.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Jar That Hums
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last sticky bit of honey off his toast.

Nell sat on the rug, sorting her yellow flowers into a neat row. It was almost bedtime.

Then the honey jar on the shelf began to glow. It hummed, soft and low, like a tiny engine.

"Finn," whispered Nell. "The jar is singing!"

The lid popped open with a soft **POP**. Out flew a tiny golden bee, no bigger than a thumb.

"Hello!" she said. "I'm Goldie. Want to fly and find out how honey gets made?"

Finn and Nell looked at each other and grinned. "Yes!" they said together.

Goldie sprinkled gold dust over them. The room seemed to spin, soft and sparkly.

Suddenly they were buzzing through the air, flying toward a sunny garden. Below them, flowers waved in yellow, pink, and purple.

Nell spotted one bright yellow flower and pointed. "That one! It's my favorite color!"

They landed softly on its big yellow petal. A fuzzy bee was already there, sipping something sweet.

"That's nectar," said Goldie. "It's sugary juice inside the flower." The bee drank it with a long, bendy tongue, like a tiny straw.

"Where does it go?" asked Finn.

"Into a special pouch, just for nectar," said Goldie. "Bees call it a honey stomach. It's not for food, just for carrying nectar home."

Finn patted his own tummy. "I wish I had one of those for toast."

Nell giggled so hard she nearly rolled off the petal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bee Kiss Trick
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! They landed at a big wooden hive. Bees zipped in and out, busy as can be.

"Follow that nectar bee," said Goldie. The bee flew inside and bumped noses with another bee.

"What is she doing?" asked Nell.

"Sharing," said Goldie. "She passes the nectar mouth to mouth, like a little bee kiss."

Finn scrunched his nose. "That's silly!"

"It's also clever," said Goldie. "Her spit mixes in and changes the nectar, bit by bit. It starts turning into honey."

Nell kissed the back of her own hand. "Mwah! Mwah!"

Finn copied her, and they both giggled until they snorted.

"Keep watching," said Goldie. "The nectar bee kisses pass it along to lots of house bees, again and again."

Finn counted on his fingers. "One, two, three bee kisses!"

"Good counting," said Goldie, smiling.

Nell tugged her flowers close. "I bet bee kisses smell like my yellow flower."

"Pretty close," laughed Goldie.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Tiny Rooms Made of Wax
chapters.text:
The house bee flew to a wall covered in tiny holes. Each hole had six flat sides, like a little room.

"Whoa," said Finn. "It's like a wall of tiny windows!"

"That's honeycomb," said Goldie. "Bees build it out of wax they make inside their own bodies."

Nell reached out and touched one gently. "It's bumpy and soft."

"Bees make the wax from little spots on their tummy," said Goldie. "Then they shape it into these six-sided rooms."

The house bee spread the nectar inside one tiny room.

"One room, filled up," said Goldie. "Time for the next trick."

Finn tugged on Goldie's wing gently. "What trick?"

Goldie just winked. "Watch the wings."

Nell pressed her nose close to the wax wall and counted the little rooms. "One, two, three, so many rooms!"

"Thousands and thousands," said Goldie proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: FLAP FLAP FLAP!
chapters.text:
Suddenly, dozens of bees lined up next to the wax room. They began flapping their wings, fast as can be.

FLAP FLAP FLAP! The sound filled the whole hive.

"Why are they doing that?" asked Nell, holding her flowers tight.

"Nectar is watery," said Goldie. "Flapping wings makes a little wind. The wind dries it out."

"Like drying wet socks on a line!" said Finn.

"Exactly," said Goldie. "Once it's dry enough, it isn't watery nectar anymore. It's thick, sticky honey."

Nell leaned close and sniffed, careful not to touch. "It smells like Finn's toast!"

Finn flapped his arms like wings. "FLAP FLAP FLAP! Make honey, Finn-style!"

He flapped so hard he tumbled onto a soft petal and laughed. Nell flapped right beside him until they both fell into a giggly heap.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Wax Lid for Winter
chapters.text:
A bee walked over and pressed a thin wax lid onto the honey room. It looked like a tiny sealed lunchbox.

"Why put a lid on?" asked Finn.

"To keep the honey clean and safe," said Goldie. "It stays sealed until the bees need it."

Nell's eyes went wide. "Need it for what?"

"Winter," said Goldie. "When it's cold, there are no flowers. No nectar to drink."

Finn frowned. "Then what do the bees eat?"

"Honey!" said Goldie. "They made it and saved it, just for that day. Smart bees."

Nell clapped her hands. "It's like saving cookies for later!"

"Just like that," laughed Goldie.

Finn patted the little wax lid softly. "Good job, bees. Nobody goes hungry."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Busy, Busy Family
chapters.text:
Goldie led them deeper into the hive, where it was busiest. Bees buzzed past in every direction, thousands of them.

"How many bees live here?" asked Finn.

"In summer, as many as twenty thousand, even sixty thousand," said Goldie.

Nell's mouth dropped open. "That's more bees than I can count!"

"Way more," giggled Goldie.

They came to one extra-big bee near the middle of the hive.

"That's the queen," said Goldie. "She lays the eggs. Sometimes more than a thousand in one single day!"

"A thousand babies a day?" Finn gasped.

"Busy mom," said Goldie.

"And almost all the other bees," said Goldie, "are girls. Worker bees. They do almost every job, finding flowers, making honey, building the wax rooms, all of it."

Nell puffed up proudly. "Girls can do anything!"

"They sure can," said Goldie, giving her a tiny high-five with one wing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
Near the entrance, one bee was wiggling in a funny little circle.

"Is she dancing?" asked Nell, already wiggling along with her.

"She is!" said Goldie. "That's a scout bee. She found good flowers far away."

"How does dancing help?" asked Finn.

"The wiggles tell the other bees which way to fly, and how far," said Goldie. "It's called the waggle dance."

Nell wiggled her hips. "Like this?"

"Pretty close!" laughed Goldie.

Finn tried too, wobbling sideways until he bumped into Nell. They both fell into a giggling heap.

"Show us where your flowers are," said Nell to the scout bee.

The scout bee wiggled toward the sunny yellow field they had visited first.

"She's pointing the way home!" said Finn.

Nell wiggled one more time, just for fun. "WIGGLE, WAGGLE, DANCE!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sweet as Honey, Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more thing before we go," said Goldie. "Did you know it takes twelve bees, working their whole lives, just to make one teaspoon of honey?"

Finn looked at his almost-empty toast plate. "That's a LOT of bee work for my breakfast."

"And honey never goes bad," said Goldie, "if you keep the lid on tight. It can stay sweet for years and years."

Nell blinked. "Even longer than my birthday?"

"Much longer," laughed Goldie.

"The bees help flowers too," said Goldie. "When they visit, little bits of flower dust called pollen stick to their fuzzy legs. It travels flower to flower, and that helps new flowers grow."

Nell looked down at her own yellow flowers and smiled. "Thank you, bees."

Goldie sprinkled gold dust over them again. "Fly and find your way home now," she said softly.

WHOOSH, and they landed right back on Finn's bedroom rug.

The honey jar sat quiet and still on the shelf, glowing just a little. Beside it lay one tiny golden feather, shimmering like a keepsake.

"Goodnight, Goldie," whispered Nell.

"Goodnight, buzzy friend," yawned Finn, climbing into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Fly and find sweet dreams.

true_facts.text: Bees called foragers fly to flowers and drink sweet nectar with a long tongue, like a tiny straw.
Bees keep the nectar in a special pouch called a honey stomach, just for carrying it home.
When bees pass nectar mouth to mouth, their spit starts turning it into honey.
Bees pour the nectar into tiny six-sided rooms called honeycomb.
Bees flap their wings fast to dry the nectar until it turns into sticky honey.
Bees put a thin wax lid on top to keep the honey clean and safe.
Bees save honey to eat in winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
A hive can have twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees living in it in summer.
The queen bee lays the eggs, sometimes more than a thousand in one day.
A scout bee does a wiggly waggle dance to show other bees where good flowers are.
It takes twelve bees, working their whole lives, to make just one teaspoon of honey.
If the lid stays sealed, honey can stay sweet for a very long time.
As bees visit flowers, bits of flower dust called pollen stick to their legs and help new flowers grow.

story.title: Omar and the Wheel Through Time
story.subtitle: A BMX kid meets every bike that ever rolled before his.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar's bike leaned in the corner, dusty from today's jumps. He'd landed his first tailwhip at the skate park. Lights out, right?

Then the back wheel started spinning. By itself. WHIRRR!

A soft glow filled the room, green and silver. A voice came from the spokes. "Evening, Omar. I'm Spoke. Want to see the very first bike ever?"

"There was a FIRST bike?" Omar sat up fast.

"In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built a wooden two-wheeler," said Spoke. "No pedals at all. Riders pushed it along with their feet, like a giant walking toy."

"That sounds hilarious," Omar said.

"People called it the 'running machine,'" Spoke said. "It even had handlebars, just like yours."

Omar grabbed his own handlebars. The wheel glowed brighter. WHOOSH! The room melted away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
Omar landed on a bumpy cobblestone street. His bike now had pedals bolted to the front wheel.

"Where are we?" he asked, wobbling.

"France, the 1860s," said Spoke. "Inventors **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement** added pedals straight onto the front wheel. People called it the 'velocipede.'"

"Vel-oss-ih-what?" Omar said.

"Just call it the 'boneshaker,'" Spoke laughed. "Riding one over these bumpy stones rattled every bone in your body."

Omar pedaled forward. CLUNK-CLUNK-CLUNK! His teeth chattered with every bump.

"THIS IS NOT SMOOTH!" Omar shouted, laughing anyway.

"Lallement even got a paper from the government in **1866**," Spoke said, "saying the pedal bike was his very own invention."

Omar pointed at a smoother dirt path. "Let's go that way — my teeth can't take much more!"

They rolled off, and the bumps finally disappeared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Big Wheel, Tiny Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
The bike under Omar suddenly grew. And grew. The front wheel rose taller than his dad.

"Whoa!" Omar yelled, looking down from way up high.

"This is a **penny-farthing**," Spoke said. "Named after two old coins — one huge, one tiny, just like these wheels."

"Why make the front wheel so big?" Omar asked.

"One turn of the pedals sends you much farther," Spoke explained. "Riders went faster than ever before."

Omar pedaled. The bike zoomed. Then it hit a bump — and tipped!

"Whoa whoa WHOA!" Omar grabbed air as the bike tilted forward.

Spoke caught the handlebars just in time. "Careful! Riders called that a 'header' — flying right off the front. It happened all the time."

Omar climbed down, knees wobbly but fine. "I'll stick to tricks closer to the ground," he said.

Spoke chuckled. "Smart kid."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
The giant wheel shrank back down. Now Omar sat on a bike with two wheels the same size.

"Much better," he said, relieved.

"In **1885**, an Englishman named **John Kemp Starley** built this," Spoke said. "He called it the 'Rover Safety Bicycle.' A chain connects the pedals to the back wheel, just like your BMX."

Omar looked down at his own chain. "So this is basically my bike's great-great-grandpa?"

"Exactly," Spoke said. "No more flying off the front. This design was so good, people everywhere copied it."

Omar pedaled smoothly, no wobbling, no tipping. He popped a little wheelie, just because he could.

"NOW WE'RE TALKING!" he shouted.

Spoke spun happily beside him. "Safety first, tricks second."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Pumped Up (1888)
chapters.text:
BUMP. BUMP. BUMP. Omar's teeth rattled again on the hard rubber tires.

"Ugh, this feels like the boneshaker again," he groaned.

"Hang on," Spoke said. "Someone's about to fix that."

A man knelt by a tricycle nearby, wrapping a rubber tube around a wheel and pumping it full of air.

"That's **John Boyd Dunlop**," Spoke said. "A vet in Scotland, in **1888**. He built an air-filled tire for his son's tricycle, to make the ride smoother."

Omar's own tires suddenly puffed up, soft and round.

He pedaled. No bumps. Just a smooth, quiet roll.

"That's SO much better," Omar said.

"His tire company is still around today," Spoke said. "You've probably seen the name Dunlop on tires."

Omar grinned. "I owe that guy a high five."

Spoke laughed. "He'd probably just want a smooth ride."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everybody's Riding (1890s)
chapters.text:
Suddenly the street filled with bikes. Dozens of them. Hundreds!

"Welcome to the **1890s**," Spoke said. "People called this the Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions of bikes were sold, all over Europe and America."

A woman zoomed past on a bike, wearing puffy pants instead of a long skirt.

"Those are called bloomers," Spoke said. "Long skirts could get caught in the gears, so riders switched to something safer."

"Smart," Omar said.

"Bikes gave women a whole new kind of freedom," Spoke said. "They could go wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted, all on their own. One famous person even said bikes did more for women's freedom than almost anything else."

Omar watched the woman pedal off, laughing with her friends.

"That's awesome," he said. "Bikes basically unlocked a whole level for everybody."

"LEVEL UNLOCKED!" Spoke cheered.

Omar fist-bumped the air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: From Bike Shop to Sky (1890s–1930s)
chapters.text:
A bell jingled above a little shop door. Omar stepped inside, surrounded by bike parts.

"This shop belongs to two brothers," Spoke said. "**Wilbur** and **Orville Wright**, in Dayton, Ohio, in the 1890s. They fixed and built bicycles for a living."

"Wright... like the airplane guys?" Omar asked.

"The very same," Spoke said. "They used tricks from building light bike frames and wheels to help build their first airplane, in **1903**."

Omar picked up a thin metal tube. "Bike parts built a FLYING MACHINE?"

"Pretty much," Spoke said.

Outside, a crowd cheered for racers speeding by on hills.

"By the 1930s, bikes got little gadgets called gears," Spoke said. "They move the chain so hills get easier to pedal up."

"And that race down there," Spoke added, "started in **1903**. The Tour de France. Racers still ride about **3,500 kilometers** across France every summer."

"That's basically a million skate park laps," Omar said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Wheels Like Mine
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a bumpy dirt track with jumps.

"NOW we're talking," Omar said, eyes wide.

"**BMX bikes** showed up in America in the **1970s**," Spoke said. "Small, tough bikes made for tricks and dirt racing, inspired by dirt bike racing."

"Finally, my people," Omar said.

"Around the same time," Spoke said, "riders in California built the first mountain bikes, with wide, bumpy tires for riding down rough trails."

Omar spotted a sleek, feather-light racing bike nearby. "Why's that one so light?"

"Modern bikes use light materials, like special metal and carbon," Spoke said. "Some racing bikes weigh less than **8 kilograms** — lighter than your backpack."

"Whoa," Omar said. "Also, how many bikes even exist now?"

"About **one billion**," Spoke said. "More than any other vehicle on Earth. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars."

Omar looked down at his own BMX, glowing softly. "Take me home, Spoke."

WHOOSH! The glow swept him back to his bedroom, bike leaning in the corner, wheel still humming quietly.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Keep your wheels turning.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built a wooden bike with no pedals — riders pushed it along with their feet.
In the **1860s**, French inventors added pedals to the front wheel, and people called it the 'boneshaker.'
In the **1870s**, the penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel.
Falling off a penny-farthing was called taking a 'header.'
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the safety bicycle, with two matching wheels and a chain.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented the air-filled tire for a smoother ride.
In the **1890s**, millions of bikes were sold across Europe and America — the Golden Age of Bicycles.
Bikes gave women a whole new kind of freedom to go wherever they wanted, on their own.
Long skirts were dangerous near bike gears, so riders switched to puffy pants called bloomers.
**Wilbur** and **Orville Wright** ran a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bike-building tricks to help build their first airplane in **1903**.
The Tour de France bike race began in **1903** and covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France.
**BMX bikes** became popular in America in the **1970s**, built for tricks and dirt racing.
Today there are about **one billion** bicycles in the world — more than any other vehicle.

new_recurring.name: Spoke
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing voice that lives in the spokes of Omar's bike wheel. Appears when the back wheel starts spinning on its own, glowing green and silver, and guides Omar through history before sending him home with a WHOOSH. Speaks in a…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Omar rode through 200 years of bicycle history with his glowing guide Spoke and landed back in his own bedroom, his BMX still humming softly in the corner.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Door
story.subtitle: A sticky, zappy, pole-flipping adventure with Pip the magnet robot

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wobbly Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada sat on her bedroom floor after dinner. Magnets from the fridge lay all around her. She liked snapping them together. CLICK! CLICK! CLICK!

Then she flipped one magnet around. She pushed it toward another. It would not click. It pushed back instead! "Hey!" said Ada. "Why won't you stick?"

A little magnet by her knee gave a shiver. It popped into a tiny round robot with blinking eyes. "Because you flipped the wrong end," the robot said. "I'm Pip. Every magnet has two ends, called poles. One end pulls. The other end pushes away."

Ada turned her magnet back around. CLICK! It stuck again.

"See?" said Pip. "One pulling end and one pushing end, matched up, stick together. Two pushing ends just push apart."

"Show me more!" said Ada.

Pip's round middle glowed like a little doorway. "Hold on tight," said Pip. "We're going to visit some magnets."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Rock That Pulled
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! Ada landed on a sunny hillside. Sheep nibbled grass nearby. A shepherd stared at the ground, confused.

His metal walking stick kept sticking to a black rock. Ada knelt down and picked the rock up. It tugged gently at Pip's little metal foot.

"This rock is called lodestone," said Pip. "It pulls on metal all by itself, no plugging in needed. People found rocks like this long ago, near a place called Magnesia."

"Is that where the word magnet comes from?" asked Ada.

"Probably!" said Pip. "Nobody is totally sure, but it's a very good guess."

Ada sprinkled tiny iron bits near the rock. They lined up in curvy lines, like stripes on a shell. "Whoa! You can SEE the pull!" she said.

"That's called a magnetic field," said Pip. "It's the invisible space around a magnet where the pulling happens. You just made it visible."

Ada tucked a tiny lodestone chip into her pocket, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Needle That Knew North
chapters.text:
The doorway glowed again. Ada and Pip popped up in an old wooden boat, floating on a calm river.

A sailor was turning in circles, lost. Ada noticed a sliver of lodestone floating on a leaf in a bowl of water. It kept turning to point the same direction.

"That's an early compass," said Pip. "People figured this out more than two thousand years ago. The floating sliver always swings to point north."

Ada tapped the bowl gently. The leaf spun, then settled, pointing the same way again. "It always comes back!" she said.

"Every single time," said Pip. "Now the sailor knows which way home is."

The sailor beamed and turned his boat the right way.

"Good job, Ada," said Pip. "You just helped him find north."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant Magnet Under Our Feet
chapters.text:
Next the doorway dropped them somewhere strange, floating high above the whole round Earth.

"Whoa," whispered Ada. "Why can I see swirly orange stuff way down in the middle?"

"That's Earth's core," said Pip. "It's the very center, deep, deep down. Hot melted iron swirls around down there. That swirling makes the whole planet act like one giant magnet."

Ada pulled her compass sliver from her pocket. Floating up in space, it still swung to point the same way.

"The needle lines up with Earth's own pulling power," said Pip. "That's why compasses always point north."

"So I'm standing on a magnet right now?" Ada laughed.

"Yep," said Pip. "A really, really big one."

Ada patted the air like she was patting the whole planet. "Good magnet," she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tiny Dancers
chapters.text:
Pip shrank the glowing doorway down, down, down, until Ada felt as small as a speck.

"Where are we now?" Ada whispered. Everything around her was fuzzy and glowing.

"Inside a piece of iron," said Pip. "Everything is made of atoms, tiny building blocks too small to see. Inside each atom, tiny specks called electrons zip around. Each one acts like a teeny tiny magnet."

Ada watched clumps of specks spinning the same direction, like dancers doing the same move.

"In iron, lots of these tiny dancers face the same way," said Pip. "That teamwork makes a strong pull."

"What about my wooden ruler?" Ada asked.

"In wood, the dancers face every which way," said Pip. "All mixed up, so the pulls cancel out. No magnet there."

Ada lined up her stuffed animals in neat rows, giggling. "Dance team, assemble!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Wire That Wiggled
chapters.text:
CLICK! The doorway opened into an old classroom. A man with a notebook was fiddling with a wire and a battery.

"That's Hans Christian Oersted," whispered Pip. "Watch his compass."

Ada leaned in. The moment he connected the wire to the battery, the little compass needle on the table jumped and swung sideways!

"Whoa, it moved all by itself!" Ada gasped. Was something wrong?

"Nothing's wrong," said Pip quickly. "Electricity flowing through a wire makes its own magnetic pull. He found that out completely by accident."

Ada grabbed a spare coil of wire, wrapped it around a nail, and touched both ends to a little battery. The nail scooped up a paperclip!

"I made an electromagnet!" Ada cheered. "A magnet I can switch on and off!"

"Just like the magnets inside doorbells, speakers, and giant junkyard cranes," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Snap Test
chapters.text:
Back in Pip's workshop, a sturdy bar magnet sat on the table.

"Guess what happens if I snap this in half?" asked Pip.

Ada thought. "Does one half just pull, and the other half just push?"

"Nope!" said Pip, and snapped it. "Each new piece gets its own pulling end and pushing end. You never get just one alone."

Ada tried it on two more magnets. Sure enough, every broken piece still had both ends.

Pip set out a spoon, a nail, a penny, and a little gold ring. "Which ones will stick to a magnet?"

Ada touched the magnet to each one. The nail jumped right to it. The others stayed still. "The nail sticks, but not the penny or the gold ring!" she said.

"Right," said Pip. "Gold, copper, and silver don't stick to regular magnets. Only certain metals do."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Fridge
chapters.text:
The doorway glowed one last time. "One more quick stop," said Pip.

They zoomed past a sleek silver train, floating just above its tracks with no wheels touching. "That train floats on magnets," said Pip. "With no rubbing on the rails, it can zoom along super fast."

Then WHOOOOSH, Ada landed back on her bedroom carpet. Magnets lay scattered just as before.

Pip shrank back down into a small bendy magnet, the kind made of squishy rubber with tiny bits of magnet mixed inside. Ada pressed it onto her fridge, right at her own height.

"Thanks, Pip," she whispered, climbing into bed. The little magnet gave one last tiny wiggle, like a wave goodnight.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together!

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends called **poles**, and that's where the pull is strongest.
Matching ends push apart, but a pulling end and a pushing end stick together.
The invisible space around a magnet where the pulling happens is called its **magnetic field**.
Sprinkling tiny iron bits near a magnet lines them up in curvy stripes, showing the field.
A natural pulling rock called **lodestone** was found near a place called **Magnesia**, maybe where the word magnet comes from.
A floating sliver of lodestone was an early **compass**, always turning to point north.
Deep down at Earth's **core**, swirling melted iron makes the whole planet act like a giant magnet.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's own pulling power.
Everything is made of tiny atoms, and inside them tiny electrons spin like little magnets.
Wrapping wire into a coil and running electricity through it makes an **electromagnet** you can switch on and off.
Snap a magnet in half and you don't get a lone pulling piece — each new piece gets both a pulling end and a pushing end.
Gold, copper, and silver don't stick to regular magnets, even though they're metal.
Fridge magnets are usually made of bendy rubber mixed with tiny bits of magnet, which is why they can bend without losing their stick.

new_recurring.name: Pip
new_recurring.rule: A tiny magnet robot who lives among the fridge magnets, shivers to life, and opens a glowing round doorway to real magnetic places and moments. Ends the night by shrinking back into a bendy magnet. Catchphrase: 'Stick together!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ada returns to her bedroom carpet and Pip shrinks back into a small bendy fridge magnet, which Ada presses onto the fridge at her own height before climbing into bed.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow That Wouldn't Sit Still
story.subtitle: A fizzy, splashy trip through sunbeams and raindrops

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Started It All
chapters.text:
It was almost bedtime. Priya was drawing rainbows on her sketchpad. Dev was spraying his water pistol at absolutely nothing, because that is what water pistols are for.

"Dev! You got my paper wet!" Priya said.

"Oops," said Dev, not sorry at all.

The sun was low and orange outside the window. Dev aimed one more squirt into the last sunbeam — and the spray lit up in every color at once.

A tiny droplet popped out of the mist, glowing like a marble made of light, with a round, giggly face.

"Hiya!" it said. "I'm Fizzle."

"You need two things to make a rainbow," Fizzle said. "**Sunshine**, and water in the air — rain, or spray from a pistol works great. The sun has to be behind you, with the water out in front."

Dev spun around so the sun was on his back and squirted again. A perfect rainbow bent across the mist.

"WHOA," said Dev.

"Want to see how it really works?" Fizzle asked. "Climb in."

Priya laughed. "Climb into a water pistol?"

"Climb into the rainbow," Fizzle said, and the room filled with mist and light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
They shrank down, down, until they floated inside one single raindrop, round as a tiny glass ball.

"Light comes in here," Fizzle said, pointing at a beam of sunlight hitting the drop's curved wall. The beam bent sideways the moment it touched the water.

"Hey, it turned!" Priya said. "Why?"

"Light moves slower in water than in air," Fizzle said. "When it slows down, it bends. Scientists call that **refraction** — a fancy word for light taking a turn."

Dev ran in a sharp zigzag, pretending to be the beam. "REFRACTION!" he yelled, bumping a beanbag.

Inside the drop, the beam bounced off the back wall, then bent again on its way out, heading straight for Priya's eyes.

"It bends twice!" Priya said. "In, bounce, and out!"

"Exactly," said Fizzle. "Every raindrop does that little dance."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Inside Sunlight
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, Fizzle held up a glass prism, shaped like a triangle.

"Sunlight looks white," Fizzle said. "But it's secretly hiding every color at once, all squished together."

"No way," said Priya. "That's like saying my white sock is secretly full of socks."

Fizzle shone a sunbeam through the glass. Out the other side came a stripe of color, stretched like a tiny painted rainbow on the wall.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** did this exact trick, back in the **1660s**," Fizzle said. "He proved sunlight is made of every color, mixed together."

Dev squirted his pistol right through the beam, just to see what happened. The colors wobbled and danced.

"Each color bends a slightly different amount," Fizzle said. "That's what pulls them apart so we can see them."

Priya grabbed her sketchpad. "I need to draw this."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Roy G. Biv Moves In
chapters.text:
Priya lined up her colored pencils on the floor. "If I was a rainbow," she said, "what order would I go in?"

"Red first," Fizzle said, "then orange, yellow, green, blue, and two purples called indigo and violet. People remember it with a name: **Roy G. Biv**."

"Like a guy who's really into crayons," Priya said, and Dev snorted.

"Red always sits on the outside edge of a rainbow," Fizzle added, "and violet always sits on the inside. Red bends the least going through a drop, and violet bends the most."

Dev squinted at the colors. "Red's on the outside 'cause it's shy," he decided.

"Close enough," said Fizzle, laughing.

Priya arranged her pencils, red to violet, in a perfect little arc on the carpet, matching the glowing one still hanging in the misty air above them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow That Never Ends
chapters.text:
"Can I ask something weird?" Priya said. "Does a rainbow have a bottom?"

Fizzle grinned. "Good question. A rainbow is actually a whole **circle**. We just can't see the bottom half, because the ground gets in the way."

Dev got down on his belly to peek underneath the misty arc, as if he might spot the missing half.

"From way up in an airplane, with no ground blocking anything, people sometimes see the whole circle, round as a hula hoop," Fizzle said.

"I'm gonna see a circle rainbow from a plane someday," Dev announced.

"Write it on your list," said Priya, patting his head.

The misty rainbow floated higher, curling almost all the way around them, before the bottom faded into the carpet like always.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Nobody Else's Rainbow
chapters.text:
Dev reached out to grab a handful of the glowing colors. His hand went straight through.

"Hey! Rude," he said to the rainbow.

"You can't ever touch one," Fizzle said. "A rainbow isn't really sitting in one spot. It only shows up at a certain angle between the sun, the water, and your own eyes."

"So if I moved over there," Priya said, pointing, "would I see a different one?"

"You'd see your very own rainbow," Fizzle said. "Nobody else sees the exact same one. Not even Dev, standing right next to you."

"We're rainbow twins who never match," Priya said. "Typical."

"Old stories say there's a pot of gold waiting at the end of one," Fizzle added. "That's probably just a fun old tale, since a rainbow's end keeps moving whenever you do."

"Story of my life," said Dev, chasing the drifting colors and never once catching them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Two for the Price of One
chapters.text:
A second, fainter arc shimmered into view above the first.

"Whoa, a copy!" Dev shouted.

"That's a second rainbow," Fizzle said. "It happens when light bounces twice inside the drops instead of once. Look close — its colors are flipped."

Priya squinted. "Violet's on the outside this time!"

"You got it," said Fizzle. "Rainbows can show up anywhere water and light team up — waterfall mist, garden hose spray, even moonlight."

"A nighttime rainbow?" Priya asked.

"A **moonbow**," Fizzle said. "They're usually so pale they look white or gray. But a camera can catch the colors hiding inside."

Dev squirted his pistol straight up, hoping for a midnight moonbow. Nothing happened — the moon wasn't out yet.

"Patience," said Priya, patting his shoulder. "Rainbows don't do requests."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
"People have told rainbow stories forever," Fizzle said, as the mist began to settle. "Some say it's a bridge for gods to cross. Some say it's a sign of a promise after a storm — a happy ending painted across the sky."

"I like that," Priya said softly. "A happy ending you can actually see."

The glow dimmed. "Sparkle on!" Fizzle said, and popped away like a soap bubble, leaving one small, ordinary drop sitting on the tip of Dev's water pistol.

Priya and Dev were back on the bedroom carpet, right where they'd started.

Priya's sketchpad lay open. Where a blank page had been, there was now a perfect rainbow, every color in order, red on the outside, violet tucked in close.

"I didn't draw that," Priya whispered.

"Rainbows don't always wait for pencils," said Dev, grinning, and gave his water pistol one last, happy squirt.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Sparkle on!

true_facts.text: A rainbow needs both **sunshine** and **water in the air**, like rain or spray, which is why they often show up after a shower.
To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you and the rain or spray in front of you.
Light goes into a raindrop, bounces off the back wall, and comes out bent — that's how a rainbow is made.
Light bends when it slows down going from air into water. That bending is called **refraction**.
Sunlight looks white, but it's secretly made of every color mixed together.
Long ago, in the **1660s**, **Isaac Newton** used a glass prism to split white sunlight into all its colors.
The color order in a rainbow is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet — remembered as **Roy G. Biv**.
Red always sits on the outside edge of a rainbow, and violet sits on the inside.
A rainbow is really a whole circle, but the ground usually blocks the bottom half from view.
Every person sees their very own rainbow, made from different drops, even if they're standing right next to each other.
You can never actually touch a rainbow, because it moves with you wherever you go.
Old stories say there's a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow — a fun old tale, since a rainbow's end always keeps moving.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow shows up above the first one, with its colors flipped around.
Rainbows can appear in waterfall mist, garden hose spray, or even faint, pale ones at night called **moonbows**.

new_recurring.name: Fizzle
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing droplet guide who appears whenever sunlight hits water spray or rain, teaches the science of light with cheerful energy, and always says 'Sparkle on!' before popping away.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Priya and Dev land back on the bedroom carpet to find a perfect rainbow has appeared on Priya's blank sketchpad page, and Dev gives his water pistol one last happy squirt.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Tide Box of Sharks
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through five hundred kinds of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Box at the Foot of the Bed
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Jack lay on his belly, holding his breath, counting in his head. He did that most nights, pretending to dive deep. Ellie sat cross-legged on her bed, brushing a shiny blue shell like it was a mermaid's hair.

"Thirty-two seconds," Jack gasped, popping up. "New record."

"Mermaids don't need to breathe," Ellie said. "They just swim."

Between their beds sat an old wooden box, the one where they kept beach treasures. Jack's biggest treasure was a smooth gray rock shaped like a tooth. Ellie's was a shiny black shell, curled at each corner like a little purse.

"Let's put them in together," Jack said. He always had ideas like that.

They dropped both treasures into the box at the same time.

The box did not just sit there. It hummed. Then it glowed, soft and blue-green, like moonlight under water.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "Is it supposed to do that?"

Water sounds poured out, waves and bubbles, though the box was bone dry. A cool mist rose up and smelled like the sea.

"Only one way to find out," Jack said, grabbing Ellie's hand.

The mist swallowed them both. **WHOOOOSH!**

The bedroom spun into blue. Sand appeared under their bare feet. Somewhere close by, something enormous moved through the water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bendy Bones
chapters.text:
They stood on a sandbar, water warm around their ankles. Something swam close, gray and quick.

"Is it going to bite us?" Ellie asked, grabbing Jack's sleeve.

The shark turned away and vanished into the blue. Easy. Gone.

"Sharks almost never bother people," said a voice. It came from the glowing box, floating beside them like a little blue lantern. "You're safe here."

Jack grinned. "The box talks now?"

"The box does a lot of things," it said.

Jack watched the shark bend and curve as it swam, smooth as a ribbon.

"Why is it so bendy?" he asked. "Fish have bones."

"Sharks do too," said the box. "But their bones are made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the part inside your ear."

Jack grabbed his own ear and wiggled it. "Like this?"

"Exactly like that," the box said.

Ellie tugged her ear too, giggling. "Mine's bendy! Am I a shark?"

"Only if you can swim backward," Jack teased.

Ellie flipped around and tried, arms waving, and went sideways instead. They laughed so hard they swallowed seawater and coughed it right back out.

"Bendy bones mean a shark can twist and turn fast," the box said. "Perfect for chasing fish, or dodging two giggling kids."

Jack puffed his chest out. "I want to swim like that."

The box glowed brighter. "Then follow the water. There's more to see."

The sandbar melted away, and a whole blue world opened in front of them, crowded with shapes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Five Hundred Kinds
chapters.text:
The blue world was busy. Shapes glided past in every size.

"There's so many!" Ellie said, spinning to see them all.

"More than **500 different kinds** of sharks swim in the ocean," the box said. "Big ones, small ones, every kind you can imagine."

A shadow passed overhead, blocking the sun like a cloud. Jack looked up and gasped. A shark the size of a school bus drifted by, mouth wide open.

"That's the whale shark," the box said. "The biggest fish in the whole sea, over **40 feet** long."

"It's going to eat us!" Ellie squeaked, clapping a hand over her mouth.

"It only eats tiny floating bits of food called **plankton**," the box said. "Too small to see. You two are far too big and wiggly for its taste."

Jack counted the spots along its side, using his fingers like a scoreboard. "That's one giant, gentle vacuum cleaner."

A streak of silver shot by so fast it left bubbles behind.

"Whoa! Was that even a shark?" Jack shouted.

"The shortfin mako," said the box. "Fastest shark there is."

"I bet I could race it," Jack said, puffing up again.

"You would lose," Ellie said sweetly, and he couldn't argue.

A tiny shark no bigger than a pencil nibbled a round bite out of something far bigger than itself, then zipped off.

"That one takes cookie-shaped bites out of giants," the box explained. "Don't worry — the giants are fine."

"Some of these whale sharks," the box added, "live to be **100 years old**, or even more."

Ellie's eyes went huge. "Older than Grandpa?"

"Maybe," said the box.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tooth That Started It All
chapters.text:
The water around them went dark and swirly, like stirring chocolate milk.

"Where are we going now?" Ellie asked, holding tight to Jack's hand.

"Back," the box said. "Long, long back. Before there were any dinosaurs at all."

Jack's mouth fell open. "Sharks are older than dinosaurs?"

"Sharks have swum in the ocean for more than **400 million years**," the box said.

Something huge moved in the murk ahead, bigger than the whale shark, with a mouth full of teeth like knives.

"That's megalodon," the box said. "The biggest shark that ever lived."

Ellie shrank back against Jack. "Is it going to find us?"

"It can't," the box said gently. "Megalodon isn't around anymore. It's **extinct** — that just means every single one of them is gone now."

Jack reached into his pocket and pulled out his smooth gray rock, the one shaped like a tooth.

"Is this one of its teeth?" he asked.

The box glowed over the rock. "Close! Real megalodon teeth were as long as a hand. We only know about megalodon from teeth like that, turned hard as stone over millions of years. We call those **fossils**. Soft parts like cartilage almost never last that long."

Jack held his rock up next to the shadowy shark shape, just to compare. Nowhere close in size.

"Good thing," he said. "Mine fits in my pocket."

Ellie peeked out from behind him, curiosity beating her worry. "Can we see it, just a little longer?"

The giant shape faded into the dark water, gone as quickly as it came. Nothing to be scared of after all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: New Teeth Forever
chapters.text:
The water brightened again. A sleek shark drifted by, mouth slightly open.

"Look!" Jack said. "One of its teeth just fell out!"

A tiny white tooth spiraled down through the water. But the shark's smile looked just as full as before.

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," the box said. "Thousands over a whole lifetime. New ones are already lined up behind, ready to move forward."

"Like a conveyor belt of teeth," Jack said.

"Exactly like that," said the box.

Ellie watched the shark's skin catch the sunlight, sparkly and rough-looking. "Is it slimy?"

"Not slimy at all," the box said. "Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps. It feels rough, like sandpaper, and helps the shark slide through water smoothly."

"Tooth-shaped bumps, everywhere?" Ellie wrinkled her nose. "Weird and cool."

"Weird and cool," Jack agreed, "is basically every shark so far."

The shark swam off, trailing a little sparkle behind it, like it had been dusted in glitter. Ellie decided that part, at least, was definitely a little bit mermaid.

"Everything in the ocean is a little bit mermaid if you squint," Jack told her, and she threw a handful of water at him for that.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Secret Senses
chapters.text:
A strange shape rounded the reef ahead — a shark with a head shaped like a hammer, flat and wide.

"What happened to its face?" Ellie burst out laughing.

"That's a hammerhead," the box said. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

"Like having eyes in the back of your head," Jack said. "Mom always says she has those."

The hammerhead swung its head side to side, scanning the sand below.

"It's hunting," the box said. "Sharks can feel tiny sparks of electricity that every animal makes, even ones hiding under the sand. Little jelly-filled dots on their snouts pick up the sparks, like a secret sense."

Jack's eyes lit up. "Let's play hide and seek! I bet I can find something hiding, using my eyes instead of sparks."

He scanned the sandy bottom hard, the way the hammerhead had, and spotted a flat fish buried under a thin layer of sand, only its eyes poking out.

"Found one!" he shouted.

"Nicely spotted," the box said. "Not bad, for a kid without sparks."

Ellie tried next and found a shrimp peeking from a shell. "I found one too!"

The hammerhead swept past them, unbothered, and melted into the blue the way all the sharks seemed to do — never any rush, never any trouble.
chapters.shout_line: I BET I CAN FIND IT!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Walking, Resting, and Rivers
chapters.text:
The water grew shallow, warm, and full of coral.

Something small scuttled across the reef using its fins like little paddle feet.

"Is that shark... walking?" Ellie gasped.

"The epaulette shark can do that," the box said. "It walks right over the reef, even in tide pools, and can go for hours with barely any air in the water around it."

Jack watched it waddle along. "That is the silliest, best thing I've seen all day."

Further along, a wide flat shark lay completely still on the sand.

"Is it sleeping? Is it okay?" Ellie asked, worried.

"It's a nurse shark," the box said. "It can pump water straight over its gills while resting. It doesn't have to swim to breathe, so it just naps right there."

"Lucky," Jack said. "I have to breathe standing up, lying down, running — it never stops."

The water around them began to taste different, less salty.

"That's strange," Jack said. "Are we near a river?"

"Good nose," the box said. "Bull sharks can live in salty ocean water or fresh river water. Some have even been found far upriver, way past where the ocean ends."

Ellie looked around at the muddy water, a little nervous, then remembered the box's words. "No rushing, no trouble," she whispered to herself, and relaxed.

"That's right," the box said warmly. "Just a shark, going about its day."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
The water cleared into a sunny, shallow bay. A woman in an old-fashioned diving mask swam alongside a shark, calm as anything, like old friends out for a walk.

"Who is that?" Jack asked.

"**Eugenie Clark**," the box said. "People called her the **Shark Lady**. She spent years studying sharks and showed the whole world that sharks are curious, and can even learn tricks."

The shark nudged a floating target with its nose, the way a dog might nudge a hand, and Eugenie Clark gave a small, pleased nod.

Jack had been waiting the whole trip to ask the question he always wondered about. "Do sharks bite people a lot?"

"Hardly ever," Eugenie Clark said, turning toward them. "People getting hurt by sharks is extremely rare. Far more sharks get hurt by people than the other way around."

"Sharks are the boss of the ocean," the box added. "Scientists call that an **apex predator** — top of the food chain. They help keep everything else in the sea balanced, by eating just enough and no more."

Ellie watched the shark circle back for another nudge. "It wants to play again."

"Then give it a trick," Eugenie Clark said, eyes twinkling.

Ellie blew a slow ring of bubbles, round as a bracelet. The shark drifted straight through the middle of it, curious as a puppy, never once coming close enough to touch.

"It copied me!" Ellie squealed.

Jack grinned at his sister. "Even the sharks think you're funny."

"Fins up," the box called softly. "Time to go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Box
chapters.text:
The bay rippled, folded, and turned to mist.

Jack and Ellie landed with a soft thump, right back on their bedroom floor, between their two beds.

The wooden box sat closed, like always, Jack's tooth-shaped rock and Ellie's curled black shell both back inside.

"Wait," Ellie said, picking her shell up carefully. "The box called this a purse. Why?"

"People call it a **mermaid's purse**," the box said, voice fading quieter now. "It's really an egg case. Some baby sharks hatch out of cases exactly like that one."

Ellie stared at the shell like she had never really looked at it before. "A baby shark used to live in here?"

"Maybe," the box said. "Isn't that the best kind of purse?"

Jack picked up his own rock, turning it over. It looked smaller now, after seeing a real megalodon. But he liked it just the same.

"Still my favorite rock," he said.

"Still my favorite purse," Ellie said, hugging it to her chest.

The box dimmed down to nothing, just an old wooden box again, waiting for the next treasure.

Ellie yawned enormously. Jack yawned right back on purpose, which made her laugh one last time.

They climbed into their own beds, treasures tucked safely under their pillows.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Fins up, and swim well.

story.title: Nora and the Glowing Tessera of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey into a buried Roman city, piece by piece.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Stepping Into Pompeii
chapters.text:
Nora sat on her bedroom carpet, way past bedtime. Tiny colored tiles were spread around her knees.

She was building a mosaic — a picture made of little tile pieces called tesserae, pressed close together like puzzle pieces.

One tile would not fit anywhere. It was round and gold, and warm, like a mug of warm milk.

Nora pushed it into the last empty gap anyway.

The tile began to hum. Then it glowed so bright the whole carpet turned gold. WHOOOOSH! The glow lifted Nora up and set her down on a sunny stone street.

"Where am I?" she whispered.

"Pompeii," hummed the warm tile, still tucked in her hand. "A real Roman town, near where the city of Naples stands today."

Nora looked down. The street had flat stones laid across it, with gaps in between.

"Why are there gaps?" she asked.

"Look closer," hummed the tile.

Nora crouched. A cart rolled by, its wheels fitting right through the gaps, while people hopped across the stones without getting their feet wet.

"They're stepping stones!" she said. "So people stay dry, but carts can still get through!"

"Exactly right," said the tile. "This was a busy town — about **eleven to fifteen thousand people**, with shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples."

Nora grinned and hopped stone to stone like a game of hopscotch.

"Which way first?" she asked.

She sniffed the air. Something smelled like warm bread.

"You choose," said the tile.

"This way!" Nora said, following her nose.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Baker's Secret
chapters.text:
The bread smell led Nora to a stone oven, round and dark like a cave.

She peeked inside — and gasped.

A whole loaf of bread sat there, still shaped in neat little sections, like a pie ready to be cut.

"Is that... old bread?" Nora asked.

"Very old," said the tile. "When the mountain nearby blew up, ash covered this town so fast it froze everything in place — paintings on walls, writing on buildings, and this very loaf, still marked by its baker."

Nora leaned in close. The loaf still had little lines pressed across the top, like a baker's signature.

"It's like time pressed pause," she said.

"Piece by piece, that's how we learn it," said the tile.

Nora noticed something else: painted words on the bakery wall, bright red letters.

"What's that say?" she asked.

"People here painted messages right on their walls," said the tile. "Ads for shops, even notes about elections. It's like an ancient bulletin board."

Nora laughed. "Walls that talk!"

She heard a trickling sound further down the street.

"What's that?" she asked.

"Only one way to find out," said the tile.

Nora followed the sound, tile glowing warm in her palm.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water for Everyone
chapters.text:
The trickling sound led Nora to a stone fountain, water bubbling from a carved spout.

"People drank from here?" Nora asked.

"They did," said the tile. "Pompeii had an advanced water system — pipes made of lead, carrying water all around town to fountains like this one."

Nora traced a pipe with her finger, following it along the wall.

"Where does it go?" she asked.

"Follow it and see," said the tile.

Nora walked the pipe's path past a bathhouse, where steam still seemed to hang in the air, all the way to another fountain two streets over.

"It goes everywhere!" she said. "Like the town's own water trick."

"Just like that," said the tile. "Everyone could get water nearby, without walking far."

Nora cupped her hands near the spout, careful not to touch the old stone too hard.

"Clever town," she said.

A distant roar of a crowd echoed from somewhere close by.

"What's making that noise?" Nora asked, eyes wide.

"Let's find out," said the tile.

Nora followed the sound, tile bouncing gently in her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Stone Circle
chapters.text:
The roaring led Nora to a huge oval building made of stone, rows and rows of seats curving around a sandy floor.

"Whoa," Nora breathed. "It's like a giant bowl!"

"An amphitheater," said the tile. "A big open theater, built around **70 BC** — one of the oldest ones we know about."

"What happened here?" Nora asked.

"Gladiator games," said the tile. "People came from all around to watch."

Nora counted the rows of seats, tracing them with her finger. "One, two, three... so many people could fit!"

"Thousands," agreed the tile.

Nora climbed a few steps and sat where an ancient Roman might have sat, imagining the crowd cheering.

"I bet it was loud," she said.

"Loud enough to hear across town," said the tile.

Nora spotted something glinting on the ground near the entrance — tiny colored squares, just like her mosaic tiles at home.

"Tessera!" she said. "Those are just like you!"

"Go on," hummed the tile. "Follow the pattern."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Tiny Tiles, Big Pictures
chapters.text:
Nora knelt by the colorful squares. They formed a floor picture — a swirling wave pattern, made entirely of tiny stone tiles.

"It's a mosaic!" she said. "Just like mine, but on the ground!"

"People here loved mosaics too," said the tile. "And bigger paintings, called frescoes, right on the walls."

Nora stepped into a nearby villa. Painted figures covered the walls — people in red robes, caught mid-movement, frozen like a photograph.

"What are they doing?" Nora asked.

"Nobody is fully sure," said the tile. "This is called the Villa of the Mysteries. The paintings may show a secret ceremony. We can guess, but we can't say for certain."

"A mystery inside a mystery," Nora said, grinning.

She traced the swirl pattern on the floor with her finger, matching colors like she did at home.

"Blue, then gold, then blue again," she said. "I can see the pattern!"

"You found it," said the tile, glowing warmer. "Piece by piece, that's how pictures — and history — come together."

Outside, the sky had gone a strange, dusty orange.

"That's new," Nora said, looking up.

"Let's go somewhere safe to watch," said the tile.
chapters.shout_line: IT'S A MYSTERY INSIDE A MYSTERY!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Day the Mountain Woke
chapters.text:
The tile's glow lifted Nora up a grassy hill, far across the water from the town, just like a real hill where someone once stood long ago.

From here, Pompeii looked small and far away. Safe.

"On **August 24th, in the year 79**, the mountain called Vesuvius woke up," said the tile. "It sent ash and rock high into the sky."

Nora watched a gray cloud rise far off, shaped like an umbrella.

"Did people see it coming?" she asked.

"A young man named Pliny the Younger watched from right where you're standing," said the tile. "He wrote two letters describing everything he saw. He was so careful that scientists still call this kind of big, sudden eruption a Plinian eruption, after him."

"Like a reporter," Nora said.

"Exactly like one," said the tile.

The ash drifted down over Pompeii, piling up fast — eventually as much as **thirteen to twenty feet deep**, burying streets, ovens, and mosaics alike.

Nora watched quietly from the safe hilltop.

"That's why everything stayed just the way it was," she said softly. "The ash tucked it all in, like a blanket."

"A very good way to put it," said the tile.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Buried Treasure, Found Again
chapters.text:
The gray cloud faded. Years and years blinked by in a blur of gold light.

"What happened next?" Nora asked.

"For almost **1,700 years**, nobody remembered Pompeii was even there," said the tile. "Until **1748**, when workers digging in a field found old stone walls underground."

Nora's eyes went wide. "They just... found a whole city?"

"Piece by piece," said the tile. "History detectives called archaeologists have been carefully digging ever since. They dig slowly, so nothing gets broken."

"Is it all dug up now?" Nora asked.

"Not even close," said the tile. "Only about two-thirds of the town has been uncovered. People are still finding new paintings today."

Nora looked back toward the hill where the town used to be. "So there's more waiting?"

"Always more," said the tile. "And the mountain is still there too — still a real volcano. Scientists watch it closely now, like checking on a sleepy giant, just to be safe."

"That's smart," Nora said.

The tile hummed softer. "Time to go home, little mosaic-maker."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The gold light swept around Nora again. WHOOOOSH!

She landed back on her bedroom carpet, tiles scattered just as before.

But one thing was different.

The mosaic she'd been building now had a finished swirl pattern in the middle — blue, then gold, then blue again, exactly like the floor in Pompeii.

"Did I do that?" Nora whispered.

The gold tile in her hand gave one last warm pulse, then settled, cool and quiet, perfectly fitted into its gap.

Nora smiled and pulled her blanket up to her chin.

Somewhere, under ash a very long time ago, a whole town had waited quietly to be found again.

Now it was her turn to wait — for tomorrow, and whatever the little gold tile wanted to show her next.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Piece by piece!

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real Roman town near where the city of **Naples** is today.
The streets had **stepping stones** so people could cross without wet feet, with gaps for cart wheels.
A whole **loaf of bread** was found still shaped by its baker, perfectly preserved.
The ash fell so fast it **froze everyday things in place** — paintings, writing, even bread.
Pompeii had **pipes carrying water** all around town to public fountains.
The town's big **amphitheater** was built around **70 BC**, one of the oldest ever found.
Colorful wall paintings called **frescoes**, including the mysterious ones in the **Villa of the Mysteries**, still cover some walls.
A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption and wrote detailed letters about it — scientists still call this kind of eruption a **Plinian eruption** after him.
The volcano **Vesuvius** erupted on **August 24, in the year 79**.
Ash and rock buried the town as much as **thirteen to twenty feet deep**.
Pompeii was forgotten for almost **1,700 years**, until workers found old walls in **1748**.
**Vesuvius is still a real volcano today**, and scientists keep a close watch on it.

story.title: Maya and the Star-Sailing Boat
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the real race to space.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Puddle
chapters.text:
It had been three whole nights since Barnacle waved his flipper from the water, right after the last rivet went in on that hummy bridge. Maya was still drawing boats about it.

She lay on her bedroom floor with her best green crayon, drawing a little paper boat on thick paper. Outside her window, one rain boot sat on the sill, half full of rainwater. The water began to glow, soft and green, like a nightlight under the sea.

**POP!** A whiskery nose popped out of the boot. It was Barnacle the harbour seal, dripping and grinning.

"All aboard, Maya," he said. "Tonight we're not going under the waves. We're going up, up, past the clouds, to the stars."

"Boats don't fly," said Maya, giggling.

"This one might," said Barnacle, and he tapped her paper boat with one flipper.

The paper boat shivered, then grew warm under her hands. The glow from the puddle poured into it like water filling a cup. Maya climbed aboard, and Barnacle hopped up beside her.

**WHOOOOSH!** The little boat shot out the window into a sky gone sparkly and dark, sailing on starlight the way it once sailed on bathwater.

They landed with a soft bump on a round, quiet little moon of rock. Below them, a beach-ball-sized silver ball floated past, beeping.

"What is THAT noise?" asked Maya, cupping her ears.

"That little ball is called **Sputnik 1**," said Barnacle. "On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union — that's a country, part of what's now Russia — sent it zooming around Earth. It was the very first machine ever to circle our whole planet from space, which is called going into **orbit**."

Maya watched it spin. "It's not much bigger than a beach ball!"

"Exactly right," said Barnacle. "About as wide as your bicycle is long. And that beep you hear? People all over the world could catch it on their ordinary radios at home."

Maya pressed her ear near the glow as it passed. **BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.** She grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

"It sounds like a tiny robot saying hello," she said.

"Seal of approval," said Barnacle, which was not even close to a real joke, but Maya laughed anyway.

She reached out and gave the little silver ball a gentle wave as it sailed by, and it beeped once more, almost like it waved back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Brave Ride
chapters.text:
A bark echoed across the dark, and Maya sat up straight. "Was that a DOG? In space?"

"Good ears," said Barnacle, steering the little paper boat closer to a second silver capsule — that's the little round pod something rides inside — drifting by. "Just one month after Sputnik 1, on **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**. Inside rode a small dog named **Laika**."

"She was the first living creature ever to circle the Earth from way up here," Barnacle went on.

Maya pressed her nose to the glowing window of their boat, hoping for a glimpse. "Was she scared?"

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle gently. "But people everywhere loved her for it. She became famous all around the world."

Maya thought about her own dog snoring at the end of her bed and felt a soft little ache for brave Laika, orbiting so far from home.

Then a bright building rose up ahead of them, all glass and antennas, humming with excitement.

"What's THIS place?" Maya asked, already reaching for her crayon to sketch its tall tower.

"That excitement you hear?" said Barnacle. "Sputnik gave the United States such a surprise that they built a brand-new space team. It started working on **October 1, 1958**. They called it **NASA**."

Maya drew a quick picture of the tower, adding little sparks around it. "Like a new team getting ready for a big race," she said.

"Precisely," said Barnacle, bobbing his whiskers proudly. "Fin-tastic drawing, by the way."

Maya rolled her eyes at the pun, but she tucked the drawing into her boat's little paper pocket anyway, right next to her sketch of Sputnik.

"Two down," she said, patting her growing stack of drawings like a captain checking her log. "Where next, Barnacle?"

"Wherever the stars point us," said Barnacle, and the little boat tilted upward again, chasing a bright streak of light across the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The First Riders
chapters.text:
The boat rocked gently, and Maya spotted two round capsules racing side by side, trailing fire.

"Someone's INSIDE those?" she asked, eyes wide.

"People, this time," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, a Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the very first human being to fly in space. He circled Earth once, in about **108 minutes** — barely longer than your favorite movie."

"That's so fast!" said Maya. "What do you call a space pilot from Russia?"

"A **cosmonaut**," said Barnacle. "That's simply their word for astronaut."

Maya rolled the word around in her mouth. "Cosmonaut," she said again, liking the sound of it.

The second capsule zoomed past them, trailing a little American flag.

"And that one?" Maya asked, pointing.

"Just a few weeks later, on **May 5, 1961**," said Barnacle, "an American named **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, riding a capsule called **Freedom 7**. His ride was shorter and didn't circle the whole planet, but up he went all the same."

Maya leaned way out over the edge of their little boat, which made Barnacle hum a worried note, though he never rushed her back.

"Careful now," he said softly, and waited while she looked her fill before settling back down on her own.

"Two firsts in one chapter," Maya said, counting on her fingers. "First person ever, and first American."

"You're keeping very good count," said Barnacle.

Maya grabbed her crayon and sketched two little capsules racing side by side, with a tiny flag on one, and underneath she wrote, in wobbly letters, FIRST AND FIRST.

"That's going right next to Laika," she said, tucking it away.

Barnacle chuckled. "At this rate, Maya, you'll run out of paper before we run out of sky."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Dare and a Flight
chapters.text:
A booming voice rolled across the stars like far-off thunder, and Maya jumped.

"Who's SHOUTING?" she asked.

"Just a president, making a promise," said Barnacle, floating them closer to a glowing patch of starlight shaped almost like a podium. "On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** dared his whole country to land someone on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the end of that decade — that's ten years."

Maya looked up at the pale, round Moon glowing above them. "That's a BIG dare," she said.

"The biggest," agreed Barnacle.

They sailed on, and soon a third capsule zipped past, this one painted with a small flower on its side.

"Who's flying THAT one?" Maya asked, already reaching for her crayon.

"That's **Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting Earth aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6**."

"Was she a pilot before, like Gagarin?" Maya asked.

"She'd worked in a factory," said Barnacle, "then trained hard to earn her seat among the stars."

Maya grinned and quickly sketched a girl in a round helmet, flying past a little flower. "She worked hard and then she flew," Maya said. "That's like practicing swimming until you finally win the race."

"A very fine comparison," said Barnacle.

Maya tucked her newest drawing in with the others, now four pictures deep. She patted the stack like a treasure chest.

"At this rate," she said, echoing Barnacle from before, "I'll need a bigger boat."

"Or a bigger ocean of stars," said Barnacle, and steered them onward into the glittering dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Floating Free
chapters.text:
Something small and round floated right past their little boat's window, trailing a long silver cord.

"Is that a PERSON?" Maya gasped, nose pressed to the glow.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**,” said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he became the first person ever to leave his spacecraft and float outside it, all alone in his space suit. That's called a **spacewalk**. He floated out there for about **ten minutes**."

Maya watched the tiny figure drift, turning slow and weightless, tethered only by that long cord.

"Wasn't he scared he'd float away forever?" she asked, her voice small.

"That cord kept him tied safely to his ship the whole time," said Barnacle gently. "And after ten minutes, he floated right back inside, safe and sound."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding, and smiled.

"I want to try floating," she said, and before Barnacle could answer, she unbuckled her little paper seatbelt and pushed gently off the bench.

**WHOOOSH.** Maya drifted up, slow as a bubble, her hair floating around her face like seaweed.

"Just like swimming," she laughed, "except there's no water to push against!"

"Better hold my flipper," said Barnacle, "unless you'd like to float all the way to the Moon without me."

Maya grabbed his flipper, giggling, and he towed her gently back down to the bench, patient as ever, not the littlest bit rushed.

"Thanks, Barnacle," she said, settling back in.

"Anytime,” he said. "Though I'll admit, out here, I'm a bit more at home in the water."

Maya patted the little paper boat beneath them. "Me too," she agreed. "But this is pretty great, too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Whole Blue Marble
chapters.text:
Their boat crested a curve of dark sky, and suddenly Maya gasped so loud Barnacle nearly dropped his pun.

"BARNACLE. Look."

There, hanging in the blackness above the gray edge of the Moon, hung a small blue and white ball, glowing soft as a nightlight.

"That's home," said Barnacle quietly. "The whole Earth, from way out here."

"It's so SMALL," Maya whispered.

"In **December 1968**, three astronauts aboard **Apollo 8** were the first people ever to fly all the way around the Moon," said Barnacle. "One of them, **William Anders**, looked back and saw exactly what you're seeing now. He snapped a photo of it rising over the Moon's edge."

"What did he call it?" Maya asked.

"Earthrise," said Barnacle.

Maya reached for her crayon without even looking, her eyes still fixed on the little blue ball. She drew it quickly: a small round Earth, peeking up over a gray curve of Moon.

"It looks so soft," she said. "Like it could fit in my hand."

"That's rather the point of the photo," said Barnacle. "It reminded everyone down there just how small and precious home really is."

Maya held her drawing up next to the real thing, comparing them carefully, tongue poking out in concentration.

"Close enough," she decided, satisfied, and tucked it in with the others.

"You know," said Barnacle, "out of everyone who's ever lived, only a tiny few have seen that sight with their own eyes."

Maya looked at her drawing one more time before folding it carefully.

"Then I'm glad I got to see it too," she said. "Even if it's just from a paper boat."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A tall, silver tower rose ahead of them, taller than anything Maya had ever seen, trailing smoke and fire at its base.

"What IS that?" she breathed.

"A rocket called the **Saturn V**,” said Barnacle. "It stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty. Two rocket masterminds helped make rockets like it possible: an American named **Wernher von Braun**, who led the team that built it, and a Soviet genius named **Sergei Korolev**, whose name was kept secret by his own country until after he died in **1966**."

"A SECRET genius?" said Maya, eyes huge. "Like a superhero with a mask?"

"A bit like that," Barnacle agreed, chuckling.

The rocket's top glowed, and a tiny ladder appeared, leading down onto gray, dusty ground.

"On **July 20, 1969**, astronaut **Neil Armstrong** climbed down that very kind of ladder and became the first person to ever walk on the Moon," said Barnacle. "He said it was a giant leap for everyone back home."

Maya squinted at the dusty gray ground below. "Can I try a leap too?" she asked.

"Go ahead," said Barnacle, "the Moon won't mind."

Maya hopped down from the boat and bounced, light as a feather in the low gravity, landing with a soft little **THUD** of moon dust.

"Buzz Aldrin walked here too, right beside Armstrong," said Barnacle, "while their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, circled alone above in their ship, named **Columbia**, waiting to bring everyone home."

"That's a big job, waiting all by yourself," Maya said thoughtfully.

"The biggest kind of patient," said Barnacle.

Maya took one more giant bounce across the dust, laughing the whole way, then scrambled back aboard, breathless and grinning, moon dust still on her shoes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Handshake and the Way Home
chapters.text:
Their little boat shuddered suddenly, and a warning light blinked on the dashboard.

"Uh oh," said Maya. "Is something WRONG?"

"Something went wrong once, for real astronauts," said Barnacle calmly. "In **1970**, a tank aboard **Apollo 13** had trouble on the way to the Moon. But the crew and their helpers on the ground worked together and fixed things up, and everyone made it safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "That's good," she said. "I'm glad they figured it out."

"So am I," said Barnacle, patting her shoulder with one flipper.

Their own little warning light blinked off on its own, and the boat steadied again, sailing smooth.

Ahead, two spacecraft drifted toward each other, slow and careful, like two puzzle pieces lining up.

"On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship met up in orbit and **docked** together," said Barnacle. "That means they joined up, nose to nose. The astronauts and cosmonauts climbed through and shook hands."

Maya watched the two crews shake hands through the glow, grinning at each other like old friends.

"After all that racing," she said, "they just... shook hands?"

"The whole race ended in a handshake," said Barnacle. "Sometimes that's the very best finish line."

Maya smiled and leaned her head on Barnacle's warm, damp shoulder, suddenly sleepy, her stack of drawings held tight in her lap.

"All aboard for home, then," said Barnacle softly, and the little paper boat turned, gliding back down through the glittering dark.

**SPLOOSH.** They landed right back in the rain boot on her windowsill, gentle as a bath.

Maya climbed into bed, her stack of space drawings fanned out on the carpet below: Sputnik, Laika, Gagarin, Tereshkova, Leonov, Earthrise, the giant leap, and the handshake.

Barnacle's nose poked once more from the glowing puddle. "Goodnight, Maya," he said. "Play well, and dream of stars."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Play well, and dream of stars.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, a silver ball about the size of a beach ball, which beeped as it circled Earth.
On **November 3, 1957**, a brave little dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to circle the Earth from space.
The surprise of Sputnik led the United States to start a new space team called **NASA**, which began working on **October 1, 1958**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person ever to fly in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, riding a capsule called **Freedom 7**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** dared his country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely within ten years.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman to fly in space, orbiting Earth aboard **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his spacecraft, staying out there for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first people to fly around the Moon, and one of them snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap.
While Armstrong and **Buzz Aldrin** walked on the Moon, their crewmate **Michael Collins** circled alone above in their ship, **Columbia**.
In **1970**, trouble with a tank aboard **Apollo 13** was fixed by the crew and their helpers, and everyone made it home safely.
On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship joined up in space, and their crews climbed through and shook hands.

new_recurring.name: The S.S. Doodle
new_recurring.rule: A paper boat Maya draws herself; it grows warm and glowing when touched by starlight or Barnacle's magic, and carries her and Barnacle wherever the night's adventure needs to go. It always returns her home gently, landing with a soft…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Maya fell asleep with eight space drawings fanned across her carpet, from Sputnik to the handshake, while Barnacle slipped back beneath the glow of her rain-boot puddle, saying goodnight.

editor_notes: Fix the three factual slips. Have Pliny watching from across the bay, with Cinder explaining he wrote it all down years later in letters to a friend. Say Tambora's ash and invisible gas made a haze that dimmed the sun. Change Olympus Mons to 'about two and a half Everests'.

Pay off the mystery and Zara's rock love together. Let Zara discover at Kilauea or Surtsey that Cinder's holes are frozen gas bubbles, so she identifies what kind of rock Cinder is. Hint at how Cinder got into her collection. This delivers the 'mysterious' tone and gives the tour a spine.
