story.title: Zara and the Rock That Remembered Fire
story.subtitle: A warm little stone takes Zara all the way around the world — and all the way to Mars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Hummed
chapters.text:
Zara knelt on her bedroom rug, rocks spread out like stars around her knees. She had quartz. She had granite. She had a shiny chunk of pyrite that looked just like gold.

Every night before bed, she lined her rocks up and gave each one a job. Tonight, there was a new rock in the pile. She did not remember picking it up. It was dark and bumpy, with tiny holes all over, like a sponge made of stone.

"Where did you come from?" Zara whispered.

The rock answered. It hummed, soft and low, and warm orange light leaked out between its holes.

Zara did not scream. She leaned closer instead, because that is exactly what a rock collector does.

A crack split open along the rock's side, glowing like a tiny mouth. "Hello," said a small, crackly voice. "I'm Cinder."

"You're a talking rock," Zara said.

"I'm a **volcano** rock," said Cinder. "A volcano is an opening in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gas sneak out from deep underground."

Zara turned Cinder over in her hands. "What's the melted rock called?"

"Down under the ground, we call it **magma**," Cinder said. "The second it bubbles up and spills outside, it gets a brand new name. We call it **lava**."

Zara grinned. Two names for one gooey rock. That was almost as good as two names for one quartz crystal.

"Want to see where I come from?" Cinder asked.

Zara did not need to be asked twice. She pressed her thumb into the warm crack, the way she'd press a key into a lock.

The crack split wider. Orange light poured across the rug like spilled juice. A soft **WHOOOOSH** of warm wind filled the room, and the rug, the quartz, the pyrite, all of it melted away into orange mist.

When the mist cleared, Zara was standing somewhere hot, with tiny ash freckles sprinkled clean across her pajamas.

She brushed one off her nose and laughed. "I think I just got cooler," she said. "I mean — warmer."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Horseshoe of Fire
chapters.text:
Zara looked down — actually down, past her own sneakers — and gasped. She was floating above a giant glowing map of the whole entire world.

Little orange dots freckled the map, mostly curling around one big ocean in a long, bent line.

"That shape," Zara said, tracing it with her finger. "It's like a horseshoe!"

"Good eye," said Cinder, glowing brighter, which Zara had already learned meant she'd gotten something right. "People call it the **Ring of Fire**. It's a horseshoe-shaped belt that wraps around the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about **75%** of every active volcano on Earth — every volcano that can still erupt."

"Why there, though?" Zara asked. "Why not just everywhere?"

"Earth's outside shell, its **crust**, isn't one solid piece," Cinder explained. "It's cracked into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**. They float on hot, slow-moving rock underneath. Where two plates push together, pull apart, or scrape past each other, that's where volcanoes love to pop up."

Zara squinted at the map. One country, shaped like a scatter of stepping stones, glowed brighter than every other spot.

"That one," she said, pointing. "It's the brightest. I bet it has the most volcanoes of anybody."

"You'd win that bet," said Cinder. "That's **Indonesia**. It has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

Zara beamed, proud of her guess. She reached out and touched the glowing dot, and it bloomed under her finger like a struck match.

"Can we go somewhere?" she asked. "Somewhere I can actually watch lava move?"

Cinder's crack curved, almost like a smile. "Pick a dot, Zara."

Zara scanned the whole map slowly. Hawaii, a little chain of islands, glowed a soft, steady orange — not angry, just warm, like a nightlight left on for her.

"That one," Zara decided. "It looks friendly."

"Good choice," said Cinder. "Hold on to your freckles."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Shield in the Sea
chapters.text:
The world melted again, and this time Zara landed on warm black rock, wide and flat as a pancake, stretching farther than she could see.

A river of orange ran slow across it, thick as honey, glowing wherever it moved.

"Lava," Zara breathed. "Real actual lava."

"This is **Kilauea**," said Cinder. "One of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It has been erupting on and off for decades, sometimes for years without ever really stopping."

Zara studied the mountain itself, and something seemed off to her. "It's not pointy," she said. "Volcanoes are supposed to look like triangles. This one's all wide and flat, like a shield."

"That's exactly what it's called," said Cinder, glowing proudly. "A **shield volcano** — wide, with gentle slopes, because its lava is thin and runny and spreads out flat. Some volcanoes, like Mount Fuji in Japan, are tall and steep instead, shaped more like a pointy party hat. Different lava makes a different shape."

Zara tucked that fact away, the way she tucked away a good rock fact at school.

"Why is it even here, though?" she asked. "Hawaii wasn't on your horseshoe map at all."

"Sharp thinking," said Cinder. "Hawaii doesn't sit on the edge of a plate. It sits over a **hotspot** — a patch of extra-hot rock rising up from deep inside the Earth. The hotspot stays in one place, while the plate slides slowly over the top of it."

Zara cupped her hands near the lava river, close enough to feel its heat, not close enough to touch it. She already knew better than that, same as she knew better than to touch a hot stove.

"Is there a biggest one?" she asked.

"Right next door," said Cinder. "**Mauna Loa**. It's Earth's largest active volcano, over **4,000 meters** tall — so tall, its top actually pokes up through the clouds."

Zara tipped her head all the way back, searching for a cloud-wrapped peak somewhere above her. "That's bigger than every rock I own put together."

"Only by a little," said Cinder, and Zara laughed so hard she nearly dropped her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Letters Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The warm island melted into cool gray. Zara landed on a hillside looking out over a bay, and across the water stood a tall mountain, puffing a thin gray feather into the sky.

"That one looks grumpy," Zara said.

"That's **Vesuvius**," said Cinder. "Back in the year **79**, it erupted so hard that it buried two whole Roman towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, under ash, thick and heavy."

Zara picked up a pinch of gray dust from the ground and let it fall through her fingers like flour. "It just buried them? Like a blanket?"

"Like a very thick, very fast blanket," Cinder agreed.

Down by the water, Zara spotted a man with a scroll, writing as fast as his hand could go, his eyes fixed on the smoking mountain.

"Who's that?" she asked.

"**Pliny the Younger**," said Cinder. "A Roman writer. He watched the whole eruption from right over there, safely across the bay, and wrote down everything he saw in letters. He described it so well that scientists still use his words today to describe this same fiery kind of eruption."

Zara watched him write, fascinated. "He just wrote down what he saw?"

"Every bit of it," said Cinder. "Sometimes the bravest thing you can do is pay close attention, and remember it right."

Zara liked that idea a lot. She held up her hand and traced letters in the warm air with one glowing finger, the way Pliny traced his across the scroll, even though her letters floated away like little puffs of smoke.

"I'm writing it down too," she said. "So I remember."

Cinder's crack curved warm, like a small, proud smile. "Then you're doing exactly what he did."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Boom
chapters.text:
Gray turned to blue ocean, and a huge **BOOM** rolled across the water before Zara even spotted the mountain.

She clapped both hands over her ears. "What WAS that?!"

"**Krakatoa**," said Cinder. "Back in **1883**, it erupted with a bang so loud that people heard it about **3,000 miles** away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara lowered her hands slowly, still a little rattled. "Three thousand miles. Is that far?"

"Think of the farthest place you know," said Cinder.

Zara thought of her grandma, who lived clear across the whole country, a long plane ride away. "Like, way past Grandma's house," she said. "Like past Grandma's house a whole bunch of times in a row."

"That's about right," said Cinder.

Zara shouted into the open air, just to test something. "HELLOOOO!" Her voice came back tiny and far away, nothing at all like a real echo.

"See?" she said. "My voice barely makes it to the end of my yard. That volcano made a sound that went practically around the whole world."

"It's still the loudest sound anyone has ever recorded," Cinder said.

Zara grinned, delighted and a little rattled at the same time, the good kind of rattled, like the drop on a rollercoaster.

"That's the loudest fact I've ever heard, too," she said, and then, because it felt exactly right, she cupped her hands and yelled it to the water.

Somewhere far off, the ocean seemed to rumble back in agreement, small and friendly this time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Snow in Summer
chapters.text:
The ocean faded into gray fields, and ash began drifting down from the sky like slow, dirty snow, except the air around Zara stayed warm, not cold at all.

She caught a flake on her palm. It crumbled, soft and light. "This isn't real snow," she said. "It's way too warm for snow."

"It's ash," said Cinder, "from a volcano called **Tambora**, back in **1815**. It was the biggest eruption anyone has ever written down in history. So much ash flew up into the sky that it blocked out sunlight, clear on the other side of the world."

"The other side?" Zara repeated.

"Far away, in Europe and in America, the very next year, **1816**, summer barely showed up at all," said Cinder. "People called it the **Year Without a Summer**. Crops struggled to grow. Snow even fell in months that should have been warm."

Zara held another flake up to the light, turning it slowly, the way she'd turn a brand new crystal to catch the sun.

"One mountain did all that? All the way from here?" she asked.

"One mountain, with enough ash," said Cinder.

Zara frowned, thinking hard. "That doesn't seem fair. All that ash, all that trouble, and nothing good came of it at all?"

"Hang on to that question," said Cinder, her crack glinting like she knew a secret Zara didn't have yet. "Ash isn't only trouble. We'll get there, I promise."

Zara tucked the flake away in her memory, right next to Pliny's letters, a little puzzle still waiting to be solved.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The ash cleared into green forest, and the ground gave one gentle shake under Zara's sneakers.

"Whoa," she said, steadying herself with a hand on a tree. "Is that going to happen again?"

"It already did, a long time ago," said Cinder gently. "No shaking now, I promise. This is **Mount St. Helens**, in the United States. On **May 18, 1980**, the biggest slide of rock and dirt ever recorded came loose and slid right down its side — and the very moment after, the mountain erupted."

Zara looked up at the mountain. Its top looked strangely flat, as if someone had sliced it clean off with a knife.

"It blew about **1,300 feet** right off the summit," Cinder said. "Scientists were studying the mountain up close at the time, trying to understand it better, so they could warn people nearby and help keep everyone safe."

Near the tree line, Zara spotted a little blinking box on a metal stand, its lights flickering in a jumpy pattern.

"What's that doing?" she asked.

"That's how volcano scientists, called **volcanologists**, watch for trouble," said Cinder. "A machine like that one feels tiny earthquakes the ground makes before an eruption starts. Up in the sky, **satellites** — cameras that circle the Earth — watch for the ground slowly swelling, like a bubble about to pop."

Zara studied the blinking lights, then grinned. "It's trying to warn everyone! Like it's saying, get ready!"

"Exactly like that," said Cinder. "That's why fewer people get hurt now than they used to. Volcanoes still surprise us sometimes, but we're much, much better at listening for their warnings."

Zara patted the metal stand gently, the way she'd pat a good, loyal dog. "Keep listening," she told it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Island That Grew
chapters.text:
Green forest melted away into gray ocean once more, waves slapping cold and foamy against black rock, and Zara noticed something strange: a patch of ocean was bubbling like a pot about to boil over.

"Something's under there," she said.

"Watch," said Cinder.

Steam burst up through the waves. Then came rock, black and steaming, hissing loudly the moment it hit the cold water.

"Back in **1963**, near Iceland, an underwater volcano kept erupting and erupting until it built a brand new island, right up out of the sea," said Cinder. "They named it **Surtsey**."

Zara's eyes went wide. "A whole new island, out of nothing?"

"Out of lava, mostly," said Cinder. "Iceland has tons of volcanoes, because it sits right on top of a crack where two giant plates are slowly pulling apart from each other."

Zara watched a fresh chunk of black rock hiss and steam as it cooled in the surf. "I was going to suggest a name," she admitted. "I was going to call it Crystal Island."

"A little late," said Cinder, her crack curving with something like a laugh. "It already has one."

"Fine," Zara sighed, though she was smiling the whole time. "Surtsey's a pretty good name too, I guess."

She watched the island keep growing, bit by steaming bit, and decided that was maybe the strangest, best thing she had ever seen a rock do: grow a whole new piece of ground, right out of the open sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Biggest Volcano of All
chapters.text:
The ocean faded to black, sprinkled all over with stars, and Zara realized she was floating somewhere that wasn't even Earth anymore.

A huge, reddish, bumpy mountain rose up below her, bigger than anything she had seen all night.

"Where ARE we?" she asked.

"**Mars**," said Cinder. "And that is **Olympus Mons**, the biggest volcano anyone has ever found anywhere in space. It's about **13.6 miles** high. That's almost three times taller than Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth."

Zara tried to picture three Mount Everests stacked up like blocks and gave up, dizzy just from thinking about it. "That's not even fair. That's cheating-big."

"Mars has weaker gravity," said Cinder. "Mountains can grow taller there without falling down under their own weight. Lucky mountain."

Zara looked around one more time at everything she had seen that night: the horseshoe map, the wide flat shield, the ash falling warm like summer snow.

"You said ash wasn't only trouble," she said. "You never finished telling me why."

Cinder's glow softened, warm and golden. "Because once ash settles down and breaks apart, it turns into some of the richest, best soil on Earth for growing things. That's why farmers still choose to live near volcanoes, ash and all. The ground always remembers how to grow things again, after."

Zara smiled, her puzzle finally solved. "So the mountain that scares you also feeds you."

"Most of the time, yes," said Cinder. "That's the whole trick of a volcano. Scary and useful, both at once."

The glow around Zara brightened into warm orange mist, familiar now, and the mist melted into the shape of her very own bedroom rug.

Zara blinked. She was home, rocks scattered around her knees exactly where she'd left them. Cinder sat cool and quiet in her palm, its little crack closed, its holes dark again.

She set it down gently among the quartz and the pyrite, right in the very middle, the place of honor.

"Goodnight, volcano rock," she whispered. "Thanks for the trip."

She pulled her blanket up to her chin, her ash freckles long since brushed away, a whole world of fire tucked safe inside one small, bumpy stone.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Shine on, little rock hound.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is an opening in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gas sneak out from deep underground.
Melted rock is called **magma** underground, but the moment it spills out, it becomes **lava**.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean that holds about **75%** of the world's active volcanoes.
Hawaii's volcanoes grow over a **hotspot** — extra-hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth that stays in one place while the land slides slowly above it.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting on and off for decades, making it one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.
**Mount Vesuvius** erupted in the year **79** and buried the Roman towns of **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum** under thick ash.
**Pliny the Younger** watched the Vesuvius eruption from across the bay and wrote it all down in letters, so clearly that scientists still use his words today.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption made a boom so loud it was heard about **3,000 miles** away.
In **1815**, **Mount Tambora** caused the biggest eruption ever recorded, and its ash helped make 1816 the **Year Without a Summer** far away in Europe and America.
On **May 18, 1980**, the biggest slide of rock and dirt ever recorded let loose from the side of **Mount St. Helens**, right before it erupted.
In **1963**, a brand-new island called **Surtsey** rose right up out of the sea near Iceland.
Iceland has so many volcanoes because it sits on a crack where two giant plates are slowly pulling apart.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found anywhere in space — about **13.6 miles** high, nearly three times taller than Mount Everest.
Ash breaks down into rich, healthy soil, which is why many farmers still choose to live near volcanoes.

new_recurring.name: Cinder
new_recurring.rule: A small, bumpy, warm volcanic rock that hums and glows when a child asks a good question or makes a good guess; a crack opens along its side like a tiny glowing mouth and it speaks in a crackly voice; pressing a thumb into the warm crack…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returned to her own bedroom rug and set the now-cool, quiet volcano rock named Cinder in the place of honor at the center of her rock collection, falling asleep with her ash freckles already brushed away.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Time Machine
story.subtitle: One boy, one pixel sprite, and the whole history of video games, before bedtime.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Screen Glows Green (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben lay on his bedroom floor, feet kicking in the air. His tablet glowed in the dark. He was drawing a tiny blocky hero, one pixel at a time. Shirt red. Eyes black. Shoes yellow. It was way past bedtime, but the hero still needed a mustache.

Then the screen flickered. Black. Green. Black again.

Lines of green fuzz swirled across it, like TV snow, but glowing. Ben sat up fast.

"Um. Hello?" he said.

A tiny pixel person popped right out of the tablet. He was blocky and green, with a smile made of three little squares.

"Name's Bit," said the sprite. "Nice mustache, by the way."

Ben blinked. "You're... from my drawing?"

"Nope. From every game ever made," Bit said. "Want to see where games started? Before Minecraft. Before Mario. Before pixels were even a thing."

Ben didn't even think twice. "YES."

The green light swallowed them both. WHOOOOSH.

They landed in a room full of humming machines, each one bigger than a fridge. A round green screen sat on a desk, with two white blobs bouncing back and forth across it.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Bit said. "A machine that draws wiggly lines with light instead of ink."

A man in glasses looked up and grinned. "Want to play tennis?"

"On that?" Ben said.

"In **1958**," the man said, "I'm William Higinbotham. I built this so visitors at my lab wouldn't get bored while they waited around."

Ben grabbed a little knob. He turned it, and his dot on the screen dipped down to meet the ball.

"You just hit it back," Bit said. "That's **Tennis for Two**. The very first video game people played just for fun."

Ben volleyed the ball back and forth, counting his hits out loud. "Six! Seven! Eight!"

"Not bad for your first game ever," Bit said.

"This is the OLDEST video game? It's just two dots!" Ben said.

"Every game starts somewhere," said Bit. "Even Minecraft started as just blocks."

"Fair," said Ben, grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spaceships on a Computer the Size of a Fridge (1962)
chapters.text:
The green light swirled again. WHOOOOSH.

They landed in a room cold as a freezer, full of blinking lights. A machine as big as a closet buzzed in the corner.

"That's a **PDP-1**," Bit said. "A computer so huge it filled a whole room, back when computers were new."

A young man typed fast, grinning at a round screen.

"What are you making?" Ben asked.

"Spaceships," the man said. "I'm Steve Russell. My friends and I are turning this giant computer into a game."

On the screen, two tiny spaceship shapes spun around, shooting little white dots at each other.

Ben leaned closer. "They're fighting! Is that a star in the middle?"

"Good eye," Steve said. "That star pulls your ship toward it. Fly too close, and you'll crash right into it."

Ben grabbed the controls and spun his ship hard, just missing the star.

"WHEW," he said. "That was close."

"In **1962**," Bit said, "Steve and his friends finished **Spacewar!**, one of the very first computer games ever made."

Ben kept dodging the star, grinning the whole time. "It's basically Minecraft, but with lasers and no crafting table."

Bit laughed so hard his pixels wobbled. "Not exactly the same. But I like how you think."

One more spaceship zipped past, and Ben whooped as his pilot looped clear around it.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box and the Bouncing Dot (1972)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. The green light dropped them in a cozy workshop, wires strung everywhere.

A man held up a plain brown box with switches on top, wired to a TV.

"I'm Ralph Baer," he said. "Folks call me the father of video games. Still makes me blush a little."

"This is a **prototype**," Bit explained. "A first try at something new, before it's all finished."

On the TV, two white squares batted a white dot back and forth.

"You can play games on a normal TV?" Ben asked. "Not just in a lab?"

"That's the whole idea," Ralph said. "Games you play right at home."

Ben grabbed a dial and bumped his square upward. The dot bounced off it. CLICK.

"In **1972**," Bit said, "Ralph's brown box turned into the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the very first video game console anyone could buy for their house."

The green light shimmered again, and suddenly they stood in a dim, noisy arcade. Machines beeped along every wall. A tall wooden cabinet glowed with that same bouncing dot.

"This one's called **Pong**," said a man with a mustache, leaning on the machine. "I'm Nolan Bushnell. My friend Ted Dabney and I started a company called Atari, the same year as the Odyssey, in **1972**."

Ben fed in a coin and grabbed the knob, batting the dot back with a satisfying CLACK.

"People loved this game so much," Bit said, "that one arcade machine supposedly got so stuffed with quarters it actually jammed shut! That part might be a bit of a tall tale, but it shows just how popular Pong got."

Ben laughed. "A game so good it ATE money?"

"Pretty much," said Nolan, grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Cartridges, Aliens, and a Hungry Yellow Circle (1977-1980)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. They landed back in the arcade, but busier now, with new machines crowding every corner.

Bit held up a flat plastic rectangle. "This is a **cartridge**. You plug it into a console, and it loads a whole new game, like swapping out a Lego set inside a box."

"In **1977**," Bit went on, "Atari made a console called the **Atari 2600**. Instead of just one built-in game, you could swap cartridges and play all sorts of games on the same machine."

Ben turned the cartridge over in his hands. "So this is when you could finally pick which game to play?"

"Exactly," said Bit.

A machine buzzed nearby, rows of blocky aliens marching across its screen.

"I made this one," said a man beside it. "Tomohiro Nishikado. I call it **Space Invaders**. Made it in **1978**, and it started a whole craze for arcades everywhere."

Ben grabbed the controls and blasted the aliens, one row at a time. They marched faster and faster the fewer there were.

"They're speeding up! That's a little spooky!" Ben said.

"Just enough to keep you on your toes," Bit said. "Nothing scarier than that."

Across the arcade, a round yellow shape chomped glowing dots along winding lines, chased by colorful ghosts.

"That's **Pac-Man**," Bit said. "A designer named Toru Iwatani made it in **1980**. Some people say he got the idea from a pizza with one slice missing."

Ben squinted at the yellow shape. "He kind of DOES look like a pizza!"

"Nobody's totally sure that story's true," Bit admitted, "but it's a fun one."

Ben grabbed the joystick and guided Pac-Man around a tight corner, just missing a ghost. "WHEW. Close one!"

"You're getting good at this," Bit said.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Big Quiet (1983)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. This time they landed somewhere much quieter. Empty shelves. Dusty store windows.

"Something's wrong here," Ben said. "Where did all the games go?"

"In **1983**," Bit explained, "so many rushed, not-very-good games got made that people stopped trusting video games for a while. Stores stopped buying them. People call it the video game **crash** — not a car crash, just a word for when something stops selling."

Ben frowned. "That sounds kind of sad."

"It was a rough patch," Bit agreed. "But don't worry. It gets better soon."

They passed a dusty truck loaded with boxes.

"People say a bunch of unsold game cartridges, including one called E.T., got driven out to **New Mexico** and buried in a big hole where trash goes," Bit said. "Diggers actually found them there in **2014**, so that part turned out to be true!"

Ben's eyes went wide. "There's buried TREASURE out there? Game treasure?"

"Buried cartridges, anyway," Bit said, smiling. "Not quite treasure. More like a time capsule nobody meant to bury."

Ben kicked gently at the dust. "Well, I bet somebody found something cool."

"They did," Bit said. "Proof that even a bad year can turn into a pretty good story."

Ben nodded slowly. "Like how my first pixel drawing looked like a potato, and now it's actually good."

"Exactly like that," Bit laughed.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984-1985)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Snow fell outside tall windows. Ben rubbed his arms.

"Where are we now?" he asked.

"**Moscow**, in **1984**," Bit said. "Home of a very clever puzzle."

A man sat at a computer, watching blocky shapes drop and lock into rows.

"I'm Alexey Pajitnov," he said. "I made a game where blocks fall, and you fit them together. I call it **Tetris**."

Ben watched a long yellow block tumble down. "Turn it sideways! It fits in that gap!"

Alexey spun the block. It slid into place. A whole row vanished with a soft FWOMP.

"You've got a good eye for this," Alexey said, impressed.

The green light swirled, and they landed in a bright toy store. A box on the shelf showed a mustached man in overalls, jumping over a turtle.

"In **1985**," Bit said, "Nintendo sold a new console called the **NES**, with a game called **Super Mario Bros.** built right in."

"A man named Shigeru Miyamoto designed Mario," Bit added. "He's still gaming's most famous character."

Ben grabbed a controller hooked to a store TV and pressed a button. The little pixel plumber jumped, bopped a question mark block, and a coin popped out, spinning. DING.

"That's basically my pixel art hero," Ben said, "just way older."

"Way, way older," Bit said. "But every hero needs a good jump."

Ben jumped Mario onto a turtle shell and did a little fist pump. "GOT IT."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Blue Blur and a Shiny Disc (1991-1994)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Blue light zipped past them so fast it left a streak in the air.

"Whoa, was that a blue blur?" Ben said.

"In **1991**," Bit said, "Sega made a fast blue hedgehog named **Sonic**, to race against Nintendo's Mario."

Sonic zoomed past again, curled into a spinning ball, and bounced clean off a loop. Ben tried to follow him with his eyes. "He's SO fast!"

"Speed was the whole point," Bit said.

The scene shifted to a living room. A gray box sat under a TV, a shiny silver disc resting beside it.

"In **1994**," Bit said, "Sony released the **PlayStation**. It used round discs instead of cartridges, which let games look and sound way more real."

Ben picked up the disc carefully, holding the edges. "It's like a mini DVD!"

"Exactly like that," Bit said.

Nearby, a row of computers sat connected by tangled wires, kids clustered around each screen.

"In **1993**," Bit said, "a game called **Doom** let friends plug their computers together and play against each other at the very same time. People called those get-togethers **LAN parties** — just a bunch of friends and their computers, all wired up in one room."

Ben grinned. "That sounds like a sleepover, but with more monsters on the screen."

"Close enough," Bit laughed. "The best part wasn't even the game. It was everybody playing together."

Ben high-fived a kid at the nearest computer, who high-fived him right back without even looking up.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Shaking Controllers and Blocky Hills (2006-2015)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Ben nearly toppled over as the green light set them down in a bright living room.

A person waved a white remote, and on the TV, a tiny tennis player swung back in reply.

"In **2006**," Bit said, "Nintendo made the **Wii**. You moved the controller with your whole arm, and the game moved along with you."

Ben swung an invisible controller hard. Bit ducked just in time.

"Careful! You nearly beaned me!" Bit said.

"Sorry!" Ben laughed.

The room melted away into something very familiar: blocky green hills, a blocky sun, a blocky sheep baa-ing nearby.

Ben gasped. "Wait. I KNOW this place."

"In **2011**," Bit said, "a game maker named Markus Persson, people called him Notch, released **Minecraft**. It ended up the best-selling video game ever made."

Ben punched a blocky tree, and wood blocks popped right out. "This is literally my favorite place in the whole world."

"Figured you'd like this stop," Bit grinned.

One more WHOOOOSH, and they stood in a bright museum hall, glass cases glowing with old consoles and cartridges.

"This is the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Bit said. "It opened in **2015**, in **Rochester, New York**, to remember all the games that got us here."

Ben spotted a tiny glowing dot behind glass, right beside a picture of Mario. "It all really did start with just two dots, huh?"

"Every single pixel did," Bit said.

The green light swelled one more time. WHOOOOSH.

Ben landed back on his bedroom floor, tablet still glowing warm in his hands. His pixel-art hero sat finished on the screen, mustache and all. Beside it, one tiny new pixel blinked — a little green dot, winking, just like the very first game Ben had ever played.

Ben smiled and pulled his blanket up. "Night, Bit," he whispered.

Somewhere in the pixels, Bit whispered back. "Catch you next level, Ben."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Catch you next level.

true_facts.text: The very first video game people played for fun was **Tennis for Two**, shown on a glowing round screen in **1958**.
In **1962**, a student named Steve Russell and his friends made **Spacewar!**, a spaceship game on a computer as big as a closet.
Ralph Baer's brown box, a first try at a home game, grew into the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game machine you could buy for your TV, in **1972**.
That same year, **1972**, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started Atari and put the bouncing-dot game **Pong** in arcades.
In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players swap in plastic cartridges to play lots of different games on one machine.
In **1978**, Tomohiro Nishikado made **Space Invaders**, with marching aliens that sped up the fewer of them were left.
In **1980**, Toru Iwatani made **Pac-Man**, a hungry yellow circle some people say was inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed games made stores stop trusting video games for a while — people call it the video game crash.
Some unsold game cartridges really did get buried in a big hole in **New Mexico**, and diggers found them there in **2014**.
In **1984**, Alexey Pajitnov made **Tetris** in Moscow, a game where falling blocks fit together into tidy rows.
In **1985**, Nintendo's **NES** came with **Super Mario Bros.** built in, starring a jumping plumber named Mario.
In **1991**, Sega made **Sonic**, a super-fast blue hedgehog, to race against Nintendo's Mario.
**Minecraft**, released in **2011** by Markus "Notch" Persson, became the best-selling video game ever made.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** in Rochester, New York, to remember the games that led here.

new_recurring.name: Bit
new_recurring.rule: A small, blocky green pixel-sprite guide who steps out of any glowing screen to lead the child through a history adventure. Dry, a little sarcastic, warm underneath. Signs off every story with the catchphrase 'Catch you next level!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ben returned to his glowing tablet with his pixel-art hero finished, mustache and all, a tiny new blinking green dot beside it, and fell asleep after Bit's whispered goodnight.

scenarios.worst_moment: Since Brazil got to keep that first trophy for good after their third title, FIFA had to make a brand new trophy in 1974 — the one still used today.
editor_notes: Give Lena a hands-on beat in Chapters 5-9. For example, she could guard the stolen trophy's empty stand, face a Pelé shot, or be shown the first yellow card. That would turn the middle from a narrated timeline into an adventure and deliver the 'exciting' tone the brief asked for.

Restore chronological order (move the Stirling Castle ball to before the Cambridge Rules) and give each chapter one focus. Cut tacked-on facts like the 1974 trophy line, so momentum builds towards 1930, then 1966, then the present.

Vary or cut the constant "the voice said" tags and replace the bolded shout-along lines with dialogue an 11-year-old would enjoy. Also fix the small slips: the Stirling ball was behind panelling, and 'soccer' was coined later than 1863.

story.title: Lena and the Keeper's Ball
story.subtitle: A ten-minute trip through every save soccer ever needed

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Ball in the Back of the Closet
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was on the carpet, diving sideways between two rolled-up socks, pretending they were goalposts.

She reached into the closet for a stray shoe and her hand closed on something round and scuffed instead — an old leather ball, laces faded, tucked behind her grandfather's winter coat. The second she gripped it, the laces lit up gold and the whole ball started to hum, low and steady, like it was bouncing without ever touching the floor.

Lena did the only sensible thing a goalkeeper does with something flying at her face. She caught it.

The carpet dissolved into packed dirt. A crowd in silk robes cheered around a leather bag being juggled from foot to foot, never touched by a single hand. "That's **cuju**," the ball hummed against her palms. "People in China were playing this more than **2,000 years ago** — one of the oldest kicking games anyone's found."

A player shanked a pass straight at her. Lena's body moved before her brain did — knee up, chest out, ball smothered dead. The crowd roared.

"Nice reflexes," the ball said. "You've got a long night of saves ahead of you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Game the King Banned
chapters.text:
The dirt field blurred into a muddy English lane, and suddenly Lena was flattened against a stone wall by what looked like an entire village sprinting after one ball.

There were no teams she could spot, no goals, just dozens of people shoving and roaring down the street after a bag stuffed with straw. "This is 'mob football,'" the ball said, bouncing nervously in her arms. "It was basically a whole town versus itself."

"That seems... unsafe," Lena said, watching a man vault clean over a cart.

"**King Edward II** thought so too. He banned it in London in **1314** — too many broken fences, too much chaos."

Lena grinned and stuck out a foot, calmly intercepting the ball-bag before it flattened a market stall, then rolled it gently back into the crowd. The mob cheered her like she'd invented the save on the spot.

"See," she told the ball, "it just needed a goalkeeper."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All
chapters.text:
Next came a tidy college courtyard, boys in blazers arguing over a ball like lawyers arguing over a contract.

"Everybody's granddad played this game by different rules," the ball explained. "Some schools let you carry it. Some didn't. In **1848**, students at Cambridge finally sat down and wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — one shared rulebook everyone could actually agree on."

A boy near her was filling in a scorebook and muttered the word "assoc" under his breath, short for "association football."

"Wait," said Lena. "Assoc... soccer?"

"Exactly," said the ball. "That nickname stuck in **1880s England**, and it's the reason half the planet calls your sport soccer instead of football."

Lena smirked. "So I'm basically playing 'assoc-ball' right now."

"Don't let it catch on," said the ball.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Man Who Wrote the Laws
chapters.text:
A gaslit office appeared next, ink bottles everywhere, a serious-looking man hunched over paper with a furious expression of concentration.

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," the ball said. "On **26 October 1863**, he helped found the **Football Association** — the group in charge of making football's rules official. Their very first rule? No more picking the ball up with your hands."

Morley looked up, spotted Lena holding the glowing ball, and apparently decided this was a perfectly normal Tuesday.

"Go on then," he said, nodding at the ball in her arms. "Show me a keeper doesn't need hands to keep a clean sheet."

Lena rolled her eyes, dropped the ball, and kicked a shot away from an imaginary goal using her shin, her foot, anything but her palms.

Morley wrote something down and almost smiled. "The **Laws of the Game**," he said. "I wrote them myself, that same year. Glad to see they're holding up."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Oldest Cup on the Shelf
chapters.text:
The scene jumped to a packed stadium, flags snapping, two teams lined up like they meant business.

"This is the **FA Cup**," the ball said, "first played in **1871-72**. It's the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world."

A year later, same stadium, different crowd — Scotland against England, nobody scoring a thing. "First official international match ever," the ball added. "**Glasgow, 1872**. Ended **0-0**."

"A nil-nil draw gets remembered forever?" Lena asked.

"Being first counts for a lot," said the ball.

By **1888**, a man named **William McGregor** was striding between clubs with a notebook, organizing England's teams into the world's very first proper football league — games scheduled, standings kept, bragging rights official.

Lena watched him work and nodded slowly. "Somebody had to make the chaos make sense."

"Somebody always does," the ball agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A World Cup Is Born
chapters.text:
Paris, 1904. A handful of men from seven countries shook hands around a table, looking extremely pleased with themselves.

"That's **FIFA**," the ball said, "the organization that still runs soccer worldwide. Founded right here."

Then the room dissolved into roaring heat and bright flags — Uruguay, 1930, the very first **World Cup**. A man with a determined mustache paced the sideline. "**Jules Rimet**," said the ball. "He pushed harder than anyone to make this tournament happen. They even named the first trophy after him."

Uruguay beat Argentina in the final, and the home crowd went completely unhinged. Someone pressed a ball into Lena's hands for a ceremonial kickoff nobody had actually planned.

She took one look at the open net, struck it clean, and the stadium erupted like she'd scored the real thing.

"Not bad," said the ball, "for someone who usually stops goals instead of scoring them."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ban That Should Never Have Happened
chapters.text:
The next field had no men on it at all — just a women's team in matching shirts, thousands of fans packed along the touchline.

"The Dick, Kerr Ladies," the ball said. "Their star player, **Lily Parr**, helped make them one of the most popular teams in all of England."

Then the crowd vanished, the gates shut, the stands went empty. Lena's stomach dropped. "What happened?"

"In **1921** the FA banned women's football completely," the ball said quietly. "It was wrong, and it lasted a very long time."

"How long?"

"Fifty years. The ban was finally lifted in **1971**."

Lena watched the gates swing back open, players streaming through them like they'd never left. "And then?"

"Then, in **1991**, the first official **Women's World Cup** was played in **China** — and the **United States** won it."

Lena pumped her fist like she'd made the winning save herself. "That's more like it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Dog Who Saved the Cup
chapters.text:
London, 1966. A glass case sat empty where the World Cup trophy should have been, and men in trench coats were sweating.

"Someone stole it," the ball said. "Right before the tournament England was hosting."

A small, scruffy dog trotted past them, nose down, tail wagging, and sniffed straight into a hedge. He emerged with the missing trophy wrapped in newspaper.

"That's **Pickles**," the ball said. "Found it safe, one week later. England went on to host **and** win that **1966 World Cup** — their only title so far."

Lena crouched to scratch the dog's ears without touching the trophy itself. "Good boy. Best save of the whole tournament."

The scene jumped forward to 1970, where a referee named **Ken Aston** held up a bright yellow card at a startled player, inspired, the ball explained, by watching traffic lights change color on his drive home. Lena laughed so hard she nearly dropped the ball she was holding.

And somewhere in black and white footage flickering past, a Brazilian forward named **Pele** lifted the trophy a third time — **1958, 1962, 1970** — the only player in history to manage that hat trick of championships.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The hum faded, the stadium lights dimmed, and Lena was on her bedroom carpet again, socks still rolled into goalposts, the old leather ball warm and quiet in her hands.

The laces had gone still, but one thread near the seam was stitched in gold now, where it hadn't been before.

"You'll keep showing up like this?" Lena whispered.

The ball gave one last soft thump against her palm, like a nod.

She set it carefully back on the closet shelf, right where she'd found it, and climbed into bed thinking about mob football and Lily Parr and a dog named Pickles, already half-planning her next training session around all of it.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a clean sheet to go earn.

true_facts.text: People in China were playing **cuju**, a kicking game, more than **2,000 years ago**.

The **Football Association** was founded on **26 October 1863** and banned carrying the ball by hand.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** wrote football's first official **Laws of the Game** that same year.
The **FA Cup**, started in **1871-72**, is still the oldest football competition running today.
The first official international match was a **0-0 draw** between Scotland and England in **Glasgow, 1872**.
**William McGregor** organized the world's first football league in England in **1888**.
**FIFA**, the group that runs soccer worldwide, was founded in **Paris in 1904**.
The first **World Cup** was played in **Uruguay in 1930**, and Uruguay won it.
**Jules Rimet** pushed hardest to create the World Cup, and the first trophy was named after him.
Star player **Lily Parr** helped make the Dick, Kerr Ladies one of England's most popular teams.
The FA's ban on women's football was lifted in **1971**, fifty years after it began.

story.title: Arjun and the Case of the Sleeping Brain
story.subtitle: A night detective, eight case files, and one very good reason to finally close your eyes.

chapters.heading: Case File One: The Boy With the Twitching Eyes (1953)
chapters.text:
Arjun was not asleep. He was never asleep at nine-forty, whatever his mother said. Under the blanket, flashlight propped on a pillow, he was deep in the last page of *Over the Boundary*, his favorite comic, where the hero smashes a six to win the match.

On his shelf sat the cricket ball he'd won last season — Man of the Match, his name scratched underneath. Tonight it was glowing green.

Arjun poked it. The ball HUMMED. The comic's ink swirled, panels sliding off the page like tiles.

A man stepped out of panel three. Trench coat, slippers, a magnifying glass shaped like a crescent moon.

"Inspector Nod," he said, tipping an invisible hat. "I investigate the strangest case in the world. Sleep. Five more minutes, you said? Lucky for you — five minutes is plenty. Case files don't wait for bedtime."

Before Arjun could answer, the floor dropped away. He landed in a bright lab, **1953**, at the University of Chicago. A boy about his own age slept on a cot, wires taped near his eyes.

"Watch," said Nod.

Under closed eyelids, the boy's eyes were darting fast, back and forth.

"His eyes are moving! Is he awake?" Arjun asked.

"Fast asleep," said Nod. "**Eugene Aserinsky** noticed exactly that, working with scientist **Nathaniel Kleitman**. They named it **REM sleep** — Rapid Eye Movement, the dreaming kind. Kleitman spent his whole life studying sleep. People call him the father of it."

Arjun grinned. "Case cracked already?"

"Case *opened*," said Nod. "Keep up."

chapters.heading: Case File Two: The Ninety-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved. Arjun stood inside something like a giant pinball machine, lights looping around a track.

"This is one night of sleep," said Nod, "speeded up. Watch the loop."

A ball of light rolled around, dipping low, then zooming through a flashing section, then dipping low again.

"Every night your brain runs this loop," said Nod. "About **ninety minutes** a lap. Quiet sleep, then **REM sleep**, back and forth, all night."

Arjun pointed at the flashing section. "That's the dreaming part?"

"Correct. Here's the strange bit." Nod tapped the glass. Inside, a tiny sleeping figure twitched, but its arms and legs stayed floppy as noodles. "During REM, the brain lights up almost like it's awake. But the body switches its muscles off. Otherwise you'd act out every dream — kicking sixes across the bedroom."

Arjun laughed. "That explains why I never actually hit the ball in my dreams."

"Science's gain," said Nod, "is your bedroom lamp's good fortune. One more case, before you ask — a fellow named **Freud** once said dreams were secret wishes in disguise. Nice story. Most scientists today think he got it wrong. Keep that one for the comics."

Arjun laughed again. Nod did not.

chapters.heading: Case File Three: The Growth Spurt Factory
chapters.text:
Next stop: a factory floor, conveyor belts humming, little packages marked GROWTH HORMONE rolling past.

"Hormone," said Nod, catching Arjun's squint, "just means a chemical message your body sends itself."

"So what's it doing here?" Arjun asked.

"This factory only runs during the **deepest, quietest stage of sleep**," said Nod. "That's when your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the chemical that helps you grow taller, heal scrapes, and build muscle."

Arjun looked down at his own arms, as if waiting for them to stretch.

"That's one reason growing kids like you need more sleep than grown-ups," said Nod. "Skip sleep, and the factory slows down."

"So if I want to actually hit the ball out of the ground someday—"

"Then somewhere a factory is waiting for you to lie down," said Nod. "Shall I tell your mother you agreed?"

"Absolutely not," said Arjun, and the factory floor folded away, laughing.

chapters.heading: Case File Four: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
They landed somewhere tiny — inside a brain, apparently, beside a pulsing clump of cells no bigger than a grain of rice.

"This," said Nod, "is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say that three times fast and I'll be impressed. Everyone just calls it the master clock. It sits right behind your eyes and tells your whole body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up."

"Like an alarm clock inside my head?"

"Exactly. It runs on a cycle called **circadian** — a word that just means 'about a day.' Roughly twenty-four hours, same as sunrise to sunrise."

Lights flickered overhead like tiny switches clicking on and off.

"In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, science's biggest award, for finding the actual genes that keep this clock ticking."

Arjun whistled. "A whole prize for a clock?"

"The clock," said Nod, "that decides when every human on Earth gets sleepy. I'd call that prize-worthy."

chapters.heading: Case File Five: The Midnight Chemist (1958)
chapters.text:
A cluttered laboratory appeared next, beakers bubbling, a scientist hunched over a dish.

"**1958**," said Nod. "Scientist **Aaron Lerner** and his team pulled a chemical out of a tiny gland and called it **melatonin**. It's the chemical that tells your body, 'it's dark, time to feel sleepy.'"

"That's why the lights going off makes me yawn?"

"Precisely. Darkness tells your brain to make more melatonin. Bright screens tell it to make less — which is why glowing comics past bedtime are, strictly speaking, evidence against you."

Arjun slid the flashlight behind his back, guiltily.

"Relax," said Nod. "I'm a detective, not the prosecution. Yet."

The beakers bubbled on, glowing faint silver, like bottled moonlight.

chapters.heading: Case File Six: The Brain's Rinse Cycle
chapters.text:
Next, Arjun found himself shrunk impossibly small, floating through winding tunnels like a brain's own plumbing.

"Two jobs happen here every night," said Nod. "First, your brain sorts the day into **memories** — filing away what you practiced, what you learned, what actually mattered. Sleep well before a big match, remember your batting tips better."

"No wonder I forget things after late nights," Arjun said.

"Second job," Nod went on, as a wave of glowing liquid swept through the tunnel, flushing old bits of waste out, "is a nightly rinse. Scientists call it the **glymphatic system** — basically a cleaning crew that washes waste out of your brain while you sleep."

"My brain gets a car wash?"

"Every single night," said Nod. "Try not to track mud through it before bed."

chapters.heading: Case File Seven: The Sleepiest Animals Alive
chapters.text:
The tunnel opened into moonlit savanna, ocean, and a cave, all at once, like three panels on one page.

"Compare notes," said Nod. "Giraffes, over there, sleep under two hours a day, in short naps, standing up."

Arjun spotted dolphins gliding with one eye open. "Why's that one eye open?"

"Dolphins and some seals sleep with half their brain at a time," said Nod. "One side rests while the other stays alert, watching for danger or keeping them swimming."

In the cave, tiny bats hung upside down, barely stirring. "Some bats sleep nearly **twenty hours** a day," said Nod. "Laziest mammals on record, officially."

"And babies?" Arjun asked, thinking of his baby cousin.

"Newborns sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours** a day, nearly half of it dreaming," said Nod. "Even bugs do something like sleeping. Tiny fruit flies rest too. Sleep is a very old habit — older than cricket, even."

"Nothing's older than cricket," said Arjun.

"We'll revisit that case another night."

chapters.heading: Case File Eight: Eleven Days Awake — and Home Again
chapters.text:
One last panel glowed ahead: a teenager grinning into an old camera, propped up with pillows, friends cheering him on.

"**1964**," said Nod. "**Randy Gardner**, seventeen, from San Diego, stayed awake about **eleven days** for a school science project. One of the longest stretches ever recorded."

"Eleven days?! That's basically a superpower."

"Not quite," said Nod, serious now. "By the end he couldn't think straight, couldn't remember simple things, felt miserable. Doctors say nobody should ever try to beat that record. It wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory, fast."

Arjun nodded slowly. "So the five-more-minutes thing isn't actually... free."

"Nothing is free after midnight," said Nod. "Oh — and if you ever wander around asleep, don't worry. Sleepwalking happens in the deep, dreamless part of the night. You're not acting out a dream. You're just taking a very confused stroll."

He tipped his hat. "People spend roughly a **third of their life** asleep. Case closed, every single night."

The lab, the cave, the clock all folded back into ink. Arjun landed softly on his own bed, comic closed on his chest, cricket ball glowing gently down to dark.

On the last page, new words had appeared in the margin: *Good job, Detective. Same time tomorrow?*

Arjun grinned, clicked off the flashlight, and actually, for once, closed his eyes.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a match to win — and, maybe, a little more sleep to spare for it.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes dart around under closed lids.
A night's sleep runs in loops about **ninety minutes** long, switching between quiet sleep and dreaming **REM sleep**.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the muscles go floppy so the sleeper can't act out the dream.
The deepest, quietest part of sleep makes the most **growth hormone**, the chemical that helps kids grow and heal.
A tiny part of the brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** works like a master clock, telling the body when to feel sleepy and when to wake up.
**Circadian**, the body's roughly day-long clock, comes from old words meaning 'about a day.'
In **2017**, scientists **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes behind that clock.
In **1958**, scientist **Aaron Lerner**'s team pulled out the sleepy-time chemical **melatonin**, which tells the body it's dark and time to rest.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day into memories, so good sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the **glymphatic system** flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** stayed awake about **eleven days** for a science project — doctors say nobody should ever try to copy that.
Dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.
Giraffes sleep under two hours a day, in short naps while standing.
People spend roughly a **third of their life** asleep.

story.title: Tom and the Gear That Remembered
story.subtitle: A ride through two hundred years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gear in the Toolbox (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom was flat on the garage floor, flashlight clenched in his teeth, hunting down why his derailleur — the little metal arm that shifts his chain between gears — kept skipping.

He dug past old tubes and patch kits and found a battered tin box he'd never seen before. Inside sat a single gear, dull bronze, bigger than his thumb. He picked it up.

It was warm. That wasn't right. Metal doesn't warm up by itself.

He turned it over again, and it hummed — a low metal note, like a wheel spinning fast. The garage light flickered green. The floor dropped away under him.

Tom landed hard on packed dirt. A man in a long coat was pushing a wooden two-wheeler along with his own feet, like a kid on a balance bike that had grown up. There were no pedals anywhere.

"You're staring," the man said, not unkindly. "Karl von Drais. This is my Laufmaschine — my running machine."

Tom checked again for pedals. Nothing. "How do you go anywhere?"

"You run," said Drais, "then lift your feet and glide." He demonstrated, scooting and coasting like it was obvious.

The gear buzzed in Tom's pocket. A small, precise voice rose out of it. "Correct date: **1817**. First two-wheeled riding machine in history. No pedals yet — just handlebars and balance."

Tom nearly dropped it. "You *talk*?"

"I'm a pinion," said the gear. "Small gear, big opinions. Call me Pinion."

Tom grinned despite himself, grabbed the handlebars — they steered exactly like his mountain bike's — and ran, then lifted his feet to glide. "It steers like mine does!"

"Keep that thought," said Pinion. "It gets better."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed again, and the dirt path turned to cobblestones.

A man was bolting a metal crank straight onto a wheel. Pedals, finally — but welded right onto the front wheel itself.

"Pierre Michaux," the man said, "and my partner, Pierre Lallement. We call it the **velocipede**."

Tom climbed on and pedaled three feet before his teeth started chattering. Every cobblestone jumped straight up through the frame.

"This is brutal," Tom said, gripping the bars.

"People call it the **boneshaker**," Lallement said, grinning, "for reasons you've just discovered."

Tom studied the wheel — solid metal rim, no cushion at all. His engineer brain clicked. "You need something soft between the wheel and the road. Like... a tube of air?"

Lallement blinked. "An interesting notion. Patent one, why don't you."

Pinion buzzed in his pocket. "Hold that thought. In **1866**, Lallement actually does patent a pedal bicycle in America. Your soft-tube idea comes later — from someone else entirely."

Tom laughed, rattling over another stone. "Can't wait to meet him."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header (1870s)
chapters.text:
The road sharpened into the 1870s, and the bicycle got ridiculous.

A front wheel towered over Tom, taller than he was. The back wheel looked like an afterthought, tiny and trailing behind.

"They call it a **penny-farthing**," Pinion said, "after two old British coins — one huge, one tiny. Guess which wheel is which."

A rider rolled past, perched high above the giant wheel like he was balancing on a unicycle with a seat.

"One turn of the pedals," the rider called down, "and you fly twice as far as on a small wheel!"

Tom squinted at the geometry. Pedals bolted straight to that huge front hub meant speed — but the rider's chin was a long way from the ground.

"What happens if you stop fast?" Tom asked.

"We call it **taking a header**," the rider said cheerfully. "You go over the front. Headfirst."

Tom pictured the physics — high center of gravity, barely any brakes — and kept both boots firmly on the dirt. "I'll admire this one from down here, thanks."

"Wise," said Pinion. "Very wise."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shape That Stuck (1885)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed, and the giant wheel shrank.

Tom found himself looking at something nearly ordinary — two wheels, same size, a chain looping between them.

A man in shirtsleeves wiped grease from his hands. "John Kemp Starley," he said. "I call her the **Rover Safety Bicycle**."

Tom circled it slowly. Even wheels. Chain drive to the back wheel. A seat low enough to touch the ground.

"This is basically my bike," Tom said, surprised.

"That's rather the idea," Starley said. "Lower, steadier, safer. No headers."

"In **1885**," Pinion added, "this shape becomes the one that sticks. Give or take a hundred and forty years of tweaks, you're still riding it."

Tom swung a leg over and pedaled a slow circle. It felt instantly familiar — handlebars, chain, two matched wheels, nothing trying to throw him over the front.

"Finally," Tom said. "Something that isn't trying to kill me."

"Give it time," Starley laughed. "You'll want it smoother yet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Vet's Idea (1888)
chapters.text:
One hum of the gear later, the road felt different before Tom even saw why.

A man knelt beside a small tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel and pumping air into it with a hand pump.

"John Boyd Dunlop," he said, not looking up. "I'm a vet, not a bicycle man. But my son's tricycle rattled his teeth loose on this garden path."

"So you gave it air," Tom said, catching on fast.

"A **pneumatic tire**," Dunlop said. "Rubber, filled with air, instead of solid rubber on a metal rim."

"In **1888**," said Pinion, "this fixes the boneshaker problem for good."

Tom rode the tricycle across the gravel path. No rattle. No jolt. Just a soft, bouncy roll, like his own mountain bike tires eating up a rocky trail.

"This is basically what my tires do," Tom said, grinning. "Just newer rubber."

"Same idea," said Dunlop. "Smoother ride, happier teeth."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everyone Gets a Bike (1890s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed into a street crowded with bicycles — hundreds of them, ridden by kids, grandparents, everyone in between.

A woman rolled past in a long skirt, then swapped to looser, split trousers before climbing onto her bike. "Can't pedal safely in skirts," she told Tom. "Gears and long fabric don't mix."

"This is the **Golden Age of Bicycles**," Pinion said. "**1890s.** Millions of bikes sold, across Europe and America."

A sharp-eyed woman nearby nodded at the crowd of riders. "Susan B. Anthony," she introduced herself. "Cycling has done more to free women to travel on their own than almost anything else in the world."

Tom thought about that — a bike as a way to just *go*, without asking anyone's permission.

Down a side street, a small shop sign read BICYCLES REPAIRED. Two brothers were truing a wheel, spinning it and tapping spokes straight.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," Pinion said quietly. "Bicycle men first."

Tom watched them bend lightweight metal tubing into a frame. "Bikes before planes," he said slowly. "The tubing, the spoked wheels — "

"Exactly the skills they'll use," said Pinion, "in **1903**, to build the first airplane that actually flies."

Tom looked at the thin, strong tubing in Orville's hands and understood, for the first time, that an engineer's best tricks move between inventions.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Up the Mountain (1903–1930s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed twice, fast, and the street turned into open road — racers strung out in a long line, climbing a hill under a hot sun.

"The **Tour de France**," Pinion said. "First raced in **1903**. Today it's about **3,500 kilometers** — over two thousand miles — across three straight weeks."

Tom watched a rider's legs pump at the exact same speed, hill or flat.

"Doesn't he need lower gears for that climb?" Tom asked.

"Not yet," said Pinion. "Wait a few decades."

Another hum, smaller this time, and the hill was still there but the bike had changed — a small metal arm now hung by the back wheel, nudging the chain between different-sized gears.

"The **derailleur**," Pinion said. "**1930s.** Shift it, and the chain jumps to an easier gear for the hill."

Tom grinned — this was the exact part he'd been digging through his toolbox for, back home.

"That's literally what I was fixing," Tom said.

"Then you already know," said Pinion, "that a tiny moving part can save your whole ride."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Marin County, and Home (1970s)
chapters.text:
One more hum, and the road turned to dirt — steep, rutted, winding down a dry California hillside.

A group of riders stood at the top with heavy old bikes, fat tires, no fear on their faces.

"Marin County," Pinion said. "**1970s.** Riders wanting to bomb down rough trails built bikes tough enough to survive it."

One rider grinned at Tom's own bike — knobby tires, sturdy frame. "Looks familiar."

"That's basically mine," Tom said. Nearby, smaller, scrappier bikes popped off dirt jumps — **BMX**, built the same decade, inspired by motorcycle racing.

"This is where my bike comes from," Tom said, watching the trail riders drop in. "All of it. The chain, the gears, the tires — two hundred years, bolted onto one frame."

"One billion bicycles exist in the world today," Pinion said. "More than any other kind of vehicle, anywhere."

The gear pulsed warm one last time.

Tom blinked, and he was back on the garage floor, flashlight still between his teeth, the derailleur still in his hands.

In his palm sat the gear, cool now, ordinary bronze. On his workbench, the tool somehow sat already tightened, perfectly adjusted.

He turned the pedal. The chain shifted clean — no skip, no catch.

"Two hundred years," Tom murmured, "just to fix one gear."

He set Pinion carefully back in the tin box, next to the patch kits, and flicked off the garage light.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a trail waiting — and a bike finally ready for it.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals — riders pushed it along with their feet.
In the 1860s, pedals got bolted straight onto the front wheel, making the rattly **velocipede**, nicknamed the **boneshaker**.
By the 1870s, the **penny-farthing** had a front wheel taller than a person, so one pedal turn carried riders much farther.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky — a sudden stop could throw a rider over the front, a fall called **taking a header**.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two even wheels and a chain — the shape bikes still use today.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop, a vet trying to smooth out his son's tricycle ride, invented the air-filled **pneumatic tire**.
The 1890s became the **Golden Age of Bicycles**, with millions of bikes sold across Europe and America.
Susan B. Anthony said cycling gave women more freedom to travel on their own than almost anything else.
In the 1890s, brothers Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle repair shop in Dayton, Ohio.
The Wrights used bicycle tricks — lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels — to help build their first airplane.
In the 1930s, the **derailleur** came along — a small part that shifts a bike's chain to an easier gear for climbing hills.
The **Tour de France**, first raced in **1903**, today covers about **3,500 kilometers** — over three weeks of racing.
In the 1970s, riders in Marin County, California, built tough, wide-tired bikes for bombing down dirt trails — the first mountain bikes.
Today, an estimated **one billion** bicycles exist worldwide — more than any other kind of vehicle.

new_recurring.name: Pinion
new_recurring.rule: A small bronze gear that turns up in Tom's toolbox or garage, warms and hums when touched, and speaks in a precise voice to narrate real history as it pulls him through time. Triggered by curiosity about how something works.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Tom wakes back in his garage with his derailleur mysteriously fixed and the talking gear, Pinion, resting quietly back in its tin box.
