story.title: Eli and the Eighteen-Year Race
story.subtitle: A busted homemade radio, a voice called Control, and the whole Space Race live on the dial.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Static (1957)
chapters.text:
Eli had been awake since eleven, chasing one sound through the homemade shortwave radio he'd built for his physics fair project, the one due in six days and still three resistors short of actually working.

Then the noise found a rhythm.

Beep. Beep. Beep. Evenly spaced, nothing random in it anywhere. Static doesn't repeat. A signal does.

He turned the dial a hair, and a green light flared behind the glass tube like something inside had been waiting for exactly that movement.

"Carrier wave," said a voice, flat and unbothered, like it had said this a thousand times before. A carrier wave, Eli knew, was just the steady background hum a radio signal rides on top of — and this one had something riding it. "You found it on the first try. Most people take longer."

Eli's hand froze on the dial. "Who—"

"Control," the voice said. "Hang on to something."

The room folded the way a picture folds when you close a laptop too fast, and then Eli was standing on open scrubland at night, cold enough to see his breath, a rocket lit up white under floodlights half a mile off.

"Where—"

"Baikonur Cosmodrome. Kazakhstan. **October 4th, 1957**," said Control. "You're about to hear the sound you were just chasing, except live."

The rocket lifted on fire with no sound at first — the light always gets there before the noise does — and then the roar arrived and shook Eli's chest. A small sphere, not much bigger than a beach ball, rode the tip of it into the dark.

"**Sputnik 1**," Control said. "First man-made object ever to make it to orbit."

Eli did the math without meaning to. The sphere was tiny, maybe **58 centimeters** wide, polished metal and antennas and nothing else. "That's the whole satellite?"

"That's the whole satellite. It doesn't need to be big. It needs to broadcast." Control's voice carried something that might have been pride, carefully disguised as boredom. "Every radio on the planet that could tune to its frequency could hear it beep. Yours included, a few minutes ago."

Eli looked up. Somewhere above the floodlights, invisible now, a beach-ball-sized machine was already circling the Earth, saying *here I am* to anyone who'd listen.

"That's the signal I built my whole radio to find," he said.

"Copy that," said Control. "Took you long enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Dog and the Agency (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Eli found himself behind a glass wall, looking into a cramped capsule with padded sides, barely big enough for the dog curled inside it.

"Her name's **Laika**," said Control. "**November 3rd, 1957**. One month after Sputnik 1. She's about to become the first living creature to make it to orbit."

Eli had been expecting more hardware, more switches. He hadn't expected something with a heartbeat. "She's not scared?"

"She's trained for it. Full life support, temperature control, enough food for the mission." Control didn't elaborate further, and Eli understood the conversation was supposed to move on, so he let it.

The capsule sealed. A dull roar somewhere behind the glass. Then nothing but readouts.

"Up she goes," Control said. "Around the world, and around it again."

Eli exhaled slowly. "One satellite that beeps, and one with a passenger. That's two shocks in a month."

"Try living in Washington D.C. that fall," said Control, and the scene dissolved into fluorescent light and a long hallway full of men in narrow ties, carrying boxes marked with three stacked letters.

"N-A-S-A," Eli read off a freshly painted door. "Let me guess."

"**October 1st, 1958**," Control confirmed. "The United States needed an agency built specifically to catch up, and fast. Sputnik did that. One beeping ball rearranged an entire government's org chart."

Eli grinned. "A ball beat the Pentagon."

"A ball **and** a dog," said Control. "Don't shortchange Laika. Copy that?"

"Copy that," Eli said, and found he liked the way it sounded.

He flipped to a blank page in his notebook and wrote two words at the top: ESCAPE VELOCITY — the speed something needs to hit so gravity can't drag it back down. He didn't know the number yet. He wrote the question anyway. Questions were usually the first useful thing in any physics problem.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Belt Nobody Expected (1958)
chapters.text:
Control dropped him into a room wallpapered in dials, every needle twitching, cigarette smoke doing a passable impression of fog.

"**January 31st, 1958**," Control said. "**Explorer 1**. America's answer, four months late and still catching up."

On a screen, a thin trace jumped and spiked with no clean rhythm Eli could find.

"That's not just a counter miscounting?" he asked, because something that irregular felt wrong for a brand-new satellite nobody had flown before.

"Look again," said Control. "What do spikes like that usually mean, in a Geiger counter?"

Eli had used a Geiger counter exactly once, during a radioactivity unit, and he remembered the rule well enough. "Radiation. If it's hitting so hard the counter can't keep up, it can actually look like it's dropping instead of climbing."

"Correct." For once Control sounded almost impressed. "Explorer 1 had just flown straight into something nobody had mapped: a doughnut-shaped ring of charged particles trapped by Earth's own magnetic field, way out past where the air runs out. They'd call it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the scientist running the instrument."

"So the counter wasn't broken. Space was just radioactive somewhere nobody expected."

"Space usually is," Control said. "You're going to want to remember that belt. Everything you fly through it later has to deal with it."

Eli scribbled *Van Allen = particles + magnetic field, not a glitch* into the notebook he was somehow still carrying, pencil and all, despite having just teleported across two decades.

"First satellite finds a new part of the solar system by accident," he said. "Not bad for a four-month delay."

"Second-best isn't nothing," Control agreed. "It's usually how real discoveries happen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: 108 Minutes and a Name No One Would Say (1961)
chapters.text:
Control brought him to a dim room full of headsets, men hunched over consoles, voices low and urgent in a language Eli didn't speak but somehow understood anyway.

"**April 12th, 1961**," Control said. "**Yuri Gagarin**. Vostok 1. About to become the first human being in space."

On the console, a dot crawled along a curved line — an orbit.

"One trip around," Control said, "roughly **108 minutes**, and then back down."

Eli watched the room hold its breath every time the signal dropped out, then exhale when it returned.

He noticed something odd: nobody in the room ever said the name of the engineer who'd designed the rocket, even though they clearly revered him. He was only ever "the Chief Designer."

"Why doesn't anyone just say his name?" Eli asked.

"Because the Soviet government decided his name was a state secret," said Control. "**Sergei Korolev** ran their entire rocket program from the shadows. Nobody outside a small circle knew who he was until after he died, in **1966**."

"A secret genius hiding behind a classified title. That's either really cool or really unfair."

"Both, usually," said Control, and didn't elaborate, which told Eli the subject was closed for tonight.

Three weeks later by the room's clocks, Control confirmed, on **May 5th, 1961**, a different console, a different flag. A capsule marked FREEDOM 7 sat on a different pad.

"**Alan Shepard**," Control said. "First American in space. Shorter flight — an up-and-down arc, not a full orbit — but it counted."

"The Soviets got the orbit. We got fifteen minutes and a splash."

"For now," Control said. "Catching up usually starts small."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Decade Clock (1961)
chapters.text:
Control set him down in sunlight this time, a crowd outside a building, a voice carrying over speakers.

"**May 25th, 1961**," Control said. "Listen."

The voice on the speakers was steady, unhurried, the kind of calm that made outrageous things sound reasonable. Eli caught the phrase: land a man on the Moon, and return him safely, before the decade is out.

"That's **President Kennedy**," Control said. "He just gave the country about eight and a half years to go from fifteen-minute hops to the Moon and back."

Eli did the arithmetic in his head without trying, the way he always did with any number that had a deadline attached. "They'd just barely gotten a guy above the atmosphere for fifteen minutes. Now there's a countdown to the Moon."

"Going to orbit is one problem," Eli went on, turning it over the way he turned over every other impossible physics problem. "Landing something on the Moon and then getting it back off the surface afterward is three or four hard problems stacked on top of each other."

"Which is why nobody serious thought the timeline was easy," Control said. "They thought it was possible. That's a different claim entirely."

Eli watched the crowd applaud, slow and uncertain, like people deciding whether to believe what they'd just heard.

"I want to see how this turns out," he said.

"You will," said Control. "Patience looks good on you. Copy that?"

"Copy that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The First Woman in Orbit (1963)
chapters.text:
Control's next doorway opened onto launch-pad quiet, a woman in a flight suit walking toward a gantry alone, like she'd done it a hundred times even though nobody ever had.

"**June 16th, 1963**," Control said. "**Valentina Tereshkova**. Vostok 6. First woman in space."

Eli watched her climb in, unhurried, like it was a normal Tuesday. "Wait — she used to work in a factory?"

"Textile factory," Control confirmed. "No pilot's license, no engineering degree. She applied, trained, and got picked anyway."

"So the first guy in space was a fighter pilot, and the first woman just... showed up and won the job."

"People do that, when the door's actually open," Control said. "She went around the planet **48 times** before she came back down. Longer than every American flight up to that point, combined."

Eli whistled low. "That's not a token flight. That's a record."

"It never was a token flight," Control said, something sharper than usual in the voice. "It just got remembered like one, for a while. Takes some digging sometimes to get the credit lined up with the achievement."

Below them, the capsule's hatch sealed with a sound like a vault closing. Eli leaned toward the glass without thinking, the way he always leaned toward big displays at the planetarium.

"Three days up there alone," he said. "No one to talk to but mission control."

"She managed," said Control. "Turns out people adapt to practically anything, given a reason big enough."

Eli made a note in his notebook, underlining her name twice. "Noted."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
Control placed him near a monitor showing a grainy black-and-white feed, a figure floating outside a capsule.

"**March 18th, 1965**," Control said. "**Alexei Leonov**. About to become the first human being to float outside a spacecraft in open space."

The figure drifted, tethered by a thin line, turning slow circles against black nothing.

Eli's pulse ticked up despite himself — there was no sound up there, no air, nothing between Leonov and raw vacuum except a suit holding pressure in. "How long's he out there?"

"**About ten minutes**," Control said.

Ten minutes didn't sound like much until Eli pictured being the guy inside the suit, a thin layer of fabric standing between him and literally nothing. "That's either the bravest ten minutes in history or the longest."

"Both, probably," Control said. "His suit puffed up out there — stiffened enough in the vacuum that getting back through the hatch took some real doing. He made it back inside with time to spare, which is the only part of this you need to lose sleep over, and you don't, because it worked."

Eli exhaled, the tension draining the moment Control said *worked*. "Ten minutes to be the first person ever to just float there and look at the whole planet with nothing between you and it."

"Most people don't get ten seconds of a view like that," Control said. "He got ten minutes. Not bad."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Photograph That Changed the View (1968)
chapters.text:
The next stop had no gravity to speak of — Eli felt the lightness in his stomach before he saw anything, floating half an inch off an imaginary floor until Control muttered something about compensating and he settled.

Through a small window, gray ground scrolled past, cratered and colorless, closer than any Moon Eli had ever seen with his own eyes.

"**December 1968**," Control said. "**Apollo 8**. First humans to orbit the Moon. Keep watching that window."

The gray horizon rolled by, and then, impossibly, a blue and white marble came up over the edge of it — small, bright, alone against black.

"That's—" Eli didn't finish the sentence. There wasn't a word ready for it.

"Earth," Control said quietly. "**William Anders** took the photo that's about to become one of the most reproduced images in human history. They're calling it 'Earthrise.'"

"We came all the way out here," Eli said slowly, "to take a picture of home."

"Turns out that's what a lot of space exploration is actually for," Control said. "You go out to look at everything else. You come back having mostly learned something about the place you started."

Eli kept his eyes on the window until the blue marble rolled out of frame again. He thought of his own backyard, his own radio, small as that marble must have looked from here. He didn't write anything in the notebook this time. Some things didn't need notes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
Control's next doorway came with heat and noise before anything else — a launch pad so vast Eli had to tilt his head back to find the top of the rocket standing on it.

"**363 feet**," Control said, before Eli could even ask. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty, torch and all. The **Saturn V**."

"Who builds something that size and expects it to fly?"

"**Wernher von Braun**," Control said. "Led the NASA team that designed it. He'd built rockets before, for a different government entirely, years earlier — not a part of the story anyone tells proudly, but it's the truth of where some of this engineering came from."

Eli filed that away without comment, the way you file a fact that's complicated enough to need more room than tonight had.

The Saturn V lit and climbed, and the ground shook under Eli's sneakers even though he was fairly sure his sneakers weren't technically present. Then the scene jumped, the way Control's jumps always did, straight to a gray surface, a ladder, a boot coming down toward dust that had never once been stepped in.

"**July 20th, 1969**," Control said. "Watch. **Neil Armstrong**, about to become the first person to walk on the Moon."

The boot touched down. Eli realized he was holding his breath for no reason at all, since he already knew how this part ended, and let it out slow.

"A giant leap," Control said, quoting the line everyone quotes, "though he was just a few feet off his own ladder when he said it."

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him down there a bit later," Control added. "**Michael Collins** stayed up above the whole time, alone in the command module — the part of the ship that never actually touches down — orbiting by himself while the other two got all the cameras."

"That sounds like the worst job on the mission," Eli said.

"Try explaining that to the twelve astronauts who walked on the Moon across the six landings that followed, between **1969** and **1972**," Control said. "Someone always has to mind the ship. Collins never once complained about it on the record."

Eli watched the flag go up, stiff with a wire frame because there was no air to let it hang properly, and thought that was somehow the most practical detail in the whole story.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown, Handshake, Home (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
Control's last jump landed Eli in a cramped capsule interior, warning lights blinking amber, three astronauts moving with the unhurried calm of people who'd rehearsed disaster a hundred times in simulators.

"**1970**," Control said. "**Apollo 13**. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon."

Eli's stomach dropped, old instinct kicking in before he remembered who was telling him this story. "Are they—"

"Alive," Control said immediately, cutting the worry off before it could grow legs. "Every one of them. Engineers on the ground redesigned their return plan from scratch, improvised a fix for the air filters out of spare parts and tape, and flew them home safe. That's the whole headline: crisis, then rescue, then home."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "So it's not actually a disaster story."

"It's a story about what a good engineer does when the plan breaks," Control said. "Which, given your hobby, you might want to remember."

One more jump — gentler this time, sunlit, two spacecraft nose to nose in orbit, hatches open, hands reaching across.

"**July 17th, 1975**," Control said. "American crew, Soviet crew, docked together on purpose, shaking hands in orbit. Eighteen years after a beeping ball started the whole contest, this is how it ended."

"Not with someone winning," Eli said slowly. "With everyone just... deciding to stop keeping score."

"That's usually how the good endings work," said Control.

The static rose around them like a tide coming in, and the launch pads and capsules and footprints blurred back into dial-light and bedroom shadow. Eli blinked, and he was sitting cross-legged on his own carpet, the homemade radio warm under his hands, headphones around his neck instead of on his ears.

The dial had gone dark. On the notepad beside him, in handwriting he didn't fully remember producing, was a string of dots and dashes he recognized immediately — the exact rhythm of the first beep he'd ever caught, copied out like a souvenir.

"Copy that," Eli said quietly, to no one, and found he meant it as a kind of thank-you.

Outside his window, it was still dark, still a school night. His physics fair project had just gotten a much better title.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, his science fair project had a new title: How to Build a Radio That Hears History.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made object to orbit Earth, launched from Baikonur on **October 4th, 1957** — just **58 centimeters** wide, yet its radio beep could be picked up on ordinary radios everywhere.
A dog named **Laika** rode Sputnik 2 into orbit on **November 3rd, 1957**, the first living creature to get there.
The Sputnik shock pushed the United States to start a brand-new space agency, **NASA**, on **October 1st, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31st, 1958**, and its instruments found a ring of radiation now called the **Van Allen belt**.

**Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space on **April 12th, 1961**, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**; **Alan Shepard** followed on **May 5th, 1961** as the first American in space, on a short up-and-down hop rather than a full orbit.
The USSR's chief rocket designer, **Sergei Korolev**, worked in total secrecy — his name wasn't made public until after his death in **1966**.
On **May 25th, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the country to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade was out.
**Valentina Tereshkova**, once a factory worker, became the first woman in space on **June 16th, 1963**, orbiting Earth **48 times**.
**Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk on **March 18th, 1965**, floating outside his capsule for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and **William Anders** took the famous 'Earthrise' photo of Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
On **July 20th, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, with **Buzz Aldrin** beside him and **Michael Collins** orbiting alone above in the command module.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried them stood **363 feet** tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty, built by a NASA team led by **Wernher von Braun**.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but engineers improvised a fix and brought the whole crew home safe.
The Space Race ended in cooperation on **July 17th, 1975**, when American and Soviet crews docked their spacecraft and shook hands in orbit.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Eli's radio went dark, leaving a hand-copied string of Morse dots and dashes on his notepad — the first beep he'd ever caught — as a souvenir, and a new title for his physics fair project.

story.title: Mia and Number Nine: A History of the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: One scuffed soccer ball, four thousand years of football, and a stats nerd who finally gets the receipts.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Cuju, China — Around 200 BCE
chapters.text:
Mia had the laptop open to a spreadsheet of her own team's shot conversion rate, rows of green and red cells stretching well past midnight. She should have been asleep two hours ago. Instead she was arguing with a pivot table about whether her left foot was actually weaker than her stats said it was.

On the shelf behind her sat the beaten-up size-4 ball her first coach had given her, scuffed down to gray, laces long gone. She'd kept it because the numbers were still legible — a 9 inked on in marker from the season she'd worn that number three years straight.

She reached over without thinking, meaning to toss it onto the bed, and the seams lit up gold under her fingers. Not a trick of the desk lamp. Stitches, actually glowing, rearranging themselves into a string of digits: -200.

"That's not a year," she said out loud, because arguing with a soccer ball felt marginally less insane than believing it. "There's no year zero. You'd need—"

"Four hundred BCE-ish, give or take a century," the ball said, in a voice like a sports commentator reading a final score. "Welcome to the all-time stat sheet, Mia. I'm Number Nine. I've been keeping tabs since before anyone called this sport anything at all."

She should have dropped it. She bounced it instead, because some part of her — the part that color-coded spreadsheets for fun — wanted to see where the data went.

The room dissolved into dust and lantern light. A dirt court. Men in long tunics kicked a stuffed leather ball between two bamboo poles, no hands allowed, roaring every time it sailed through.

"Cuju," said Number Nine, spinning lazily in her grip. "A kicking game, played in Han China **over 2,000 years ago**. A lot of historians call it the oldest ancestor soccer's got."

Mia watched a player flick the ball up with his heel, juggle it twice, then thread it dead center between the poles. The crowd completely lost it.

"That's a better first touch than half my varsity team," Mia muttered.

"Write it down," said Number Nine. "I keep the receipts. You're just visiting them."

She grinned, and bounced the ball again before she could talk herself out of it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A King's Ban and a Castle's Secret
chapters.text:
The next bounce landed her mid-riot.

Mud, noise, and about forty men hauling an inflated pig's bladder — the squishy, air-filled sac that used to get stitched inside old leather balls — down a London street like it owed them money. Mia ducked an elbow that wasn't aimed at her but might as well have been.

"This is **mob football**," said Number Nine, sounding delighted. "Whole villages against each other. No ref, barely any rules, and absolutely no sideline."

"This is a riot with a ball in it," Mia said, watching a man get shouldered straight into a fruit cart.

"King Edward II thought so too. He banned it in London in **1314** — too much property damage, not nearly enough actual football."

Mia laughed despite herself. "So the first rule in soccer history is basically 'please stop.'"

"Pretty much."

The scene blurred, and when it settled she was standing in a quiet stone room lined with tapestries — somebody's castle, judging by the drafts coming off the walls. Number Nine nudged her attention toward a dusty rafter overhead, where something round and leathery had been wedged for who knew how long.

"Stirling Castle, Scotland," said the ball. "That thing up there might be the oldest football in the world — leather stitched around a pig's bladder for bounce, hidden away sometime in the **1540s**."

Mia reached up and turned it over in her hands. Lopsided, soft with age, nothing like the machine-stitched spheres crammed in her gear bag. "Might be?"

"Nobody's got a receipt for that one. History doesn't always keep score as neatly as I do."

"That's the most honest thing you've said all night."

"I'm always honest. I'm just not always certain." Number Nine's stitches flickered, almost like a shrug. "Put it back gently. That one's close to five hundred years old and doesn't owe you a juggling trick."

Mia set it back in the rafter exactly where she'd found it, careful as she'd be with a trophy, and felt, for a second, like she'd shaken hands with the game's great-great-great-grandfather.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Settle an Argument
chapters.text:
They landed in a courtyard full of shouting, except this argument had no ball in it at all.

Young men in university gowns stood in two clumps, each side insisting their old school's version of football was the only correct one. One side wanted to carry the ball. The other wanted it kicked only, no hands, ever, under any circumstances.

"Cambridge, **1848**," said Number Nine. "Every school had brought its own rules from home, and nobody agreed on anything. Shin-kicking was legal in some versions. That tells you how bad it had gotten."

Mia watched two students nearly come to blows over whether tripping an opponent counted as clever defending or just plain mean. "This is like three different stats sites reporting three different numbers for the exact same game."

"Close enough. So a handful of Cambridge students sat down and tried to write one shared rulebook — the **Cambridge Rules**."

"Tried?"

"The full details didn't all survive, and historians argue about exactly what it said. But it's generally agreed they made the attempt, and other people borrowed from it later. That part mattered, even if the paper itself is fuzzy."

Mia liked that answer more than a tidy one would have. Real data was messy too; she'd spent enough nights reconciling two conflicting box scores to know a suspiciously clean story usually meant somebody hadn't checked it hard enough.

She watched one young man finally slap a sheet of paper down on the table, silencing the group, at least for a minute. "Somebody just needs to write it down properly and make everyone agree to disagree less," she said.

"That's the next stop, actually," said Number Nine. "Bounce me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tavern Meeting
chapters.text:
They landed in a smoky room above a London tavern, a dozen serious-looking men arguing over a sheet of paper like it was a contract worth a fortune.

"October 26th, **1863**," said Number Nine. "The **Football Association** — the FA — gets born tonight. Right here."

A man at the head of the table, thin and precise-looking, was writing fast, crossing things out, writing again. "That's Ebenezer Cobb Morley," said Number Nine. "He's about to personally write the first official **Laws of the Game** — the rulebook that practically everyone after this one copies."

Mia leaned over his shoulder, careful not to actually touch anything four centuries of ghost-rules apparently didn't want touched. One line stood out, underlined twice: no carrying the ball with your hands.

"That's the rule that splits it from rugby forever," she said.

"Correct. Before tonight, 'football' meant about six different games wearing a trench coat. After tonight, this version finally gets its own name."

"Which is?"

"Association football. Give it twenty years and some English schoolboys will get bored of saying the whole thing."

Mia's eyebrows went up. "Let me guess. They shortened it."

"To 'assoc.' Then to 'soccer.' Both words — **soccer** and **association football** — are the same sport in different jerseys, both from about the same decade, just **1880s** England being lazy with syllables."

Mia grinned. She'd spent her whole life hearing American commentators get side-eyed for saying "soccer," never once knowing the word was English through and through. "Wait till I tell my coach that one."

"Tell Morley first. He's still writing."

She watched him finish the page, set down his pen, and exhale like a man who'd just solved a very long equation. Mia knew that exhale. She made the exact same one closing a spreadsheet at one in the morning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Nil-Nil in Glasgow
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like cut grass and nerves.

"FA Cup, **1871-72**," said Number Nine, as men in long shorts jogged onto a pitch ringed by a modest, hopeful crowd. "First tournament of its kind. Still running today, which makes it the oldest football competition on Earth."

"A hundred and fifty-some years and it's never once stopped?" Mia asked.

"Wars, pandemics, nothing's killed it yet. Somebody always finds a pitch."

They didn't stay for the final whistle. Number Nine spun her forward a few months, into colder air and a bigger, louder crowd — Glasgow, a banner reading SCOTLAND somewhere up in the stands.

"**1872**," said the ball. "First official international match ever played. Scotland versus England."

Mia watched ninety minutes of genuinely committed effort produce exactly nothing. The final whistle blew on a flat, featureless scoreline.

"0-0," she said, checking twice like the number might change on her. "The first international match in the history of the sport, and it's a scoreless draw."

"Welcome to football."

"As a stats person, I respect it. As a fan, I would like a refund."

"Nobody asked for a refund in **1872**. They just agreed to do it again."

Mia watched the two captains shake hands, completely unbothered, like 0-0 was a perfectly respectable outcome between gentlemen. Somewhere down the line, she thought, some future version of herself would build an entire personality around arguing that shot quality mattered more than final scorelines — and this flat, boring draw was the very first entry in a database that was about to get extremely long.

"Keep the receipt," she told Number Nine.

"Already have it. I have all of them."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A League, Then a World
chapters.text:
They landed inside an office that smelled like pipe tobacco and ambition.

A man was sketching columns onto a chalkboard — teams, listed vertically, points scrawled beside each one.

"William McGregor," said Number Nine. "**1888**. He's organizing the Football League — the world's first — so that instead of one-off matches, clubs play each other all season long, building a table that actually means something at the end of it."

Mia stared at the chalk columns like she'd come home. Wins, losses, points. "That's literally a leaderboard."

"It's the ancestor of every leaderboard you've ever refreshed at midnight."

She almost laughed. Her entire spreadsheet habit, it turned out, had a great-great-grandfather, and his name was William McGregor, and he'd built it out of nothing but chalk and stubbornness.

The scene shifted again, this time to a room in Paris, men from seven different countries signing papers around a long table, none of them fully agreeing on the language they were arguing in.

"**1904**," said Number Nine. "FIFA. Soccer's world governing body, born right here, from seven countries that wanted one shared set of rules — not just for one league, but across borders entirely."

"So first it's one club against another," Mia said slowly, working it out loud the way she worked out a formula. "Then it's a league. Then it's whole countries. It's just... scaling up, over and over."

"That's exactly what it is. You're basically watching a spreadsheet grow more tabs."

"Please never say the word 'tabs' to me again."

"Noted. Bounce me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ban Nobody Could Justify
chapters.text:
The crowd noise hit her before the picture did — actual roaring, thousands of voices, for a game Mia hadn't expected to find at all.

Women in long shorts and buttoned jerseys tore down a muddy pitch while a packed stadium howled their names.

"Dick, Kerr Ladies," said Number Nine. "English women's team, early twentieth century. Their best player's right there — **Lily Parr**. She helped make this team one of the most popular sides in the whole country, full stop, not just in women's football."

Mia watched Parr strike a ball with a left foot that looked, even across decades, genuinely unfair to defend against. The stands were packed tighter than half the men's matches she'd seen on television. "Then why have I literally never once heard of her?"

Number Nine's glow dimmed, just slightly. "Because in **1921**, the FA banned women's football in England. Said it wasn't suitable. No real reason that held up under any scrutiny — it just happened, and that was that, for a very long time."

Mia's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"No. It wasn't."

She didn't say anything for a second, just watched Parr take a corner, drop it perfectly onto a teammate's head, and the crowd come apart.

"How long did the ban last?"

"Fifty years. The FA finally lifted it in **1971**."

"Fifty years." Mia did the math without meaning to — more than three times her own age, of a sport simply not letting people play it. "And after that?"

"After that, it built back, slower than it should have had to. In **1991**, China hosted the first official Women's World Cup. The United States won it."

Mia looked at Parr once more before the scene faded, filing the name away like a stat too important to ever misplace again. "Keep her on the sheet," she told Number Nine. "Permanently."

"She was never off it. Some records just get buried longer than they should be."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Thirteen Teams and a Boat Ride
chapters.text:
Heat hit her first, thick and bright, a stadium under a sun that didn't do subtlety.

"Montevideo, **Uruguay**, **1930**," said Number Nine. "The first FIFA World Cup. Thirteen teams total, most of Europe's best declining the boat trip, so it's mostly the Americas represented. Uruguay's the host."

Mia watched the host team work the ball with controlled chaos, defenders overlapping like they'd rehearsed it, which, apparently, they had. "Home advantage is a real stat, you know. Crowd noise genuinely changes decision-making on the field."

"Then you'll like the final. Uruguay versus Argentina."

The whistle blew; the stadium detonated into noise before the ball had even crossed the line once. Mia couldn't follow every pass through the roar, but she didn't need the play-by-play to read the scoreboard at the end: Uruguay had won it, the very first champion the sport ever crowned.

A man in a suit stood near the trophy presentation, looking exactly as relieved as a tournament organizer should.

"Jules Rimet," said Number Nine. "FIFA's president. He's the one who pushed this whole tournament into existing in the first place. They name the trophy after him."

Mia studied the small gold statue being handed over, unglamorous by modern standards, nothing like the gleaming thing she'd seen lifted on television every four years of her life. "That's it? That's the whole trophy?"

"That's the start of it. Trophies get better sequels. Bounce me — this one's got a plot twist."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Stolen Cup and a Very Good Dog
chapters.text:
They landed in London, gray skies, a glass display case standing conspicuously, suspiciously empty.

"Somebody's missing something," Mia said.

"In **1966**, somebody stole the World Cup trophy. Right off its display, days before England was due to host the whole tournament."

Mia blinked. "They just... took it?"

"For about a week, yes. Then a dog named **Pickles** found it, wrapped in newspaper, under a garden hedge, out on an ordinary walk with his owner."

"A dog solved it."

"A dog solved it. England got its trophy back in time, hosted the tournament, and then won it outright — their only title to date."

The scene rolled forward, and suddenly she was watching a different World Cup entirely, 1970 judging by the kits, a referee reaching into his pocket and holding up a small bright square of color at a player.

"Yellow card," said Number Nine. "A referee named Ken Aston invented the whole system — yellow and red — straight off a traffic light he happened to be sitting at when the idea hit him. It debuted at this tournament."

"Stop and go. That's such an obvious idea I'm genuinely annoyed nobody thought of it sooner."

"Most good ideas are, in hindsight."

She watched a player in yellow and green dismantle an entire defense in three consecutive touches, the crowd rising before the shot had even gone in.

"Brazil," said Number Nine. "They'll finish with five World Cup titles total, more than anyone — **1958**, 1962, this one in **1970**, plus two more down the line. And that man right there has been on three of the winning squads himself. First player ever to manage it."

"Pele," Mia said, like naming a fact she'd always half-known but never actually watched happen in front of her.

"Brazil kept this particular trophy for good after that third win — tournament rules at the time. FIFA had to make an entirely new one in **1974** for everybody else to fight over."

Mia watched Pele get lifted onto someone's shoulders, grinning, and thought that out of everyone she'd met tonight, he looked the most like he was genuinely having fun doing something that mattered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Final Whistle
chapters.text:
The seams dimmed, and the roaring crowd noise thinned back into the ordinary hum of her bedroom, laptop fan still running, spreadsheet still glowing faintly on the screen like it had never once blinked.

Mia sat up straight, the ball warm and quiet in her hands again, just an old size-4 with a marker 9 and no laces. She turned it over out of habit, checking the seams. No glow now. Just leather.

"You still there?" she asked, feeling slightly ridiculous saying it out loud.

"Always," said Number Nine, voice barely above a whisper now, like a commentator signing off after extra time. "I don't go anywhere. I just wait for someone who actually checks the stat sheet."

Mia glanced at her spreadsheet — her own tidy little percentages — and thought about Lily Parr's name sitting unrecorded for fifty years, and a man writing rules by candlelight, and a dog finding a trophy under a hedge, and a scoreless draw that somehow mattered more than most 5-0s ever would.

She opened a new tab and started a second sheet. Not stats this time. Names. Dates. The whole long chain of people who'd built the game she played every single Saturday without ever once wondering who'd come before her.

"You're going to fall asleep at your desk," said Number Nine.

"In a minute."

"That's what you said an hour ago."

Mia smiled, set the ball gently back on the shelf, number-side out, and kept typing a little longer before she finally closed the laptop. Somewhere past the window, the sky was already turning the pale gray that meant morning wasn't far off, and she had a match to play in a few hours that suddenly felt like it carried a little more history on its shoulders than it had the night before.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match couldn't come soon enough.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a ball-kicking game with no hands allowed, was played in China **over 2,000 years ago** and may be soccer's oldest known ancestor.
Medieval **mob football** got so wild and destructive that King Edward II banned it in London in **1314**.
A lopsided leather ball found hidden at **Stirling Castle** in Scotland might date all the way back to the **1540s**, possibly making it the oldest football in the world.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **October 26, 1863**, and its very first rule banned players from carrying the ball with their hands.
FA founder **Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote the first official **Laws of the Game** that same year.
The word **"soccer"** actually comes from **"assoc,"** a schoolboy nickname for association football from **1880s England**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
In **1888**, **William McGregor** organized the **Football League**, the world's very first football league, built on a simple win-loss points table.
**FIFA**, soccer's world governing body, was founded in **Paris in 1904** by seven European countries.
Star player **Lily Parr** helped make the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** one of the most popular football teams in all of England.
The FA finally lifted its ban on women's football in England in **1971**, fifty years after the ban began.
The first **FIFA World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host team beat Argentina in the final.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London and found safe about a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
Brazilian forward **Pele** is the only player ever to be part of three different World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.

new_recurring.name: Number Nine
new_recurring.rule: A scuffed, laceless size-4 soccer ball marked with a '9,' once given to Mia by her first coach. Its seams glow gold and show numbers when something historic is about to happen; it speaks like a dry, deadpan sports commentator, calls…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Mia set the quiet, un-glowing ball back on her shelf, started a new list honoring overlooked names like Lily Parr, and closed her laptop knowing her Saturday match now carried a little more history behind it.

story.title: Noah and the Night Server
story.subtitle: One gamer, one glowing controller, and the strangest level ever loaded: his own brain.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Error 0451
chapters.text:
It was 1:47 a.m., which Noah was fairly sure did not officially exist, and he was three songs deep into a playlist he'd sworn he'd only listen to for "five more minutes" two hours ago.

His headset glitched mid-track. Not static — a rhythm. Blink-blink-blink-pause, like something breathing in Morse code.

The controller on his desk lit up on its own. Two little sync lights at the top blinked fast, side to side, side to side, exactly like a pair of eyes flicking under closed lids.

Text crawled across his phone screen where the song title should've been: **LOADING: SLEEP.EXE**.

Noah picked up the controller, mostly to make it stop, and the floor of his room dropped away like a cutscene nobody warned him about.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Boy Who Wouldn't Stay Still
chapters.text:
He landed in a dim lab that smelled like old paper and coffee. A kid about his age was asleep on a cot, wires taped near his eyes, while two grown men in white coats watched a pen scratch lines on rolling paper.

"That's **1953**," said the controller, now somehow talking, in the voice of a very patient tutorial. "University of Chicago. Those two are **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman**. They noticed something everyone else had been sleeping right through."

Noah leaned in. The sleeping boy's eyes were darting back and forth under his eyelids, fast, like he was watching an invisible tennis match. "Wait — his eyes are moving? He's asleep."

"Exactly what Aserinsky thought," the controller said. "They named it **rapid eye movement**, or REM, for short. Turns out a night's sleep isn't one long blackout. It's built from repeating **cycles about ninety minutes long**, flipping between calm, quiet sleep and active, dreaming REM sleep."

Noah checked the paper chart, found the up-and-down wave pattern repeating like a level map. "So sleep has stages. Like a dungeon with rooms."

"Nobody's ever put it that way," the controller admitted. "But sure."

chapters.heading: Level 3: Locked Controls
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into something closer to Noah's own bedroom, except now there were two versions of him on the bed — one awake-looking, eyes darting, and one completely limp, like a character with the inputs disabled.

"During REM sleep," the controller said, "the brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake. But the body's muscles go slack. Locked. So you can't get up and act out whatever your brain's running."

"So I'm basically in spectator mode," Noah said. "Brain's live, controller's unplugged."

"Close enough that I'm stealing it," said the controller.

A deeper, slower wave rolled across the limp Noah's chart — not REM, the quiet stage beneath it. "That one matters too," the controller added. "The deepest non-REM stage is when the body releases the most **growth hormone** — the chemical that helps you actually get taller and heal. One reason growing kids need more sleep than they think they do."

Noah glanced at the limp version of himself, unimpressed by its own growth spurt. "Could've told me that before I stayed up for the server reset last Tuesday."

"I did," said the controller. "You were asleep. Ironic."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Clock With No Hands
chapters.text:
Next stop: somewhere dark red and pulsing, deep inside a screen shaped like a brain. A tiny cluster of light sat just behind Noah's eyes, blinking on its own clean rhythm.

"That little cluster runs the whole schedule," the controller said. "Sleep, wake, hunger, all of it. Scientists call the whole system **circadian** — from Latin words meaning roughly 'about a day,' because it resets close to every 24 hours."

"So I've got an internal server clock," Noah said. "Why does it keep thinking 3 a.m. is a great idea for one more match?"

"Because you keep overriding it with a screen," the controller said, unbothered. "In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that keep that clock ticking. Turns out it's not a metaphor. It's real code, running in your cells."

Noah watched the cluster pulse, steady as a loading bar that never stalls. "Okay, that's actually kind of insane."

"Everyone's got one," said the controller. "Yours just keeps getting jet-lagged by your own phone."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Night Shift
chapters.text:
The scene shifted again to a cluttered old lab, glass vials lined up like loot drops.

"**1958**," the controller said. "A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team isolated **melatonin** — the hormone that tells your body it's bedtime — straight out of a small gland deep in the brain."

"The sleepy-time chemical," Noah said. "Basically my body's 'quest complete, go rest' notification."

"Not bad," the controller said. "And while that notification's running, your brain's doing cleanup work too. Sleep helps sort the day's experiences into actual long-term memory — which is why a good night's sleep helps you remember what you practiced on guitar, not just what you played badly at 11 p.m."

Noah winced, recognizing several specific chord mistakes.

"There's also a literal rinse cycle," the controller went on. "A system that flushes waste out of the sleeping brain overnight, like clearing your cache."

"So my brain's basically defragging."

"If that helps you respect it more, yes."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Leaderboard
chapters.text:
A glowing scoreboard appeared, listing sleep times for animals Noah definitely hadn't expected to see ranked.

"**Bottlenose dolphins and some seals**," the controller read, "sleep with only half the brain at a time. One eye stays open, watching for danger or just keeping the body swimming."

"That's cheating," Noah said. "Dual-core sleeping."

"**Giraffes** barely bother," the controller continued. "Some get by on under two hours a day, in short naps while standing."

"And at the absolute bottom of effort," it said, scrolling down, "small bats — up to **20 hours a day**. Practically professionals."

"What's at the very top of this leaderboard?" Noah asked.

"Fruit flies," the controller said. "They show sleep-like rest too, which tells scientists sleep has been around in living things for an extremely long time. Longer than giraffes. Longer than dolphins. Maybe longer than almost anything."

Noah stared at the tiny fly icon sitting calmly at the very top, undefeated. "I've been outslept by a bug."

"Everyone eventually is," the controller said.
chapters.shout_line: I'VE BEEN OUTSLEPT BY A BUG

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Eleven-Day Run
chapters.text:
The next room had a single teenager sitting at a desk, grinning through eyes that looked like they'd forgotten how blinking worked.

"**1964**," the controller said, tone shifting slightly, more careful now. "**Randy Gardner**, seventeen, San Diego. Science-fair project. He stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight — one of the longest stretches ever properly documented."

"Eleven days," Noah repeated. "No sleep. That's basically a world record."

"It is," the controller said. "And doctors do not want anyone chasing it. Going that long without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory, fast. Randy got studied carefully and recovered. Nobody's recommending a repeat run."

Noah glanced at his phone, suddenly less proud of his own personal best.

"One more thing while we're here," the controller added. "Sleepwalking happens during deep, dreamless sleep — not during dreaming. So if someone wanders around asleep, they're not acting out a dream. They're just... running on autopilot, controls half-online."

"And back in **1899**," it added, almost as an afterthought, "a scientist named **Sigmund Freud** published a whole book arguing dreams reveal secret wishes. It's a famous read. Most of that specific theory hasn't held up — call it a legendary take, not a confirmed one."

"So basically," Noah said, "dreams are cool, but don't trust the guy who wrote the first big book about them."

"Harsh," said the controller, "but accurate."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Respawn
chapters.text:
The lab blinked out. Noah's own ceiling swam back into focus above him, familiar glow-in-the-dark star stickers and all.

The controller sat warm in his hands, lights settling into a slow, steady pulse — the kind his phone made right before it finally, mercifully went to sleep.

"One last stat," the controller said. "Add it all up over a lifetime, and a person spends roughly **a third of their life asleep**. Not wasted time. Maintenance time."

Noah set it down on the nightstand, next to a phone that had given up trying to glow at him.

"So every night's basically a patch update," he said.

"Closer than you'd think," the controller said, light fading to a dim standby glow. "Good night, Noah. Or — good morning, technically. You've got maybe five hours left to actually install this one."

Noah didn't argue. For the first time in weeks, he put the headset down before the clock said something embarrassing.

Tomorrow there was a new level to beat, a new song to learn, and — for once — an actual full cycle of sleep standing between him and both.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's run would go better. Tonight, the controller could handle the respawn.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes dart under his eyelids.
A night's sleep is made of repeating **cycles about ninety minutes long**, switching between quiet sleep and active, dreaming REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go **completely limp** so the sleeper can't act out dreams.
The deepest stage of non-REM sleep triggers the most **growth hormone**, one reason growing kids need extra sleep.
A tiny cluster of brain cells works as the body's **master clock** for sleeping and waking.
The word **'circadian'** comes from Latin words meaning **'about a day.'**
In **2017**, **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep the body's internal clock running.
The sleepy-time hormone **melatonin** was first isolated in **1958** by scientist **Aaron Lerner**'s team.
Sleep helps sort the day's experiences into **long-term memory**, which is why good sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
**Bottlenose dolphins and some seals** sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.
**Giraffes** are among the shortest sleepers of any large animal, sometimes under **two hours a day**.
Some small **bats** sleep up to **20 hours a day**, making them some of the sleepiest animals known.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science project — a record doctors say nobody should try to repeat.
People spend roughly **a third of their life** asleep, added up over a lifetime.
